liyeque.name: Que of Li Ye
liyeque.sub: Zitong · Eastern Han single stone que
liyeque.lede: At the foot of Mount Changqing, a tapering stone que shaft carries the memory of Li Ye. Only one que survives; the capstone seen today is a later replacement.
facts: Generally dated to the early Eastern Han and traditionally to the 12th year of Jianwu (36); it is entered here with an approximate year, and the later capstone is not counted as original Han fabric.
A single stone que survives, its shaft about 2.45 m tall. The south face originally carried an inscription and the Qing-dynasty Record of Moving the Que; the other three faces are plain.
In the 25th year of Daoguang in the Qing (1845), county magistrate Zhou Shutang found the damaged shaft and moved it to the Shrine of Li Jieshi for protection. The plate depicts its present form.

taishique.name: Taishi Que of Dengfeng
taishique.sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Zhongyue Temple
taishique.lede: The stone que before Zhongyue Temple freeze Han-dynasty buildings in stone. The main and subsidiary que join at different heights, and the surviving stone eaves and que inscriptions still point to the mountain-worship rites of two thousand years ago.
facts: Built in the 5th year of Yuanchu in the Eastern Han (118) as the spirit-way que in front of the temple of Mount Taishi.
The east and west que face each other; each consists of a taller main que joined to a lower subsidiary que.
The stone blocks imitate a timber roof, and the shafts retain pictorial carvings, studded boss patterns and Han inscriptions.

5th year of Yuanchu, Eastern Han

shaoshique.name: Shaoshi Que of Dengfeng
shaoshique.sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Mount Shaoshi
shaoshique.era: Reign of Emperor An of Han
shaoshique.lede: The paired que at the foot of Mount Shaoshi are remnants of an ancient road for mountain worship. Their stone eaves join at different heights, and the carved chariots and horses, animal taming and cuju football leave fragments of Eastern Han life outside the temple gate.
facts: The Zhengzhou Municipal Bureau of Cultural Relics records construction in the 2nd year of Yanguang (123); other estimates place it between 118 and 123, so the timeline uses an approximate year.
The east and west que are both two-tier main-and-subsidiary que, each made up of a base, a shaft and a stone capstone.
The carved scenes include equestrian acrobatics, hunting, elephant taming and cuju, making the que physical evidence for the study of Eastern Han life and ritual.

qimuque.name: Qimu Que of Dengfeng
qimuque.sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Qimu Temple
qimuque.lede: The Qimu Que stands below Wansui Peak on Mount Song, on the approach to the long-vanished Qimu Temple. Its damaged top and uneven stone blocks preserve the marks of time, while its inscription carries the legend of Yu the Great taming the floods into the ritual world of the Han.
facts: Built in the 2nd year of Yanguang in the Eastern Han (123) by Zhu Chong, Grand Administrator of Yingchuan, as the spirit-way que in front of Qimu Temple.
The common name is Qimu Que, also Kaimu Que; the name “Houmu Que” written by the user has been corrected here from the place-name context.
The north face of the west que preserves the Qimu Que inscription and a rain-prayer inscription. This drawing shows the south face and keeps the losses of the surviving damaged top.
captions: Qimu Que · South face of the west que
Surviving damaged top · Eastern Han stone carving

gaoyique.name: Que of Gao Yi
gaoyique.lede: Beside Hanbei Road in Ya'an, the stone que in front of the tomb of Gao Yi hold the forms of Han timber architecture in red sandstone. The west que preserves the stepped outline of a main que joined to its side que.
facts: Built in the 14th year of Jian'an in the Eastern Han (209) as a ceremonial structure in front of the tomb of Gao Yi, Grand Administrator of Yizhou.

There were originally paired east and west que, and the western main-and-subsidiary que is the better preserved. The plate draws the west que from photographs and does not reconstruct the damaged east que.
The que imitates timber construction with bracket sets, an upper story and eaves; its carvings include historical stories, mythical beasts and processions.

jl_jiangjunfen.name: General's Tomb, Ji'an
jl_jiangjunfen.yearNote: 450 is an ordering placement for the remains of a stone-chamber tomb of about the 5th century, not a precise construction year; the traditional identification of the tomb's occupant is not treated as established fact.
jl_jiangjunfen.place: Jilin · Ji'an · Southern foot of Longshan
jl_jiangjunfen.lede: Huge stones are stacked into seven square tiers, with buttress stones leaning against the steps at the base and the entrance to the burial chamber opening in the upper part. The General's Tomb belongs to the Goguryeo remains and should not be relabeled Northern Wei simply because the dates are close.
facts: The plate is checked against the seven main tiers and does not count each course of masonry as a separate tier.
Identifications of the tomb's occupant differ; this entry does not directly assert that it is the tomb of King Jangsu, and it does not mix in images of the Taiwang Tomb.
The surviving gray-brown stone blocks, joints and pale buttress stones are drawn from a single photograph without digital retouching; this is not an archaeological reconstruction.

sx_yungang.name: Yungang Grottoes
sx_yungang.era: Northern Wei · Period of the Five Caves of Tanyao
sx_yungang.yearNote: Placed by the c. 460–470 construction phase of the Five Caves of Tanyao, to which Cave 20 belongs; 465 is used only for ordering.
sx_yungang.lede: After the front wall of Cave 20 collapsed, its principal figure was left exposed. The broad shoulders, full face and robe leaving the right side of the chest bare preserve the solemn mass of early Northern Wei colossal images.
facts: Caves 16 to 20 are known collectively as the Five Caves of Tanyao, the earliest group of large caves at Yungang.
This plate shows only the central seated Sakyamuni of Cave 20 and keeps the actual damage to the arms and in front of the knees.
The domed ushnisha, long ears and asymmetrical drapery are clues for identifying the principal figure; the flanking standing figures and niche walls are not drawn.

songyue.name: Songyue Temple Pagoda, Dengfeng
songyue.lede: Fifteen tiers of brick eaves recede along a curve, giving the Songyue Temple Pagoda an outline close to an upright writing brush. Its twelve-sided body and flame-shaped door lintels preserve traces of early Chinese pagodas absorbing a range of formal vocabularies.
facts: The pagoda was built in the late Northern Wei; a 2021 conservation study dated its construction to between 511 and 520, while older accounts often give 523.
The plan is twelve-sided, with fifteen tiers of multi-eaves stacked above the body and an outline that tapers upward in a curve.
The ground story has arched doorways on the four cardinal faces and pagoda-shaped niches on the other eight; at the top is a finial of lotus petals and spire rings.
captions: Songyue Temple Pagoda · Front view

hn_gongyi.name: Gongxian Grottoes
hn_gongyi.yearNote: 520 is only an approximate ordering point for the late Northern Wei sculptural phase and is not taken as an exact inscribed date for any cave or niche.
hn_gongyi.place: Henan · Gongyi · Siwan Village, Heluo Town
hn_gongyi.lede: The central pillar of the Gongxian Grottoes encircles the path of worship. In Cave 1 the principal figure and attendants project from the stone wall, their hanging drapery, mandorlas and serene faces preserving the forms of late Northern Wei sculpture.
facts: Excavation: The grottoes were begun in the Northern Wei, with further work in the Eastern Wei, Western Wei, Northern Qi, Tang, Song and other periods.
Cave layout: Cave 1 is a square central-pillar cave with niches cut into the pillar faces; thousand-Buddha and worship-procession reliefs are distributed over the four walls.

Imagery: Cave 1 preserves reliefs of the emperor and empress worshipping the Buddha. This drawing takes the principal figure and flanking attendants on one face of the central pillar and does not bring the adjacent wall reliefs into the composition.

xinchangdafo.name: Great Buddha Temple, Xinchang
xinchangdafo.yearNote: 516 is the 15th year of Tianjian in the Liang, when the image was completed; 486 is the date of origin linked to Senghu's vow, and another account places the start of carving in the Jianwu era of the Qi. The temple's founding in the Eastern Jin is kept distinct from later restorations.
xinchangdafo.lede: Broad knees support a calm body as the stone Maitreya sits cross-legged in a rock chamber on Mount Shicheng. Carved by successive generations of monks during the Qi and Liang of the Southern Dynasties, it is a valuable surviving example of early large-scale Buddhist sculpture in Jiangnan.
facts: Qi–Liang creation: After Senghu made his vow, Sengshu and Sengyou continued the work, completing it in the 15th year of Tianjian in the Liang (516); it was formerly called the Stone Buddha of Three Generations.
Cliff-cut image: The Maitreya is carved from the rock face of Mount Shicheng, seated in full lotus with both hands resting between the knees; the knees are about 10.6 m apart.

Later care: The image has been redecorated and repaired over many periods and conserved several times in the modern era. The plate shows the historical stone image as it is today and excludes the modern reclining Buddha of the scenic area.
captions: Great Buddha Temple, Xinchang · Stone Maitreya
Southern Dynasties Qi–Liang · 486–516

hn_xiaonanhai.name: Xiaonanhai Grottoes
hn_xiaonanhai.yearNote: The Palace Museum records excavation from the 1st to the 6th year of Tianbao in the Northern Qi; 553 is only an approximate ordering point within this range and does not mark the exact completion year of any one cave.
hn_xiaonanhai.lede: In the cliff face, low and small cave openings still show carved lintel decoration and damaged figures beside the doors. The three Xiaonanhai caves preserve important evidence for Northern Qi Buddhist sculpture and Pure Land imagery.
facts: Date: According to the Palace Museum, the grottoes were excavated from the 1st to the 6th year of Tianbao in the Northern Qi (550–555) and finally completed by the monk Sengchou.
Three caves: The east, middle and west caves are all square with truncated-pyramid ceilings and three niches on three walls; the Buddha groupings include Vairocana, Amitabha and Maitreya.

Plate scope: The line drawing takes the part of the cave-door facade visible in photographs, keeping the cracks in the rock and the damaged carvings beside the door; the sculptures inside the caves are not added.
captions: Xiaonanhai Grottoes · Detail of the cliff face at the cave door

xiangtang.name: Xiangtangshan Grottoes
xiangtang.lede: A broad, round Buddha face, heavy shoulders and fine drapery folds are enclosed by a flame-shaped mandorla. The Great Buddha Cave of North Xiangtang preserves the serene mass of Northern Qi sculpture in the rock walls of Mount Gu, and its losses also bear the marks of a long history.
facts: Early Northern Qi: The Great Buddha Cave is one of the earlier large caves at North Xiangtang. Research usually places it in the reign of Emperor Wenxuan of the Northern Qi, about the 550s; the exact founding inscription has been lost.

Central-pillar cave: Cave 9 is a stupa-pillar cave with a central square pillar, the Buddhas of the Three Ages carved on three of its faces; the plate shows the principal figure on the front face, about 3.5 m tall.

Present condition: The principal figure's hands and part of its drapery are lost, but the round head halo and flame mandorla remain recognizable; the carvings of the cave group have suffered weathering, looting and later repairs.

hn_dapishan.name: Great Cliff Buddha of Mount Dapi
hn_dapishan.sub: The Great Stone Buddha of Xun County, seated against the cliff
hn_dapishan.yearLabel: Later Zhao, Northern Qi or other views
hn_dapishan.yearNote: Proposed dates include the Later Zhao and the Northern Qi. Here 560 serves only as an ordering point based on the Northern Qi start-of-carving view recorded in 2004 material from Cultural Relics Press and does not indicate a confirmed start date; a 2026 Henan Daily on-site conservation report adopts the Later Zhao view. The disagreement is retained and should not be read as a settled Northern Qi date.
hn_dapishan.lede: The Great Buddha of Mount Dapi is carved from the mountain cliff, its right hand raised and its left resting on the knee. Its date of carving is variously judged as Later Zhao, Northern Qi and other periods, and its present surface carries later repairs and painting.
facts: Differing dates: Older conservation sources record carving begun in the Northern Qi and completed in the early Tang; recent conservation reports adopt the Later Zhao view. This entry keeps the differing judgments.

Colossal cliff figure: The figure sits in a pendant-leg posture, the right hand in the abhaya mudra and the left on the knee; the plate draws only the part visible in the photograph, from the head to the knees.

Conservation: It was repaired in the 10th year of Zhengtong in the Ming; a new round of conservation of the figure began in 2025, and the line drawing is based on photographs taken in 2024 before the work.
captions: Great Cliff Buddha of Mount Dapi · Visible part from head to knees
Date of carving disputed · Drawn from 2024 photographs of its condition

sx_tianlongshan.name: Tianlongshan Grottoes
sx_tianlongshan.yearNote: The front portico of Cave 16 shown here belongs to the Northern Qi (550–577); 560 is an approximate ordering point. Sui and Tang dates of other caves are not applied.
sx_tianlongshan.lede: Two stone columns and the inverted-V members above them preserve traces of Northern Qi timber construction in the mountain rock. The front portico of Cave 16 extends the significance of Tianlongshan from sculpture to architectural form.
facts: The Tianlongshan Grottoes were built in phases including the Eastern Wei, Northern Qi, Sui and Tang; this plate takes Northern Qi Cave 16.
The portico columns, lotus-petal column bases and inverted-V bracket sets (puzuo) are carved from the rock, imitating the timber forms of the time.
The plate keeps the weathered losses at the entrance and draws only part of the portico; it does not add sculptures lost from the caves or modern reconstructed figures.
captions: Tianlongshan Cave 16 · Carved stone portico

hb_yicihui.name: Yicihui Stone Pillar
hb_yicihui.sub: Northern Qi stone pillar with a three-bay stone hall on top
hb_yicihui.yearNote: Its present location is Shizhu Village, Gaoli Township, Dingxing County; Yi County, given as the location in the old national listing, is an outdated administrative attribution. The Northern Wei wooden predecessor is kept separate from the Northern Qi stone structure.
hb_yicihui.lede: The Yicihui Stone Pillar raises a small stone hall on a tall stone column, and its stone imitation of timber construction preserves details of Northern Qi architecture. The long eulogy on the shaft recounts charitable burials and relief in a time of turmoil, and it also gave the monument its name.
facts: Date: The surviving stone structure was erected in the 2nd year of Daning in the Northern Qi (562); an earlier wooden predecessor pillar dates to the Northern Wei.
Form: The shaft carries a stone disc and a three-bay stone house; the roof, eave rafters, bracket sets and other parts are all rendered in carved stone.
Inscription: The eulogy on the pillar records the warfare at the end of the Northern Wei and the charitable burials and food relief that followed; the original stands in Shizhu Village, Dingxing.

hn_lingquan.name: Lingquan Temple Grottoes
hn_lingquan.sub: Armored guardians flanking a Sui cave doorway
hn_lingquan.yearNote: Uses the excavation date of the Dazhusheng Cave, not a single date for all the Lingquan Temple caves.
hn_lingquan.place: Henan · Shanying Town, Long'an District, Anyang
hn_lingquan.lede: The Dazhusheng Cave at Lingquan Temple was excavated in the 9th year of Kaihuang in the Sui. On either side of the doorway, armored divine kings hold weapons, their long beards falling to their chests; in low relief they carry the guardian imagery of the Northern Dynasties on into the Sui.
facts: Dazhusheng Cave: The excavation of this cave was directed by Lingyu and is dated to the 9th year of Kaihuang in the Sui (589); the surrounding cliff niches and images vary in date.
Paired guardians: The divine kings Kapila and Narayana are carved on either side outside the door. The two differ in posture and in what they hold, and each is drawn from its own photograph.

Partial plate: The plate selects the two low-relief figures beside the door, keeping their damaged outlines and the cracks in the rock; it does not add the doorway between them or the Buddhas inside the cave.

hb_anjibridge.name: Zhaozhou Bridge (Anji Bridge)
hb_anjibridge.sub: Side elevation of an open-spandrel stone arch bridge
hb_anjibridge.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau's description gives 605–616, and another account gives 595–605; 610 is only an approximate ordering point within the Sui and does not indicate an exact completion year.
hb_anjibridge.lede: A single low, flat arch spans the Xiao River, with four small arches opened in its shoulders. The Zhaozhou Bridge turns the demands of load-bearing and drainage into a clear outline, its deck rising gently above.
facts: The Anji Bridge is the Zhaozhou Bridge. It was first built in the Sui, and traditional records associate it with Li Chun.
One main arch, with two small arches on each shoulder, forms an open-spandrel, single-span stone arch bridge.
The deck balustrade panels and parts of the structure have been repaired over time, and the plate follows the present state; sources differ slightly on the span of Sui construction dates.

sd_simen.name: Four Gates Pagoda of Shentong Temple, Jinan
sd_simen.sub: Sui single-story stone pagoda · Arched doors on four sides
sd_simen.yearNote: Takes the inscription inside the stone pagoda, “made in the 7th year of Daye,” corresponding to 611; the Eastern Wei inscription of 544 on a Buddha image inside is not equated with the date of the pagoda itself.
sd_simen.lede: There are no stacked stories, only arched doors on four sides and a pyramidal roof of masonry stone. With its plain, massive chamber, the Four Gates Pagoda preserves the outline of Sui stone architecture to this day.
facts: Dating evidence: An inscription reading “made in the 7th year of Daye” was found inside the top of the pagoda, corresponding to 611; the Eastern Wei images inside predate the structure and are not treated as the same date.
Form: A single-story pavilion-type stone pagoda, square in plan with a door on each side; Buddha images are set around the central pillar, facing the four directions.
Plate scope: Shows the exterior of the whole stone pagoda; the Buddha images inside are not enlarged as a separate subject.

kaiyuan.name: Kaiyuan Temple, Zhengding
kaiyuan.era: Founded in the 10th year of Zhenguan
kaiyuan.lede: The pagoda and the bell tower face each other to the left and right in front of the main hall, a transitional example of Tang monasteries shifting from a “pagoda-centered” to a “hall-centered” layout. It is the only such layout left in China.
facts: Xumi Pagoda: Founded in the 10th year of Zhenguan in the Tang (636), it is a square nine-tier multi-eaved pagoda 42.5 m tall overall, plain and unornamented, and a typical Tang square multi-eaved pagoda.

Bell Tower: The only Tang bell tower surviving in China, two stories high and three bays wide, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a height of 14 m; the lower story has brick walls and the upper story is timber-framed.
In 1933 Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin came to Zhengding and identified the lower story of the bell tower here as surviving Tang structure.

sn_xingjiao.name: Xuanzang Pagoda of Xingjiao Temple
sn_xingjiao.sub: Square five-story brick pagoda · Relic pagoda of Xuanzang
sn_xingjiao.yearNote: 669 is the construction year of the Xuanzang Pagoda; the two disciples' pagodas at Xingjiao Temple each have their own histories, and the plate does not treat the three pagodas as a single subject of one date.
sn_xingjiao.lede: The square brick pagoda narrows story by story, with brickwork under the eaves imitating timber columns and architraves. Xuanzang's relics are enshrined here; of the three pagodas at Xingjiao Temple, the plate takes only the central Xuanzang Pagoda.
facts: Main subject: The relic pagoda of Xuanzang, built in the 2nd year of Zongzhang in the Tang (669); the three pagodas were not all built in the same year.
Form: A square five-story pavilion-style brick pagoda with corbeled eaves; brick columns and architraves imitate timber architecture.
Plate scope: Only the tall central pagoda is drawn; the disciples' pagodas to its left and right are not included.

longmenshiku.name: Longmen Grottoes
longmenshiku.era: Fengxian Temple completed in the 2nd year of Shangyuan
longmenshiku.lede: Carving began after the Northern Wei moved its capital to Luoyang in the 17th year of Taihe (493) and continued into the Tang. The great niche of Fengxian Temple was begun in the 3rd year of Xianheng (672) and completed in the 2nd year of Shangyuan (675), with Wu Zetian donating twenty thousand strings of cash from her cosmetics allowance. The 17-meter Vairocana sits at the center, and the nine figures, with disciples, bodhisattvas, heavenly kings and guardians, stand in a single row — of all the niches in the grottoes, the one most like a hall.
facts: The Vairocana is 17.14 m tall overall, with a head 4 m high and ears 1.9 m long; it sits in full lotus on a lotus throne, and its round head halo is carved with lotus-petal and flame patterns.

The niche is about 36 m wide, with nine figures arranged symmetrically: Kasyapa and Ananda stand in attendance, Manjushri and Samantabhadra are 13.25 m tall, the heavenly kings trample demons, and the guardians are 9.75 m tall.

The two hills of Longmen hold more than 2,300 surviving caves and niches and over 100,000 statues. The Northern Wei Guyang Cave (493) and Central Binyang Cave came first, and the Tang Ten-Thousand-Buddha Cave (680) later; the site was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2000.

xiuding.name: Xiuding Temple Pagoda
xiuding.era: Founded in the Northern Qi · Rebuilt in the Tang
xiuding.lede: A single-story square brick pagoda is covered entirely with 3,775 molded decorative bricks, rhombuses, rectangles and triangles fitted together into a net of relief. Archaeologists have called it “the true first flower pagoda of China.”
facts: First built in the 1st year of Tianbao in the Northern Qi (550) and rebuilt in the Tang; the decorative bricks of the surviving body were all fired in the Tang, so it is called a Tang pagoda.
It is 20 m tall overall, with a body 9.3 m high and 8.3 m wide, close to a cube; it is capped by corbeled eaves and a four-sloped pyramidal roof, with an inverted-bowl finial on top.
The decorative bricks show guardians, apsaras, the Azure Dragon, the White Tiger, monks and scrolling vines in more than seventy designs, fitted together with tight joints.

sn_qianling.name: Wordless Stele of Qianling
sn_qianling.sub: Stele with chi-dragon head · Later inscriptions
sn_qianling.yearLabel: Tang · Exact year of erection undetermined
sn_qianling.yearNote: The date of and motive for erecting the stele are interpreted differently; 700 is only an approximate Tang ordering point, not an established year of erection. The stele is not entirely blank today: inscriptions have been added since the Song and Jin.
sn_qianling.lede: When first erected, the tall stele bore no main text, and its chi-dragon head and single block of stone give it a solemn outline. Visitors' inscriptions from the Song and Jin onward gradually accumulated on its face, so the name “wordless” does not mean it is still blank today.
facts: Material: Carved from a single block of limestone, with eight chi dragons carved on the head and a rectangular stone base.
Inscriptions: It originally had no main text, and inscriptions were added one after another from the Song and Jin onward; the name is not a literal description of the present stele face.
Date: A Tang survival whose exact year of erection is undetermined; the plate does not treat the approximate ordering year as historical fact.
captions: Front and base of the Wordless Stele of Qianling · Line drawing
Tang · Tang dynasty · Exact year of erection undetermined

xian.name: Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, Xi'an
xian.sub: Da Ci'en Temple · Seven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda
xian.era: Founded in the 3rd year of Yonghui · Rebuilt in the Chang'an era of the Wu Zhou
xian.yearNote: First built in 652; dated by the seven-story form of the rebuilding in the Chang'an era of the Wu Zhou, with later brick casing and repairs described separately.
xian.lede: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda stands in Da Ci'en Temple, a brick pagoda built by Xuanzang to house the Buddhist scriptures he brought back from India. First built in the 3rd year of Yonghui (652), it was rebuilt with seven stories in the Chang'an era of the Wu Zhou (701–704). Its pavilion-style body tapers story by story, and its present appearance also reflects later brick casing and repairs.
facts: A square seven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda about 64.5 m tall overall; the brick walls render the form of a timber pavilion with columns and architraves in low relief.
Each story has arched openings on its main faces; the tapering body and corbeled brick eaves give a clear outline, and the finial survives at the top.
The subject drawn is the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda itself, excluding the temple's other buildings; it is catalogued separately from the Small Wild Goose Pagoda of Jianfu Temple.
captions: Line drawing · Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, pavilion-style brick pagoda
Seven stories · About 64.5 m tall overall

sn_xiangji.name: Shandao Pagoda of Xiangji Temple
sn_xiangji.sub: Tang square pagoda · Present form with damaged top
sn_xiangji.era: Built in the early Tang, repaired over the centuries
sn_xiangji.yearNote: Sources give differing interpretations: construction in 681 with repairs in 706, or construction in 706. The year 706 follows Table 1 of the Palace Museum Journal as an ordering reference, without asserting that the whole present pagoda is original fabric of that one year. The damaged top is kept, and the original thirteen stories are not reconstructed.
sn_xiangji.lede: Layered brick eaves gradually draw the square pagoda inward, and its damaged top still bears the marks of time. The Shandao Pagoda has shared the history of Xiangji Temple, and its present form is not reconstructed to a full thirteen stories.
facts: Date: Sources give two interpretations, 681 and 706, for the building and repair of the pagoda; the timeline uses an approximate Tang placement.
Form: A square brick pagoda, now with eleven stories and layered projecting eaves; the top is damaged.
Present form: Remains repaired over the centuries; the two upper stories that have vanished are not added.

Tang · Tang dynasty · Construction date disputed

xian_small.name: Small Wild Goose Pagoda, Xi'an
xian_small.sub: Jianfu Temple · Thirteen-tier multi-eaved brick pagoda
xian_small.era: Jinglong era of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang
xian_small.yearNote: Founded in the Jinglong era of the Tang; 707 is used as the starting point for ordering, and the drawing shows the thirteen-tier form with the damaged top left after Ming-dynasty earthquakes.
xian_small.lede: The Small Wild Goose Pagoda, originally called the Jianfu Temple Pagoda, was built in the Jinglong era of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang (707–710). The square brick pagoda narrows upward through dense corbeled brick eaves. It originally had fifteen tiers, but Ming-dynasty earthquakes destroyed the top two; thirteen tiers and a damaged top remain today.
facts: A square multi-eaved brick pagoda with thirteen surviving tiers, about 43.4 m tall in its damaged state, with ground-story sides about 11.38 m long; the ground story is tall and the upper eave tiers are closely set.

The pagoda has been through several earthquakes, and its 14th and 15th tiers at the top have been lost. The plate follows the present damaged top and does not restore the vanished tiers or add a finial.

The subject drawn is the Small Wild Goose Pagoda of Jianfu Temple itself, excluding the galleries of the Xi'an Museum and the temple's other buildings; visits are recorded separately from the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda of Da Ci'en Temple.
captions: Line drawing · Small Wild Goose Pagoda, multi-eaved brick pagoda
Thirteen surviving tiers · Surviving height about 43.4 m

gs_bingling.name: Bingling Temple Grottoes
gs_bingling.era: Carved in the 19th year of Kaiyuan, Tang
gs_bingling.yearNote: The plate shows the Great Buddha of Niche 171, dated to its carving in the 19th year of Kaiyuan in the Tang (731) as stated by experts of the conservation institute. The upper body is carved stone and the part below the abdomen is clay sculpture, with later repairs; the dates of the early Western Qin caves are not substituted for the date of this figure.
gs_bingling.lede: The Great Buddha sits upright against the rock cliff, its broad kasaya leaving large, quiet planes. The hand resting on the knee on one side is still intact, while the other side keeps its present damage; the caves and plank walkways above are not drawn in.
facts: Main subject: The Great Maitreya Buddha of Niche 171.

Date: The plate shows the Great Buddha of Niche 171, dated to its carving in the 19th year of Kaiyuan in the Tang (731) as stated by experts of the conservation institute. The upper body is carved stone and the part below the abdomen is clay sculpture, with later repairs; the dates of the early Western Qin caves are not substituted for the date of this figure.

Plate scope: The complete seated Maitreya, with curled hair, long ears, broad kasaya and pendant legs. The present state is kept, with one hand intact on the knee and damage on the other side, rather than showing both hands whole; only the shallow rock niche close around the body is retained, and Cave 169 and the walkways are not drawn.

hn_fengxue.name: Fengxue Temple
hn_fengxue.sub: A High Tang pagoda beneath nine tiers of multi-eaves
hn_fengxue.yearNote: Entered by the date of the surviving Tang main structure of the Seventh Patriarch Pagoda, not mixed with the Song Hanging Bell Pavilion or the Jin Middle Buddha Hall.
hn_fengxue.lede: The Seventh Patriarch Pagoda stands at the center of Fengxue Temple, built in memory of Chan Master Zhen. A tall square lower story supports nine tiers of multi-eaves, and the spire rings of the finial still keep a clear outline.
facts: High Tang body: The Seventh Patriarch Pagoda was built in the 26th year of Kaiyuan in the Tang (738) as the relic pagoda of Chan Master Zhen.
Square, nine tiers: The pagoda is 24.17 m tall, a square hollow brick pagoda whose outer eaves recede tier by tier in a slightly curved outline.
Coexisting periods: The temple also has a Song-dynasty Hanging Bell Pavilion and a Jin-dynasty Middle Buddha Hall; this plate draws only the Tang pagoda.

hb_daodejing.name: Daodejing Pillar of Longxing Daoist Temple
hb_daodejing.sub: Detail of the shaft and lotus base
hb_daodejing.yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hb_daodejing.lede: On the octagonal stone column, the scripture unfolds line by line across the stone faces, with cracks running through the characters and lotus petals. Although Longxing Daoist Temple no longer exists, this Tang pillar still keeps a Daoist classic in its original county town.
facts: The pillar was erected in the 26th year of Kaiyuan in the Tang (738) and is carved with the Daodejing and Emperor Xuanzong's commentary.
The octagonal shaft rests on a lotus base. The calligrapher is traditionally said to be Su Lingzhi; the entry keeps this traditional attribution without treating it as a confirmed signature.

In the reference photograph the upper part is hidden by the beams of a protective pavilion, so this drawing takes only the visible shaft and lotus base and does not add the pillar top or the modern pavilion.

haichunxuan.name: Haichunxuan Pagoda, Dongtai
haichunxuan.era: Built in the Tang, repaired in the Song · Founding year yet to be determined
haichunxuan.yearNote: 750 is only an approximate mid-Tang placement on the timeline and does not represent an evidenced construction year; construction supervised by Yuchi Jingde is treated only as legendary history.
haichunxuan.lede: Beside the waters of Xixi, seven tiers of brick eaves recede one above another, giving the pagoda a plain, steep outline. The Haichunxuan Pagoda has witnessed changes in the Jianghuai salt works and coastline, and it carries the long accumulation of Tang construction and Song repairs.
facts: Dating: The national protection listing classes it as Tang, and local sources record Song repairs; the specific founding year is not settled on the basis of legend.
Form: A seven-story octagonal brick pagoda about 20.8 m tall; the lower walls are tall, while the upper stories recede closely and have small niches.

Names: Also called the Guangfu Temple Pagoda and the Yuchi Pagoda. The county gazetteer's account of construction supervised by Yuchi Jingde is legendary history; the surviving brick body and exterior outline must be understood together with repairs over the centuries.

Tang pagoda · Song repairs

nanchan.name: Main Hall of Nanchan Temple
nanchan.lede: The earliest surviving timber building in China. When Emperor Wuzong of Tang suppressed Buddhism in the Huichang era and monasteries throughout the empire were almost all torn down, it escaped because it stood in a remote small village.
facts: Three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, a gentle roof slope and deeply projecting eaves, it is a typical small Tang hall.
The seventeen Tang sculptures inside are as old as the building and form the most complete group of Tang sculpture in mainland China.
Only four Tang timber buildings survive, all in Shanxi — this journey takes in two of them.
captions: Line drawing · Three bays wide
Single-eaved hip-and-gable

sx_longshan.name: Longshan Grottoes
sx_longshan.sub: Cave of the Great Master of the Three Heavens · Principal figure
sx_longshan.era: Tang niche figures · Later Yuan extensions
sx_longshan.yearNote: The niche of the Great Master of the Three Heavens is dated to the Tang following on-site signage and Jinyuan culture and tourism materials, and 800 is only an approximate placement; the Yuan-dynasty main body of the grotto group is described separately.
sx_longshan.lede: Longshan is known for its Daoist grottoes, whose figures with high topknots and broad robes differ from the great Buddhist images. This drawing selects the central seated figure of the early Cave of the Great Master of the Three Heavens, keeping the subdued outline of its weathered face.
facts: Within the grotto group, the niche of the Great Master of the Three Heavens and the Xuanzhen niche belong to the Tang according to local culture and tourism materials; most of the other main parts were made in the Yuan.
This drawing shows only the principal figure of the Cave of the Great Master of the Three Heavens, from the topknot to the crossed knees, and does not represent the complete group of three figures.

The Yuan extensions are associated with Quanzhen Daoism. The plate's colors follow the Tang niche figure drawn, and the national listing date for the whole group is not substituted for the date of the individual figure.

sd_longhu.name: Dragon and Tiger Pagoda of Shentong Temple, Jinan
sd_longhu.sub: Tang carved body · Later replacement top
sd_longhu.era: Tang body, top repaired in later periods
sd_longhu.yearNote: The base and carved body are attributed to the Tang on the basis of form, and the exact founding year is unknown; 800 serves only as an approximate placement on the Tang timeline. The brick top is a later addition, so the whole pagoda cannot be called original fabric of one date.
sd_longhu.lede: Dragons, tigers and apsaras climb the stone walls of the pagoda, the fine carving set off by a massive Sumeru plinth. The Tang stone body of the Dragon and Tiger Pagoda carries a later replacement top, so repairs of different periods are layered in a single pagoda.
facts: Dating: The base and body are usually attributed to the Tang on the basis of architectural and carving style; the exact founding year is unknown, and 800 is only an approximate placement on the timeline.
Surviving layers: The carved stone body and the later brick top should be considered separately; the whole pagoda cannot be treated as original fabric completed in one year.
Form: A square pagoda chamber with doorways on four sides and stacked Sumeru plinths. Its name is the Dragon and Tiger Pagoda; it is not the twin pagodas of Lotus Pond in Kaohsiung.
captions: Dragon and Tiger Pagoda of Shentong Temple, Jinan, whole view · Line drawing
Tang · Tang dynasty · Date uncertain

guangren.name: Temple of King Guangren, Ruicheng
guangren.lede: On the high Longquan terrace beside the ancient city of Wei, the Five Dragons Temple keeps the local cult of the water deity with a small Tang timber main hall; its beam frame is spare and its roof slopes are gentle.
facts: The main hall is a surviving Tang timber structure, usually dated by a stele of the 6th year of Dahe in the Tang (832) and by the features of its frame.
The hall is five bays wide and four rafters deep, with no interior columns, and the beam frame is entirely exposed.
Bracket sets are placed only on the column heads, with no intercolumnar sets; the present walls, doors, windows and roof show later repairs.
captions: Front of the main hall, Temple of King Guangren · Redrawn from photographs
Tang timber structure · Five bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; walls and roof repaired over time

longxingchuang.name: Dharani Pillar of Longxing Temple, Hangzhou
longxingchuang.sub: Tang stone pillar · Detail of the shaft
longxingchuang.era: 2nd year of Kaicheng · Upper part repaired in the Qing
longxingchuang.lede: Beside a busy street, an octagonal stone pillar still carries scriptures carved in the Tang. Cracks run across its faces, and characters and repair seams overlap, leaving more than a thousand years of preservation and repair on the same stone.
facts: Tang date: The pillar was erected in the 2nd year of Kaicheng (837) and also bears an inscription of the 5th year of Dazhong (851); there were originally two, and one survives.
Later repairs: The shaft, base and other parts retain Tang components, while the upper part is a Qing repair; the surviving whole cannot simply be regarded as its original form of 837.

Partial plate: The plate selects the octagonal shaft and its supporting stone, showing the visible cracks and damage; the scripture is suggested with sparse strokes and is not a readable transcription.

chongsheng.name: Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple, Dali
chongsheng.sub: Dali · Qianxun Pagoda and the north and south pagodas
chongsheng.lede: At the eastern foot of the Cang Mountains, the Qianxun Pagoda and two smaller pagodas to the north and south stand in a triangle. The central square pagoda rises tall and straight, while the octagonal pagodas on either side are somewhat shorter, preserving the different outlines of Nanzhao and Dali Kingdom pagodas.
facts: The Qianxun Pagoda is generally dated to the reign of Quanfengyou of Nanzhao (823–859); it is a square sixteen-tier brick pagoda 69.13 m tall, and the catalogue orders it by this approximate date.
The north and south pagodas are dated separately to the Dali Kingdom; each is octagonal with ten tiers and 42.19 m tall, and they are not recorded as built in the same year as the Qianxun Pagoda.

The plate groups the three pagodas as seen from the east, with the Qianxun Pagoda in the center, the south pagoda on the left and the north pagoda on the right; the finials, bodies and bases of all three are drawn in full.
captions: Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple · Group view from the east
Qianxun Pagoda with sixteen tiers, the smaller north and south pagodas with ten each

foguang.name: East Hall of Foguang Temple
foguang.lede: In June 1937, Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin read the inscription “female disciple Ning Gongyu” beneath a beam in the hall, and the Japanese scholars' claim that “China has no Tang timber buildings left” was overturned.
foguang.quote: “This is the only Tang timber building we have encountered in all our years of searching… the foremost treasure among China's ancient buildings.” — Liang Sicheng, Notes on the Architecture of Foguang Temple on Mount Wutai
facts: Seven bays wide, with a single-eaved hipped roof. The bracket sets are nearly half the height of the columns and the eaves project nearly four meters — proportions never seen again in later periods.
Tang architecture, sculpture, murals and inscriptions survive together in a single hall, which Liang Sicheng called the “four wonders.”
The dharani pillar in front of the hall is inscribed “11th year of Dazhong,” another piece of conclusive evidence for the dating.
captions: Line drawing · Seven bays wide
Single-eaved hipped roof

protection.scope: East Hall of Foguang Temple

sh_tangchuang.name: Tang Dharani Pillar, Songjiang
sh_tangchuang.sub: Dharani pillar of the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra
sh_tangchuang.lede: Tier upon tier of stone pedestals raise a slender octagonal shaft, with carved scripture alternating with reliefs of lotus petals, coiled dragons and Buddhas. Erected in the 13th year of Dazhong in the Tang, this pillar still stands on a school campus in the old town of Songjiang.
facts: Built in the 13th year of Dazhong in the Tang (859), it is the oldest above-ground cultural relic surviving in Shanghai; it was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1988.
It is about 9.3 m tall overall, with 21 surviving stone sections; the octagonal shaft is engraved with the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra and donors' inscriptions.

Pedestals, waisted sections, canopies and waist eaves are stacked in alternation, carved with lotus flowers, coiled dragons and Buddhist figures. The plate simplifies the weathered reliefs and scripture and is not a facsimile of the inscription.
captions: Octagonal stone pillar · Stacked carvings
Tang · 13th year of Dazhong (859)

hlj_shideng.name: Balhae Stone Lantern of Xinglong Temple
hlj_shideng.era: Balhae period · Date of construction unknown
hlj_shideng.yearNote: 800 is only an ordering placement for a Balhae-period stone carving, not an exact date of making; surviving repaired components and the temple's later buildings are not all treated as Balhae originals.
hlj_shideng.place: Heilongjiang · Ning'an · Xinglong Temple, Bohai Town
hlj_shideng.lede: A lotus base, a long stone column, an octagonal lamp chamber and a pavilion-style cap make up a freestanding carved stone lantern for an ever-burning flame. It is catalogued as Balhae period; the later temple behind it does not become ancient original fabric along with the lantern.
facts: The stone lantern is a freestanding carving; the plate draws only this subject and excludes the modern railing and the temple background.
The stone is now gray and weathered; the yellow-green patches on the cap and base are lichen, not glazed tiles or painted timberwork.

The openwork windows visible in the lamp chamber and the low reliefs on the base are treated differently, the latter kept solid. On the map it is grouped under a representative point for Ning'an City, not the exact coordinates of the lantern.

gongchen.name: Gongchen Pagoda, Lin'an
gongchen.lede: In the 1st year of Zhenming in the Later Liang (915), Qian Liu, King of Wuyue, built a pagoda on Mount Gongchen, where his rise had begun. Square and five stories high, of brick imitating timber, it is the earliest surviving square pagoda in Zhejiang, and it still looks Tang.
facts: It is 25.3 m tall overall, with a five-story body 22.06 m high; brick engaged columns, architraves and bracket sets imitate a timber pavilion-style structure.
Each story has cusped kunmen openings on all four sides and corbeled eaves; the finial is iron.
Qian Liu was born in Lin'an, and Mount Gongchen takes its name from him; only the site of Gongchen Temple beside the pagoda remains.
captions: Line drawing · Square, five stories

longmen.name: West Side Hall of Longmen Temple
longmen.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Yuantou Village
longmen.lede: From the fifty-three years of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, only five timber buildings survive in all of China, and three of them are in the Zhuozhang River valley. The West Side Hall of Longmen Temple is the earliest of these and the only one with an overhanging gable roof — a small three-bay hall whose architraves do not project beyond the corner columns and whose columns carry no pupaifang plate beam, still the Tang way of building.
facts: Built in the 3rd year of Tongguang in the Later Tang (925), or by another account in the 2nd year of Qingtai (935); three bays wide and four rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof.

Within the single temple of Longmen stand buildings of six periods, Five Dynasties, Song, Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing: the Mahavira Hall dates to the 5th year of Shaosheng in the Song (1098), the Hall of Heavenly Kings to the Jin and the Dipankara Buddha Hall to the Yuan.
Bracket sets sit only on the column heads, in the simple doukou tiao form, with no intercolumnar sets — even sparer than at Nanchan Temple.
captions: Line drawing of the West Side Hall · Three bays wide

hb_zdwenmiao.name: Dacheng Hall of the Zhengding County Confucian Temple
hb_zdwenmiao.yearNote: The subject drawn is dated to the late Tang–Five Dynasties; the numerical year is only an approximate ordering point.
hb_zdwenmiao.lede: A low, gentle roof covers the five-bay hall, and massive beams and brackets show beneath the eaves. The date of the Dacheng Hall of the Zhengding County Confucian Temple comes from judgments of its structural form, not from the date the Confucian temple was later established.
facts: The Dacheng Hall is usually dated to the late Tang to Five Dynasties; the national protected site listing gives its date as Five Dynasties.
Five bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the outer columns are enclosed in the walls, and four column shafts are visible on the front.

This entry is the Dacheng Hall of the county Confucian temple, distinct from the Zhengding prefectural Confucian temple; the date of the temple's establishment in the Hongwu era of the Ming is not used to date the ancient hall.

tiantai.name: Tiantai Hermitage
tiantai.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Wangqu Village
tiantai.lede: A small three-bay hall long counted as one of the “four Tang timber buildings.” Only when an inscription was found on a beam during repairs in 2014 was it learned that it was built in the 4th year of Changxing in the Later Tang (933) — twenty-six years after the end of the Tang, yet still in the Tang manner.
facts: Three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the four front columns stand outside the wall, the eaves project deeply and the corners sweep high.
The bracket sets are extremely simple, using only doukou tiao on the column heads and no intercolumnar sets; the interior is open to the roof, so the beam frame can be seen at a glance.
In front of the hall stand a Tang stone pillar and Ming and Qing steles; small as it is, the hall is the most “Tang” of the three Five Dynasties buildings in the Zhuozhang River valley.

dayun.name: Amitabha Hall of Dayun Monastery
dayun.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Shihui Village
dayun.lede: The Amitabha Hall, built in the 5th year of Tianfu in the Later Jin (940), retains more than twenty square meters of Five Dynasties murals inside — among China's surviving temple murals, the only ones from the Five Dynasties.
facts: Three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the bracket sets are five-puzuo with two projecting arms, with one intercolumnar set in each bay.

The Five Dynasties murals on the east wall and on the back of the fan-shaped screen wall, including the Vimalakirti Sutra transformation tableau, are unique survivors of mural painting between the Tang and the Song.
The Shuanglin Temple–style stone dharani pillar and the gate in front of the temple are later, but the beam frame of the Amitabha Hall is still original Five Dynasties fabric.
captions: Line drawing of the Amitabha Hall · Three bays wide

fuzhouwuta.name: Black Pagoda, Fuzhou
fuzhouwuta.place: Fujian · Fuzhou · Gulou District · Eastern foot of Mount Wu
fuzhouwuta.lede: Granite is stacked into a seven-story pavilion-style tower, each story with a narrow gallery and balustrade panels. The Black Pagoda is named for its dark stone, and together with the White Pagoda on Mount Yu opposite it is one of two familiar landmarks of old Fuzhou.
facts: Five Dynasties Min Kingdom: Construction began in 941 with nine stories planned, but stopped at seven after Wang Yanxi was killed in 944; the present pagoda is recorded by its completion at seven stories.
Stone imitating timber: An octagonal seven-story granite pagoda about 32.86 m tall, with engaged columns at the corners and stone eaves projecting at each story.
Galleries and niches: Balustrade panels enclose a gallery around the outside, the walls are pierced with doors and niches, and a gourd-shaped finial crowns the top.
captions: Black Pagoda, Fuzhou · Chongmiao Baosheng Jianlao Pagoda

wenfeng.name: Wenfeng Pagoda
wenfeng.lede: In the fifty-three years of the Five Dynasties, few timber buildings survived in the Central Plains, and this brick pagoda is a rare relic of that turbulent age. Wider at the top than at the bottom and shaped like a parasol canopy, it has almost no parallel among China's ancient pagodas.
facts: Five stories and octagonal, it widens story by story, each story projecting outward on corbeled brick eaves; the top story is the widest.
The top is not an ordinary finial but a Tibetan-style lama stupa about ten meters tall.
The eight faces of the body carry brick carvings of the life of the Buddha; a stair inside leads to the top for a distant view.
In the Qianlong era of the Qing, Huang Bangning, prefect of Zhangde, inscribed the words “Wenfeng songxiu” (the literary peak rises in elegance), and the pagoda was renamed after them.

hb_cangzhoulion.name: Iron Lion of Cangzhou
hb_cangzhoulion.sub: Original iron lion surviving at the old city (damage retained)
hb_cangzhoulion.yearNote: The enlarged replica made in 2011 for Lion City Park is not used; the real damage, the lotus basin on its back and the necessary supports follow photographs.
hb_cangzhoulion.lede: The thousand-year-old cast-iron lion carries a lotus basin on its back; its damaged body stands together with a supporting steel frame, recording both Later Zhou casting technique and a long history of conservation.
facts: Date: The lion's body bears the inscription “cast in the 3rd year of Guangshun of the Great Zhou,” corresponding to 953; it is a large cast-iron survival of the Later Zhou.
Form: The giant lion raises its head with open mouth, wears saddle ornaments and carries a lotus basin on its back; the original has obvious breaks and losses at the head, legs and feet.
Present state: The plate follows 2020 photographs of the original, keeping the damage and the steel-tube supports; it does not use the newly cast replica of 2011 or restore the missing parts.
captions: Original iron lion of Cangzhou
Damage and protective supports retained as in 2020 photographs

protection.scope: Iron Lion of Cangzhou · Original iron lion surviving at the old city (damage retained)

zhakoubaita.name: Zhakou White Pagoda
zhakoubaita.era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Wuyue
zhakoubaita.lede: The Zhakou White Pagoda carves the columns, tie beams, bracket sets and tiered eaves of a timber pavilion-style pagoda in miniature in white stone. Its nine-story body tapers up from a Sumeru plinth, and weathered stone eaves and an iron finial together outline this Wuyue structure on the bank of the Qiantang River.
facts: Conservation sources date the pagoda to the late Wuyue of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; no specific year of construction is firmly assigned.
It is an eight-sided, nine-story stone pagoda imitating a timber pavilion, each story made up of a balcony platform, a body and eaves.

The base is carved with the Nine Mountains and Eight Seas and with Buddhist sutras, and the body with reliefs of Buddhas, bodhisattvas and other figures; the plate keeps the present damage and does not complete it as a new pagoda.
captions: Zhakou White Pagoda
Nine-story stone pagoda imitating timber · Wuyue, Five Dynasties

huqiuta.name: Yunyan Temple Pagoda, Tiger Hill
huqiuta.era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Wuyue
huqiuta.lede: On the summit of Tiger Hill, the brick eaves of the Yunyan Temple Pagoda recede tier by tier, and its seven-story body keeps traces of timber-style columns, tie beams and bracket sets. The pagoda's lean and the successive changes to its brick and timber structure together make up the present form of this old Suzhou pagoda.
facts: The present pagoda was begun in 959 and completed in 961; the national listing dates it to the Five Dynasties, and historically it belongs to Wuyue.
It is a seven-story, eight-sided brick pagoda imitating a timber pavilion; its timber eaves have been lost, while the brick eaves and balcony platforms remain.
The body has long leaned to one side; repairs over the centuries and modern reinforcement are recorded separately from the date the original pagoda was built.
captions: Tiger Hill · Yunyan Temple Pagoda
Near-frontal view · Wuyue, Five Dynasties (959–961)

qixia.name: Relic Pagoda of Qixia Temple
qixia.era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Southern Tang
qixia.lede: The Relic Pagoda of Qixia Temple raises its sculpted body on upturned lotus petals; five stone eaves recede upward, and a carved finial stands at the top. Buddha niches, guardians and narrative reliefs on the base give this Southern Tang stone pagoda both an architectural and a sculptural scale.
facts: The surviving stone pagoda is a Southern Tang rebuilding, dated to the Five Dynasties in the national listing; its Sui-dynasty timber predecessor is recorded separately from today's stone pagoda.
It is an octagonal five-story multi-eaved stone pagoda resting on a Sumeru plinth and upturned lotus, with five stone eaves stacked above the body.
The body is carved with doors and with figures such as heavenly kings and guardians, and the base with Buddhist stories; the plate renders the reliefs as simplified line drawing.
captions: Qixia Temple · Relic Pagoda
Five-story stone pagoda · Rebuilt in the Southern Tang

lingyin.name: Stone Pagodas and Dharani Pillars of Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou
lingyin.lede: The stone pagodas freeze tiers of timber eaves in stone, while the dharani pillars stack scripture and Buddha images on tall columns. This group of Wuyue survivals at Lingyin Temple dates from across the founding of the Northern Song, yet still belongs to Jiangnan under the rule of the Qian family.
facts: The stone pagodas were built in 960; two survive, octagonal and nine stories high, rendering in stone the columns, tie beams, bracket sets and projecting eaves of a pavilion.

The dharani pillars were built in 969, and two also survive; their shafts are carved with scripture, and the pedestals and upper parts are stacked in tiers. They belong to a different construction date from the stone pagodas.

The plate selects one stone pagoda and one dharani pillar and sets them side by side for comparison from historical photographs; the timber halls of the present temple have their own history of later rebuilding.
captions: Stone pagoda and dharani pillar · Comparative line drawing

sx_zhenguo.name: Zhenguo Temple, Pingyao
sx_zhenguo.yearNote: Dated to the 7th year of Tianhui of the Northern Han. Although 963 already falls within the Northern Song reckoning, this part of Shanxi still belonged to the Northern Han, so the hall is not reassigned as a Song structure.
sx_zhenguo.lede: The roof of the Ten-Thousand-Buddha Hall looks exceptionally broad, its deep eaves carried out by huge bracket sets. The small three-bay hall preserves the scale and character of Northern Han timber construction.
facts: The Ten-Thousand-Buddha Hall was built in the 7th year of Tianhui of the Northern Han (963) and is a surviving timber structure of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.
Three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the massive bracket sets (puzuo) and deeply projecting eaves form striking proportions.
Zhenguo Temple, together with the Ancient City of Pingyao and Shuanglin Temple, makes up a World Heritage Site; the plate selects the Ten-Thousand-Buddha Hall alone.
captions: Ten-Thousand-Buddha Hall, Zhenguo Temple · Front view
7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han · 963

hualin.name: Hualin Temple, Fuzhou
hualin.era: 2nd year of Qiande, Northern Song · Built under Wuyue
hualin.place: Fujian · Fuzhou · Gulou District · Southern foot of Mount Ping
hualin.lede: At the southern foot of Mount Ping, the Main Hall of Hualin Temple raises its broad roof on four sturdy front eave columns. In the 2nd year of Qiande in the Northern Song, the Wuyue prefect Bao Xiurang built this temple; its huge bracket sets and deeply projecting eaves bear the marks of Tang and Five Dynasties timber construction and of Fujian building practice.
facts: Founded in 964 and first named Yueshan Jixiang Chan Monastery, it was built by Bao Xiurang, prefect of Fuzhou under the Wuyue kingdom; it was renamed Hualin Temple in 1444.
The surviving Main Hall is three bays across the front with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; 18 timber columns together form the body of the hall, and the bracket sets use massive timbers.
Listed in the 2nd batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level in 1982.

chongming.name: Chongming Temple, Gaoping
chongming.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Hexi Town · Guojiazhuang Village
chongming.lede: At the eastern foot of Mount Shengfo, the low, gentle roof of the Middle Buddha Hall rests on huge bracket sets. This small three-bay hall, completed in the 4th year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (971), has not a single interior column. Looking up at the beam frame, one sees short timbers joined in midair into long beams, the old builders' way of spanning a large space with small timber.
facts: Three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the Middle Buddha Hall is a Northern Song structure, while the rear hall is a later building.

The column-head bracket sets are seven-puzuo, with two projecting arms and two descending cantilevers (ang), and the eaves project deeply; there is no pupaifang plate beam and the architraves do not project beyond the corner columns, retaining early timber practice.

Inside, a paired-beam system carries the roof frame, and some beams are joined end to end in sections, popularly called “broken beams”; this construction leaves the three-bay interior open and free of columns.
captions: Line drawing of the Middle Buddha Hall · Three bays wide
Seven-puzuo · Single-eaved hip-and-gable · Northern Song

protection.scope: Chongming Temple, Gaoping · Middle Buddha Hall · Mount Shengfo

longxing.name: Longxing Temple
longxing.sub: Moni Hall · Hall of Great Compassion · Revolving Sutra Cabinet
longxing.lede: Longcang Temple, founded in the 6th year of Kaihuang in the Sui, was expanded by imperial order under Emperor Taizu of Song, and a 21-meter bronze Guanyin was cast. It is the most completely preserved example of Northern Song official-style architecture.
facts: The Moni Hall (4th year of Huangyou, 1052) is cross-shaped in plan, with porches projecting on all four sides, gable ends facing forward and a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof — Liang Sicheng called it “the only example of its kind in the land.”

The bronze Thousand-Armed, Thousand-Eyed Guanyin in the Hall of Great Compassion is 21.3 m tall, with forty-two arms; cast in the 4th year of Kaibao in the Song, it is the greatest of Song bronze castings.
The Revolving Sutra Cabinet is the earliest surviving rotating sutra repository, and is itself a small pavilion of Song fine joinery.
Inside the Moni Hall is a Ming-dynasty suspended sculpture of a backward-seated Guanyin; Lu Xun once kept its photograph on his desk and called it the “Goddess of Beauty of the East.”
captions: Line drawing of the Moni Hall · Seven bays wide
Double-eaved hip-and-gable · Porches on four sides

hn_jidu.name: Jidu Temple
hn_jidu.sub: A Song-dynasty Sleeping Hall at the source of the Ji River
hn_jidu.yearNote: Based on the date of the timber Sleeping Hall; the Sui founding history of Jidu Temple is not applied to the Song hall.
hn_jidu.lede: Jidu Temple honors the god of the Ji River, and its Sleeping Hall preserves timber construction of the 6th year of Kaibao in the Northern Song. Under the low, gentle roof, massive bracket sets and a simple column grid support a five-bay facade.
facts: Northern Song Sleeping Hall: The Sleeping Hall was built in 973 and is the main timber structure in the temple with a clear Song date.
Five bays, hip-and-gable: The hall is five bays wide and four rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the front eaves retain large bracket sets.
Conservation: Professional conservation and repair were carried out in modern times, and the plate is drawn from photographs of its present state after repair.
captions: Sleeping Hall of Jidu Temple · Front elevation
6th year of Kaibao, Northern Song (973) · Five bays wide, hip-and-gable roof

hn_fanta.name: Fan Pagoda, Kaifeng
hn_fanta.sub: Surviving three-story main body and small pagoda
hn_fanta.yearNote: 974 is the year the Song main body was built; the small pagoda on top and the repaired details are not dated by this year.
hn_fanta.lede: Only three stories of the broad hexagonal body remain, yet they still carry layered brick carvings and Buddha niches. The incomplete outline of the Fan Pagoda records the demolition and repairs that followed the building of this Song pagoda.
facts: The Fan Pagoda was built in the 7th year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (974), and its tall lower three stories survive.
The hexagonal body is covered with Buddha-image bricks and timber-style details, and on top is a small pagoda rebuilt in a later period.
The plate draws the three-story main body and the small pagoda surviving on top as they are now, without restoring the original nine stories as a complete pagoda.
captions: Fan Pagoda, Kaifeng · Surviving three-story main body and small pagoda
Song · 974 · Later repairs

sh_longhuata.name: Longhua Pagoda
sh_longhuata.sub: Eight-sided, seven stories · Brick-and-timber pavilion-style pagoda
sh_longhuata.era: 2nd year of Taiping Xingguo · Rebuilt by Qian Chu of Wuyue
sh_longhuata.yearNote: The main body of the surviving pagoda is placed by its rebuilding by Qian Chu of Wuyue in the 2nd year of Taiping Xingguo (977); the national listing dates it to the Song. The timber eaves, railings and other parts have been repaired over the centuries, and the legend of a founding in the Three Kingdoms period is not taken as the date of the surviving pagoda.
sh_longhuata.lede: Seven tiers of flying eaves unfold story by story around the pagoda core, with timber railings and yellow walls alternating around it. The Longhua Pagoda carries on the ancient body rebuilt under Wuyue while keeping, through repairs over the centuries, the layered outline of a brick-and-timber pavilion-style pagoda.
facts: Traditionally said to have been first built in the Three Kingdoms period, the main body of the surviving pagoda was rebuilt by Qian Chu, King of Wuyue, in the 2nd year of Taiping Xingguo in the Northern Song (977); the legendary date and the surviving main body are recorded separately.
A pavilion-style brick-and-timber pagoda, eight-sided and seven stories high, about 40.4 m tall overall; the body tapers story by story, with timber eaves and balcony railings on the outside.

After many repairs, the exterior timberwork is not all the same age as the ancient brick body. The plate depicts the present appearance from daytime photographs and includes only the old pagoda, not the temple's later halls.
captions: Eight-sided, seven stories · Brick-and-timber pavilion style
Rebuilt under Wuyue · Northern Song date (977)

luohanshuangta.name: Twin Pagodas and Main Hall Ruins of Luohan Monastery, Suzhou
luohanshuangta.sub: Seven-tiered, eight-sided twin pagodas · Song stone columns
luohanshuangta.era: Begun in the 7th year of Taiping Xingguo
luohanshuangta.lede: Two slender brick pagodas stand side by side, their long iron finials reaching into the sky. The main hall beside them has vanished, but its stone columns and column bases still mark the scale of the hall on the original site.
facts: The twin pagodas were begun in the 7th year of Taiping Xingguo in the Northern Song (982) and completed in the Yongxi era; both are seven-tiered, eight-sided pavilion-style pagodas.
The brick bodies imitating timber taper story by story, rendering the pavilion form with columns, tie beams, bracket sets and brick eaves, and the long finials give a striking outline.
Main hall ruins: The hall has been destroyed, but stone columns and carved column bases remain; the plate selects a few of these remains and presents them alongside the twin pagodas.
captions: Twin Pagodas of Luohan Monastery · Remains of stone columns
Northern Song · Begun in the 7th year of Taiping Xingguo

sx_youxian.name: Youxian Temple, Gaoping
sx_youxian.era: Chunhua era, Northern Song · Vairocana Hall
sx_youxian.yearNote: Local culture and tourism accounts give 990, but no inscription recording a founding at that time has been found for the front hall; the period 990–994 is used as an approximate placement, without claiming a precise completion year.
sx_youxian.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mount Niu, Zaili Village, Hexi Town
sx_youxian.lede: The Vairocana Hall of Youxian Temple sets wide eaves over thick walls, with its three bays of doors and windows compactly arranged. The bracket sets beneath the eaves and the frame of naturally curved timbers preserve the practice of local craftsmen in the early Northern Song.
facts: Chunhua-era Song structure: The Vairocana Hall is usually dated to the Chunhua era of the Northern Song and was repeatedly repaired from the Jin and Yuan onward; the halls of the temple are not all of one date.

Thick walls, deep eaves: Three bays and six rafters, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and deeply projecting eaves; the brick walls stand close to the plane of the eave columns, unlike the look of halls with a front porch.
Built with curved timber: The dingfu transverse beams are worked from naturally curved timber, the beam frame preserves features of local craftsmanship, and there is also a Yuan repair inscription.
captions: Youxian Temple · Vairocana Hall
Chunhua era, Northern Song · c. 990–994

protection.scope: Youxian Temple, Gaoping · Vairocana Hall · Mount Niu

songyangyanqing.name: Yanqing Temple Pagoda, Songyang
songyangyanqing.lede: The hexagonal body of the Yanqing Temple Pagoda tapers tier by tier, with balcony galleries running around it and two broad eaves spreading at the base. A slender iron finial stands atop the seven-tier brick-and-timber structure, showing the form of early pavilion-style pagodas in southwestern Zhejiang.
facts: Work on the pagoda began in the 2nd year of Xianping in the Northern Song (999) and was completed in 1002; this entry is recorded by its Song brick core.
The pagoda is a six-sided, seven-tier pavilion-style brick-and-timber structure; the ground story has a double-eaved peristyle (fujie), so eight eave lines can be counted on the complete exterior.
Major repairs began in 1983 and were completed in 1991; the repair history of today's timber eaves and galleries must be distinguished from the Northern Song body.
captions: Songyang · Yanqing Temple Pagoda
Six sides, seven tiers · Double-eaved peristyle at the base

yuanqi.name: Yuanqi Temple, Lucheng
yuanqi.era: Founded in the 6th year of Tianbao, Tang · Surviving Song structures
yuanqi.place: Shanxi · Lucheng · Bank of the Zhuozhang River · Xin'an Village
yuanqi.lede: The temple sits atop a solitary peak beside the Zhuozhang River and was founded in the 6th year of Tianbao in the Tang (747). The surviving Mahavira Hall and Qinglong Pagoda are both Song: hall and pagoda stand side by side on the clifftop, and looking up from the valley, the pagoda's silhouette catches the eye first.
facts: The Mahavira Hall is three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and high-swept corners, typical of Song halls in southeastern Shanxi.
The Qinglong Pagoda is an octagonal seven-tier pavilion-style brick pagoda of Song construction; pagoda and hall stand side by side on the east side of the temple, not on the central axis.
The temple holds a Tang stone dharani pillar and a damaged Northern Wei stele; after the game “Wukong” became a hit, it became one of the game's real-world locations.
captions: Line drawing · Hall and pagoda side by side
Single-eaved hip-and-gable · Octagonal, seven tiers

gd_meian.name: Mahavira Hall of Mei'an, Zhaoqing
gd_meian.sub: Song timber frame · Present flush gable roof
gd_meian.yearNote: Mei'an was founded in 996; 1000 is only an approximate ordering point for the Song structure, without asserting that every component of the surviving hall was completed in the same year. The Mahavira Hall retains features of Song timber construction; its roof was changed to a flush gable roof in later repairs, and the plate follows the present state.
gd_meian.lede: The timber frame of the five-bay hall retains features of Song architecture, while its roof bears the changes of later repairs. The small hermitage does not impress by its size; what is worth seeing is precisely its timber structure and its accumulated layers of history.
facts: Main subject: The complete Mahavira Hall of Mei'an.

Date: Mei'an was founded in 996; 1000 is only an approximate ordering point for the Song structure, without asserting that every component of the surviving hall was completed in the same year. The Mahavira Hall retains features of Song timber construction; its roof was changed to a flush gable roof in later repairs, and the plate follows the present state.

Plate scope: The present flush gable roof and the five-bay Song timber body of the hall, three bays deep; it is not changed back to the hip-and-gable roof of the original construction, and the incense burner and trees are not drawn.

ruiguang.name: Ruiguang Pagoda, Suzhou
ruiguang.era: Built from the 1st year of Jingde to the 8th year of Tiansheng
ruiguang.lede: Beside Panmen Gate, seven tiers of eaves recede one above another, and the body and its exterior timberwork together form the outline of a Jiangnan pavilion-style pagoda. It has undergone Song alterations and modern restoration, so its date must be read from the early brick body.
facts: Northern Song construction: The foundation was laid in the 1st year of Jingde (1004) and the pagoda was completed in the 8th year of Tiansheng (1030); it was later altered and repaired.
The seven-tier, eight-sided brick body bears the load, while the exterior timber eaves and galleries display the pavilion form; the present state includes parts restored in modern times.
Pagoda treasures: Objects found inside the pagoda, such as the Pearl Relic Pillar, are now in the Suzhou Museum and can be read alongside the pagoda's building history.
captions: Ruiguang Pagoda · Seven tiers, eight sides
Northern Song body · Later timber eaves

baoguo.name: Baoguo Temple, Ningbo
baoguo.lede: The Main Hall of the 6th year of Dazhong Xiangfu in the Northern Song (1013) is the earliest surviving timber building south of the Yangtze. It was originally a three-bay hall with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; in the Qing a peristyle was added all around, producing the five-bay, double-eaved hall seen today — the central three bays are still Song construction from a thousand years ago.
facts: The plan is deeper than it is wide, and three caisson ceilings in the front bay of the interior hide the beam frame, which is why it is popularly called the “Beamless Hall.”

The melon-ribbed columns are each assembled from four smaller pieces into one large column, the earliest surviving example of composite columns in China; the bracket sets are seven-puzuo, with two projecting arms and two descending cantilevers.
“Birds do not roost, insects do not bore, spiders spin no webs and no dust settles on the beams” — legend credits the timber, but in fact it is the cross-draft through the hall.
No Buddha images are enshrined in the temple; it is now a museum of ancient architecture.
captions: Line drawing of the Main Hall · Five bays wide
Double-eaved hip-and-gable · Peristyle added in the Qing

sx_chongqing.name: Chongqing Temple, Zhangzi
sx_chongqing.era: 9th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song · Thousand-Buddha Hall
sx_chongqing.place: Shanxi · Zhangzi · Mount Ziyun, Ju Village, Setou Town
sx_chongqing.lede: The Thousand-Buddha Hall of Chongqing Temple sits on the slope of Mount Ziyun, its wide eaves covering three plain bays of thick walls. The Northern Song timber structure stands next to the temple's Song painted clay arhats, so the different dates of architecture and sculpture can be read side by side in one small temple.
facts: Song structure of 1016: The Thousand-Buddha Hall dates from the 9th year of Dazhong Xiangfu in the Northern Song; it is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and the surviving main structure is recorded as Song.

Wide eaves, thick walls: The walls lie close to the plane of the eave columns; the central timber door and the vertical-bar windows on either side are tucked under the great eaves, and the bracket sets beneath the eaves are sturdy and clear.
Song sculpture next door: The temple's Dashi Hall and its eighteen arhats bear a date of 1079, and the walls and other halls have later repairs; this drawing depicts only the Thousand-Buddha Hall.
captions: Chongqing Temple · Thousand-Buddha Hall
9th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song · 1016

hb_xiude.name: Xiude Temple Pagoda
hb_xiude.sub: Surviving brick pagoda combining pavilion and flower-pagoda forms
hb_xiude.yearNote: The county gazetteer says the pagoda was completed in 1020; the provincial cultural heritage bureau dates it only to the Song and records six tiers with no surviving finial. Later photographs were checked against the surviving tiers, and the common seven-story account is not used to reconstruct it.
hb_xiude.lede: Xiude Temple is long gone, but an unusual brick pagoda still stands south of the town of Quyang. A plain lower story supports a middle section covered with small pagodas, and the upper part narrows into a pavilion-style body, joining flower pagoda and pavilion in a single outline.
facts: Date: The surviving body is dated to the Song; the county gazetteer records the pagoda's completion in 1020, and the Sui-dynasty predecessor temple is treated as separate history.
Form: An octagonal brick pagoda combining the pavilion and flower-pagoda types, its middle section covered with reliefs of small pagodas.
Site: Large numbers of stone sculptures from the Northern Dynasties to the Sui and Tang were once excavated at the temple site; they are earlier than the surviving Song pagoda.
captions: Quyang · Xiude Temple Pagoda
Present body · Pavilion and flower pagoda combined

jiwang.name: Jiwang Temple, Wanrong
jiwang.place: Shanxi · Wanrong · Nanzhang Township · Taizhao Village
jiwang.lede: A low, spreading hipped roof covers a five-bay facade, and a deep gallery encloses the ritual space within. The temple is dedicated to Houji, the ancestor of agriculture, and its main hall, framed without full-length great beams, preserves a distinctive Northern Song structural solution.
facts: Northern Song structure: Official sources date the main hall to the Northern Song and record that the temple was founded no later than the 1st year of Tiansheng (1023).
Five-bay hipped hall: The main hall is five bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof, and bracket sets on the column heads and between the columns carry the deep eaves.

“Beamless Hall”: The popular name comes from the absence of full-length great beams inside; it still has a timber beam frame and is not a masonry beamless hall. It was listed in the 5th batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level in 2001.
captions: Jiwang Temple, Wanrong · Main Hall
Five-bay hipped hall · Northern Song structure

haiqing.name: Ashoka Pagoda of Haiqing Temple
haiqing.place: Jiangsu · Lianyungang · Foot of Huaguo Mountain
haiqing.lede: The Ashoka Pagoda of Haiqing Temple tapers upward through nine tiers of corbeled brick eaves, its tall ground-story chamber and tiers of arched doors setting a clear rhythm. This brick pagoda at the foot of Huaguo Mountain preserves its Northern Song outline, plain and upright in appearance.
facts: The pagoda had a Tang predecessor; the present pagoda is recorded by its rebuilding in the 1st year of Tiansheng in the Northern Song (1023), and the Tang history is not taken as the date of the main structure.
The body is eight-sided with nine tiers; its brick eaves are corbeled tier upon tier, and the arched doors and low top form its present outline.
Repairs in the 1970s found a stone casket, a silver coffin, porcelain vases, relics and other objects in the pagoda core; they are now kept by the Lianyungang Museum.
captions: Haiqing Temple · Ashoka Pagoda

hb_tuoluoni.name: Zhaozhou Dharani Pillar
hb_tuoluoni.yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hb_tuoluoni.lede: Octagonal shafts, canopies and lotus petals are stacked tier upon tier, so that the Zhaozhou Dharani Pillar resembles a stone pagoda made of scripture and carving. The original Kaiyuan Temple no longer exists, but the pillar still stands at a street crossing in the town.
facts: The pillar was built in the 5th year of Jingyou in the Northern Song (1038); it is octagonal in plan with seven tiers in all.
The shaft is carved with scripture, and between the canopies and pedestals are carvings of Buddhas, apsaras, lotus petals and more.
The plate depicts the surviving stone pillar, keeping its partial damage, and does not confuse it with the Bailin Temple Pagoda in Zhao County or with Kaiyuan Temple in Zhengding.
