lingxiao.name: Lingxiao Pagoda of Tianning Temple
lingxiao.era: Founded in the Tang · Rebuilt in the 5th year of Qingli, Song
lingxiao.lede: First built in the reign of Emperor Daizong of Tang, it was rebuilt on the ruins of the Tang pagoda in the 5th year of Qingli in the Song (1045), and its upper part was repaired again in the 5th year of Huangtong in the Jin (1145). The lower four stories are Song brick and the upper five are Jin brick and timber — two dynasties stacked in one pagoda.
facts: An octagonal nine-story pavilion-style pagoda of mixed brick and timber, 41 m tall, standing on an octagonal platform.

From the fourth story a timber central mast rises straight to the top, linked to the outer eaves on each story by eight radiating paliang beams; this is the only surviving example of the method in China.

With the Xumi Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, the Flower Pagoda of Guanghui Temple and the Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple, it is one of the “Four Pagodas of Zhengding”; this journey takes in three of them.

hn_tieta.name: Iron Pagoda, Kaifeng
hn_tieta.yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hn_tieta.lede: Thirteen tiers of closely set eave lines slowly converge toward the top. The Iron Pagoda of Kaifeng is not cast in iron; its dark brown glazed bricks gave this Song pagoda the name it still bears.
facts: The Youguo Temple Pagoda was built in the 1st year of Huangyou in the Northern Song (1049); it is an octagonal thirteen-story pagoda of glazed brick.
Its surface is assembled from molded glazed bricks forming bracket sets, doors, windows and ornament, and the closely spaced eaves create a steady rhythm.
The plate is based mainly on a photograph of the whole pagoda, supplemented by close-ups of the ground story; it keeps the thirteen stories and does not reconstruct the earlier timber pagoda.

fotou.name: Fotou Temple, Pingshun
fotou.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · South bank of the Zhuozhang River · Chedang Village
fotou.lede: A small temple on the south bank of the Zhuozhang River, of which only a Northern Song Buddha hall remains. The hall is just three bays and 131 square meters, yet it fully preserves its Song beam frame, and the four walls inside carry Yuan paintings of the Twenty-Four Devas.
facts: Three bays wide and four rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the column-head bracket sets are four-puzuo, with one intercolumnar set.
The Yuan murals of the Twenty-Four Devas inside the hall are rare Yuan murals in the Zhuozhang River valley.
Together with Chunhua Temple, the Temple of the Holy Mother of the Nine Heavens and Huilong Temple, it is one of the Song and Jin temples in Pingshun.

baosheng.name: Baosheng Temple
baosheng.yearNote: 1050 is only an approximate Northern Song placement on the timeline, not an exact date of sculpting; the original 1961 national listing gives Northern Song, and the traditional attribution to Yang Huizhi of the Tang is not treated as settled authorship.
baosheng.lede: Arhats sit among undulating rocks and clouds, their lean faces and the folds of their broad robes still full of spirit. The surviving half of the sculpted wall at Baosheng Temple models figures and landscape together into the wall surface.
facts: Northern Song sculpture: The first national listing of 1961 dated the arhat sculptures of Baosheng Temple to the Northern Song; the claim that they were created by Yang Huizhi of the Tang is a traditional attribution.
Nine figures, half the set: Nine seated arhats survive, arranged irregularly across the sculpted wall, each with a different posture and expression; this drawing selects one of them.

Landscape in the wall: Rocks, clouds, caves and other features form the background of the sculpted wall, with the figures set into the landscape; the date of today's protective hall is counted separately.

hb_puli.name: Puli Temple Pagoda
hb_puli.sub: Square seven-story body and balcony eaves
hb_puli.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau clearly gives the 3rd year of Huangyou; the surviving seven stories are kept, and other pagodas of the same name are not confused with it.
hb_puli.lede: Puli Temple no longer exists, but its square brick pagoda still stands on a high stone platform in Lincheng. The thousand-Buddha carved bricks of the ground story and the band of standing figures on the second story give clear layering to the body as it tapers story by story.
facts: Date: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Relics Bureau dates it to the 3rd year of Huangyou in the Northern Song (1051); after repairs in the Jiajing and Wanli eras of the Ming, it still retains the form of a Song pagoda.

Stories: The body has seven stories, with a balcony platform below the second story, and from the third story up it approaches the multi-eaved type; in counting stories, the balcony eaves are not treated as a separate story.

Brick carving: The ground-story walls are inset with square carved bricks of Buddha images, and the second story has standing Buddhas and corner guardians; this drawing simplifies the dense ornament to keep the outline.

liaodi.name: Kaiyuan Temple Pagoda, Dingzhou
liaodi.era: Begun in the 4th year of Xianping · Completed in the 2nd year of Zhihe
liaodi.lede: Work began in the 4th year of Xianping under Emperor Zhenzong of Song (1001) and the pagoda was completed in the 2nd year of Zhihe (1055), fifty-four years in all. At 83.7 meters it is the tallest surviving brick pagoda in China; Dingzhou lay on the Song–Liao frontier, and from the top one could watch Khitan troop movements, hence the name “Liaodi” (gauging the enemy).
facts: An octagonal eleven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda, 83.7 m tall overall, tapering story by story, with stairs inside leading to the top.
Arched doors and false windows alternate on each story, and above the corbeled brick eaves rise balcony platforms, story after story, all in brick masonry.

In the 10th year of Guangxu in the Qing (1884), the northeast side of the body collapsed, leaving a gaping breach for more than a century until it was fully repaired at the end of the twentieth century; hence the saying of its “beauty of imperfection.”
captions: Line drawing · Octagonal, eleven stories

sd_pizhi.name: Pizhi Pagoda of Lingyan Temple, Jinan
sd_pizhi.sub: Octagonal, nine stories · Brick pagoda with twelve eaves
sd_pizhi.era: Rebuilt from the 5th year of Chunhua · Completed in the Jiayou era
sd_pizhi.yearNote: The pagoda inscription records rebuilding in the 5th year of Chunhua (994); image inscriptions of 1057–1058 provide the basis for completion in the Jiayou era, and 1057 is used as an approximate placement on the timeline.
sd_pizhi.lede: The Pizhi Pagoda stands amid the mountain scenery of Lingyan Temple, its octagonal body tapering story by story. The lower three stories each have two brick eaves and the upper six one each, so the nine-story body shows twelve tiers of eaves; an iron finial and fine chains close the outline at the top.
facts: The surviving pagoda is a Northern Song rebuilding. The pagoda inscription records that work began in the 5th year of Chunhua (994), and image inscriptions of the Jiayou era provide the basis for its completion date.
Octagonal with nine stories, double eaves on the lower three and single eaves on the upper six, twelve eaves in all; the brick eaves organize the outline with timber-style details.

The plate is drawn from daytime photographs of the surviving pagoda, keeping the gray-brown brick and stone, the dark eaves and some ochre-red door and window frames; it is not a reconstruction of historical paintwork.
captions: Octagonal, nine stories · Double eaves on the lower three

hb_yuquan.name: Iron Pagoda of Yuquan Temple
hb_yuquan.sub: Northern Song iron pagoda · Octagonal, thirteen tiers
hb_yuquan.yearNote: The iron body is dated by its casting in the 6th year of Jiayou in the Northern Song (1061), while the finial on top is a later Qing-dynasty replacement; the drawing distinguishes the components of the two periods and does not date the modern temple buildings to the Song along with it.
hb_yuquan.lede: Thirteen tiers of small eaves recede one by one, and the cast-iron bracket sets also imitate timber construction. The dark brown rust of the body differs from the finial added later at the top.
facts: Main subject: The thirteen-story iron pagoda of Yuquan Temple, Dangyang.

Date: The iron body is dated by its casting in the 6th year of Jiayou in the Northern Song (1061), while the finial on top is a later Qing-dynasty replacement; the drawing distinguishes the components of the two periods and does not date the modern temple buildings to the Song along with it.

Plate scope: The octagonal thirteen-story pavilion-style iron pagoda, with its complete finial and story-by-story taper; only the iron pagoda and its short base are drawn, not the tall retaining wall or the surrounding trees.

hn_xiangshan.name: Guanyin Pagoda of Xiangshan Temple
hn_xiangshan.era: Northern Song · Rebuilt in the 1st year of Xining
hn_xiangshan.yearNote: Takes the rebuilding in the 1st year of Xining in the Song recorded by the municipal culture and tourism bureau; the original founding date of the temple and pagoda is unknown, and repairs continued in later periods.
hn_xiangshan.lede: Two tiers of closely set small niches support an octagonal body that tapers story by story. The Song pagoda of Xiangshan Temple and the stele written by Cai Jing preserve the Guanyin faith of the Central Plains in brick and stone.
facts: Surviving Song pagoda: According to the Pingdingshan Municipal Culture and Tourism Bureau, the pagoda was rebuilt by imperial grant in 1068; it is octagonal with nine tiers and 33 m tall, and has been repaired repeatedly since.
Form: Corbeled brick eaves with balcony platforms above them; small Buddha niches line the lower walls and the upper stories have doorways, tapering tier by tier.
Scope drawn: The plate takes the body visible today from two photographs; the part of the ground story hidden by the neighboring hall is left blank, and the hidden base is not reconstructed.

sx_kaihua.name: Kaihua Temple, Gaoping
sx_kaihua.era: 6th year of Xining, Northern Song · Mahavira Hall
sx_kaihua.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mount Sheli, Wang Village, Chenqu Town
sx_kaihua.lede: The Mahavira Hall of Kaihua Temple spreads its broad eaves on the mountainside. The three-bay Song hall also preserves Northern Song painted decoration and sutra-tableau murals, so timber structure and the painters' brushwork meet in a single space.
facts: Xining-era Song hall: There is evidence for the construction of the Mahavira Hall in the 6th year of Xining (1073); it is three bays and six rafters, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and the eave columns of the central bay are square.
Song sutra tableaux: The murals inside were painted in the late Northern Song, about 1092–1096; their date is recorded separately from the 1073 timber structure.
Painted timberwork: Remnants of Song painted decoration still survive on the beam frame, and together with the murals they preserve the interior decorative scheme of a Northern Song monastery.

hb_jingzhouta.name: Relic Pagoda of Kaifu Temple
hb_jingzhouta.yearNote: The provincial bureau gives 1079 alongside the 3rd year of Yuanfeng, a clerical error in the date; it should be the 2nd year of Yuanfeng. 1079 is used, with the source checked against the stele record.
hb_jingzhouta.lede: The thirteen-story octagonal brick pagoda tapers story by story, its tiers of arched windows and bands of timber-style bracketed eaves raising a clear Song pagoda outline in the town of Jingzhou.
facts: Date: The surviving body is dated by its rebuilding in the 2nd year of Yuanfeng in the Northern Song (1079), with repairs in the Jin, the Ming and modern times.
Stories: An octagonal thirteen-story pavilion-style brick pagoda about 63.85 m tall, each story's elevation organized by arched doors and bands of timber-style bracketed eaves.
Finial: The top retains an iron finial net and stacked bronze gourds; the national listing name is the Relic Pagoda of Kaifu Temple, and it is popularly called the Jingzhou Pagoda.

Thirteen-story octagonal body with iron finial net and bronze gourds

sh_fangta.name: Pagoda of Xingshengjiao Temple, Songjiang
sh_fangta.sub: Square Pagoda Park · Nine-story square pagoda
sh_fangta.yearNote: Uses the construction range of 1068–1093 recorded in the Songjiang Yearbook 2019; 1080 is used only as an approximate placement on the timeline, not as a confirmed completion year. The temple's founding in 949 is recorded separately from the Northern Song construction of the pagoda.
sh_fangta.lede: On the square body, nine tiers of timber eaves spread like layered wings. Xingshengjiao Temple no longer has its original extent, but this Northern Song brick-and-timber pagoda still stands with slender proportions in the old town of Songjiang, where locals simply call it the “Square Pagoda.”
facts: Xingshengjiao Temple was founded in the 2nd year of Qianyou in the Later Han of the Five Dynasties (949), while the pagoda was built in the Xining and Yuanyou eras of the Northern Song (1068–1093); the two are not conflated as one date.

The pagoda is square in plan and of brick-and-timber construction, a nine-story pavilion-style pagoda about 42.65 m tall overall; the brick walls are divided into three bays by timber-style columns, with a cusped kunmen opening in the middle.

Each story has timber waist eaves, a balcony platform and railings, and an iron finial stands at the top. It has been repaired through the Yuan, Ming, Qing and modern times, and the plate shows its surviving form.
captions: Square, nine stories · Brick-and-timber pagoda
Northern Song · Xining and Yuanyou eras

qinglian.name: Qinglian Temple, Jincheng
qinglian.sub: Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple
qinglian.lede: On the slopes of Mount Xiashi beside the Dan River, Qinglian Temple is divided into upper and lower compounds. Stone inscriptions in the Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple record the 4th year of Yuanyou in the Northern Song; the small three-bay hall stands on a high platform, its stone columns carrying deep eaves. Farther down the mountain, the Lower Temple still preserves Tang painted sculptures.
facts: The Sakyamuni Hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; an inscription on the stone door frame provides the basis for dating it to the 4th year of Yuanyou in the Northern Song (1089).

Square chamfered stone columns carry five-puzuo bracket sets with one projecting arm and one descending cantilever, and there are no intercolumnar sets; the central bay has a door and the two side bays have vertical-bar windows.

The Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple holds four Song sculptures, and the Maitreya Hall of the Lower Temple six Tang sculptures. In one temple, upper and lower, timber structures and painted sculptures each preserve the appearance of different dynasties.

Single-eaved hip-and-gable · 4th year of Yuanyou, Northern Song

sx_wubian.name: Wubian Temple, Taigu
sx_wubian.sub: White Pagoda · Ancient City of Taigu
sx_wubian.lede: The White Pagoda in the ancient city of Taigu tapers gently, its octagonal body imitating a pavilion with brick-carved bracket sets, projecting eaves and balcony platforms. The Song pagoda and the later rebuilt temple together form an old landmark on the city skyline.
facts: Yuanyou-era White Pagoda: The surviving White Pagoda was built in the 5th year of Yuanyou in the Northern Song, that is, 1090; the legend of the temple's founding in the Western Jin cannot be taken as the date of the pagoda.

Seven outside, nine inside: The pagoda is an octagonal pavilion-style pagoda; conservation sources record seven stories on the outside and nine inside, with brick-carved eaves and platforms imitating timber bracket sets.
History of temple and pagoda: The temple was repaired in the Ming and Qing, and its halls were rebuilt after a late-Qing fire; the plate takes only the White Pagoda, which preserves the Song style.

hn_chongfa.name: Chongfa Temple Pagoda
hn_chongfa.sub: A Song pagoda raised on tiers of balcony platforms and lotus petals
hn_chongfa.yearNote: Dated by the pagoda's completion in 1098; a foundation's materials give 1093 for the building of the underground crypt and 1095 for the start of the body. Some secondary sources wrongly equate 1093 with the 1st year of Shaosheng; this erroneous conversion is not adopted.
hn_chongfa.lede: The Chongfa Temple Pagoda rises tier upon tier in the old city of Yongcheng. The octagonal nine-story brick pagoda imitates a timber pavilion, tracing the rhythm of a Song pagoda body with closely set eaves and balcony platforms.
facts: Song body: The pagoda was completed in the 5th year of Shaosheng in the Northern Song (1098); the temple's history is earlier than this surviving pagoda.
Octagonal, nine stories: The pagoda is 34.6 m tall, each story with projecting eaves, a balcony platform, doors and windows; eaves and platforms are counted separately, and the body has nine stories.
Brick imitating timber: The pagoda renders columns, bracket sets and railings in brickwork, and inside it preserves glazed Buddha-image bricks and other components; it was repaired in later periods.

anyue.name: Anyue Rock Carvings
anyue.lede: One knee raised, one hand resting lightly on the stone platform: seated at ease in the posture of royal ease, the Water-Moon Guanyin of Pilu Cave leaves the composure of Song stone carving on the rock face.
facts: Principal figure drawn: The Water-Moon Guanyin of Pilu Cave, popularly called the Purple Bamboo Guanyin; this is not a panorama of the Anyue rock carvings.
Royal ease: The right knee is raised with the right hand hanging over it; the left hand rests on the platform and the left foot hangs down onto the lotus pedestal, in a relaxed posture.

Treasures of the two Songs: The Pilu Cave sculptures were carved during the Northern and Southern Song, with work continuing into the Ming and Qing; they were listed in the 5th batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level in 2001.

hn_xiaoshang.name: Xiaoshang Bridge
hn_xiaoshang.era: Song main structure · Repairs over the centuries
hn_xiaoshang.yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate ordering point for the surviving Song main structure. The county gazetteer records the bridge as built in the 4th year of Kaihuang in the Sui; Mao Yisheng considered a founding in the early Sui credible but the form of the surviving bridge still open to study, and Luo Zhewen judged the style and carving of the surviving bridge body to be Song remains.
hn_xiaoshang.lede: A low, gentle main arch has one small spandrel arch opened in each shoulder. The red-stone bridge body and balustrade panels of many periods together record the building and repair of the bridge over the Xiaoshang River.
facts: Distinguishing dates: The founding of the bridge is traditionally traced to the Sui; Luo Zhewen judged the architectural style and surface carving of the surviving main structure to be Song remains.
Structure: The bridge is 21.3 m long and 6.45 m wide, with a segmental main arch flanked by one small spandrel arch on each side, making it an open-spandrel stone arch bridge.
Repairs over time: Repairs in 1994–1995 cleaned and reset many kinds of components; the present balustrade panels and posts include pieces from the Song, Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing periods.

sn_daqin.name: Daqin Temple Pagoda, Zhouzhi
sn_daqin.era: Surviving pagoda dated to the Song
sn_daqin.yearNote: The 6th batch of the national listing places the surviving Daqin Temple Pagoda in the Song; 1100 is only an approximate Song ordering point. Discussions of the temple's origins or of the Church of the East do not prove that today's pagoda was built in the Tang.
sn_daqin.lede: The seven-story octagonal brick body leans slightly, its corbeled eaves narrowing tier by tier. The present dating of the Daqin Temple Pagoda should be considered separately from the temple's earlier origins; the plate records only the pagoda as it stands today.
facts: Dating: The 6th batch of the national listing of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level places it in the Song; the exact year of construction is undetermined.
Form: An octagonal seven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda; the surviving body leans slightly.
Historical distinction: Discussions of the temple's origins and its links with the Church of the East are not taken directly as a Tang date for the surviving pagoda.

jinci.name: Jinci Temple
jinci.era: Renovated in the 1st year of Chongning, Northern Song
jinci.lede: Beneath two tiers of flying eaves, eight carved wooden dragons coil around the front columns. With its deep, broad colonnade and layered bracket sets, the Hall of the Holy Mother preserves the spatial order of a Northern Song hall.
facts: Seven bays, double eaves: The Hall of the Holy Mother is seven bays wide and six bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
Surrounding peristyle: A gallery runs all around the outside of the hall, the front gallery especially deep and broad; the eight front eave columns are decorated with carved coiling dragons.

Date of renovation: Renovated in the 1st year of Chongning in the Northern Song (1102), when the layout of the surviving main structure took shape; the plate shows the Hall of the Holy Mother and excludes the Flying Bridge over the Fish Pond.

sx_faxing.name: Faxing Temple, Zhangzi
sx_faxing.era: Northern Song · Song sculpture of the 1st year of Zhenghe
sx_faxing.yearNote: Takes 1111, the year the central Song sculpture of Sakyamuni drawn here was made, not the founding year of the temple or the 1081 enlargement of the Yuanjue Hall. The temple was moved to its present site in 1984–1996, and the painted sculptures have been repaired and redecorated over the centuries; the replica outer eaves of the present hall are not taken as original fabric of 1081.
sx_faxing.place: Shanxi · Zhangzi · Mount Cuiyun, Cilin Town
sx_faxing.lede: At the center of the Yuanjue Hall, the seated Sakyamuni sits cross-legged on a lotus throne, its drapery folds and gestures still keeping the composure of Song sculpture. The plate draws only the principal figure and its pedestal as they are now, recording this group of painted sculptures preserved through the temple's relocation.
facts: Date of the Song sculptures: The Song sculptures in the hall are dated 1111, and records name the sculptor Feng Zongben and the painters Chen Daorong and Lü Rong; this drawing takes only the central Sakyamuni.

Hall and figures dated separately: The Yuanjue Hall was dismantled and enlarged in 1081, before the Song sculptures were made. The hall, the sculptures and later redecoration each have their own dates.

Relocation and protection: The temple was moved to Mount Cuiyun in 1984–1996; the outer eaves of the Yuanjue Hall were reproduced conjecturally from surviving Northern Song structures, so today's entire exterior cannot be regarded as original Song fabric.

hn_chuzu.name: First Patriarch Hermitage of Shaolin Temple
hn_chuzu.sub: Front of the Main Hall of the First Patriarch Hermitage
hn_chuzu.yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hn_chuzu.lede: Stone columns support deep timber eaves, and in just three bays the Main Hall of the First Patriarch Hermitage preserves the layers of Song construction. The carved column shafts and massive bracket sets give this hermitage commemorating Bodhidharma a distinctive appearance.
facts: The Main Hall was built in the 7th year of Xuanhe in the Northern Song (1125) and belongs to the Shaolin Temple building group of the Dengfeng “Center of Heaven and Earth” World Heritage Site.
Three bays with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; carved stone columns support the timber structure, and the column-head bracket sets are prominent in scale.

The plate takes the front elevation as its subject, with the roof checked against a view from another angle; only the First Patriarch Hermitage is included, and the Shaolin Pagoda Forest is not split off and counted separately.

liuhe.name: Liuhe Pagoda, Hangzhou
liuhe.era: Rebuilt in the 26th year of Shaoxing, Southern Song
liuhe.lede: The King of Wuyue built it in the 3rd year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (970) to subdue the tidal bore of the Qiantang River; the surviving brick body was rebuilt in the 26th year of Shaoxing in the Southern Song (1156) and completed in the 1st year of Longxing (1163). The thirteen tiers of timber eaves on the outside were added in the 25th year of Guangxu in the Qing (1899).
facts: Mixed brick and timber, octagonal, 59.89 m tall overall; the brick body has seven stories and the exterior thirteen tiers of eaves — “thirteen outside, seven inside” — with balcony railings around each story.

The brick carvings of flowers, birds and beasts on the Sumeru plinths inside the pagoda match the patterns recorded in the Yingzao Fashi (Treatise on Architectural Methods), making them physical evidence for the study of Song architecture.
In 1934 Liang Sicheng drew up a “slimming” plan for the pagoda, removing the Guangxu-era timber eaves to restore the original appearance of the Song pagoda; it was never carried out.

xuanmiao.name: Sanqing Hall of Xuanmiao Temple
xuanmiao.sub: Suzhou · Nine-bay Southern Song main hall
xuanmiao.lede: The Sanqing Hall of Xuanmiao Temple raises two tiers of hip-and-gable eaves over a broad nine-bay body, and the ridge-end ornaments and the three-halberd (pingsheng sanji) ornament on its long ridge draw the silhouette skyward. This Southern Song hall remains an early timber structure of striking scale in the old city of Suzhou.
facts: The Sanqing Hall was rebuilt in the 6th year of Chunxi in the Southern Song (1179); this date must not be confused with the original founding of Xuanmiao Temple.
The hall is nine bays wide and six bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and stands on a broad platform.
The plate isolates the Sanqing Hall, keeping its double eaves and long-ridge silhouette, and leaves out the temple's front gate and the incense-burner pavilion before the hall.

dazu.name: Dazu Rock Carvings
dazu.era: Southern Song, Chunxi to Chunyou eras
dazu.lede: On the cliff face of Baodingshan, Guanyin's arms spread out in every direction. The principal figure lowers her gaze with palms joined, and the dense array of hand gestures and ritual implements condenses the conception of Southern Song craftsmen into a single niche.
facts: Detail shown: The principal figure of the Thousand-Armed Guanyin in Niche 8 at Dafowan, Baodingshan, with the adjacent arms; not a view of the whole niche.
Southern Song work: The figures were carved between the Chunxi and Chunyou eras and belong to the Baodingshan grottoes, whose construction was directed by Zhao Zhifeng.
Radiating composition: The whole niche occupies about 88 square meters of cliff face; the arms spread to both sides and upward, each hand holding an object.
captions: Dazu Rock Carvings · Thousand-Armed Guanyin at Baodingshan
Southern Song · Detail of the principal figure and radiating arms

feilaifeng.name: Feilai Feng Grottoes
feilaifeng.yearNote: 1200 is only an approximate timeline position for the traditional Southern Song dating, not the year of carving. The niche has no dated inscription, and some research proposes an early Yuan date; the year 966 is not used to impose a date.
feilaifeng.lede: Beside Lengquan Creek, the Budai Maitreya laughs openly as he leans on his cloth sack, while the arhats in the rock niche each wear their own expression. Niche 68 brings Buddhist sculpture into vivid human moods and is the most familiar face of Feilai Feng.
facts: One niche, many figures: The complete Niche 68 centers on the Budai Maitreya, with nine arhats ranged on each side; this plate shows only the principal figure and the four nearest arhats.

Sack and prayer beads: The principal figure, chest and belly bare, rests his right hand on the sack and holds prayer beads in his left, expressing devotion to Maitreya through the image of the monk Budai.

Disputed date: Popular accounts adopt a Southern Song date, while some research argues for the early Yuan; the niche bears no exact dated inscription, and no single year can stand for the carvings of the whole hill.
captions: Feilai Feng Niche 68 · Budai Maitreya and adjacent arhats (detail)
Southern Song (traditional dating; an early Yuan date is also proposed)

zijinan.name: Zijin'an Temple
zijinan.yearNote: 1200 is only an approximate timeline placement within the Song tradition of arhat art, not an exact year of sculpting; the heritage listing dates the statues to the Song–Ming, and Lei Chao and his wife are the traditionally attributed sculptors.
zijinan.lede: Tucked away in a hollow of Dongshan, sixteen arhats each have their own expression and pose. Tilted heads, lowered eyes and lightly interlaced fingers give the quiet clay figures the liveliness of everyday people.
facts: Song–Ming statues: The heritage listing dates the arhat statues of Zijin'an to the Song through Ming; they are traditionally said to be the work of Lei Chao and his wife in the Southern Song, but the authorship is unsettled.
Sixteen arhats: The arhats line both sides of the hall, differing in drapery, sitting posture and expression; this plate shows the upper body of the Venerable Panthaka.
Repairs through the ages: The statues have been repaired over time, and what is seen today includes painting and repairs from different periods; the surviving hall is dated separately.
captions: Zijin'an · Venerable Panthaka (upper body, detail)
Song–Ming · Repaired over successive periods

feiying.name: Feiying Pagoda
feiying.lede: The outer pagoda of Feiying Pagoda wraps an inner stone pagoda in seven octagonal stories of timber eaves, its broad ground-floor gallery eave supporting a body that tapers story by story. Railings between the stories and a slender finial trace a landmark silhouette of the old city of Huzhou.
facts: The plate focuses on the outer pagoda, entered as a Southern Song rebuilding; sources give two dates for the rebuilding, the Jiatai era and the beginning of the Duanping era, so no single year is forced.
The outer pagoda is a seven-story octagonal pavilion-style pagoda of brick and timber that encloses a freestanding stone pagoda, forming the famous “pagoda within a pagoda.”

It has been repaired many times over the centuries; the conservation work of 1982–1987 retained its mixed brick-and-timber structure, and repair dates must not be taken as the pagoda's original construction date.

Full elevation · Rebuilt in the Southern Song

fj_renshou.name: Renshou Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
fj_renshou.sub: West pagoda · Octagonal five-story stone pagoda
fj_renshou.era: 1st year of Shaoding to 1st year of Jiaxi
fj_renshou.yearNote: The surviving stone pagoda was built in 1228–1237, and the completion year 1237 is used; the Five Dynasties timber pagoda was its predecessor and is not used as the date of the surviving structure.
fj_renshou.place: Fujian · Quanzhou · West Pagoda Court of Kaiyuan Temple
fj_renshou.lede: Completed earlier than the east pagoda, the west pagoda raises a slender finial on five stone stories. Renshou Pagoda stands alongside Zhenguo Pagoda, yet each has its own character in its bracket sets and relief subjects.
facts: Surviving structure: Renshou Pagoda (the west pagoda) was rebuilt as a stone pagoda in 1228–1237, in the Southern Song.

Alike yet different: Like the east pagoda it is octagonal with five stories; the third, fourth and fifth stories have fewer intercolumnar bracket sets, and the Sumeru plinth favors floral and animal motifs.
Scope of the plate: Only the west pagoda is drawn, in full; it is not combined with the east pagoda or with the Mahavira Hall, which already has an entry.

fj_zhenguo.name: Zhenguo Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
fj_zhenguo.sub: East pagoda · Octagonal five-story stone pagoda
fj_zhenguo.era: 2nd year of Jiaxi to 10th year of Chunyou
fj_zhenguo.yearNote: The year used is 1250, the completion of the surviving granite pagoda; 865 marks the founding of the timber pagoda, and the brick pagoda of 1227 is not the surviving five-story stone pagoda.
fj_zhenguo.place: Fujian · Quanzhou · East Pagoda Court of Kaiyuan Temple
fj_zhenguo.lede: Five stone eaves unfold outward tier upon tier, their imitation-timber bracket sets carved from granite. Completed in the Southern Song, the east pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple still sets Quanzhou's stone-carving tradition against the skyline of West Street.
facts: Surviving structure: Zhenguo Pagoda (the east pagoda) was rebuilt as a granite pagoda in 1238–1250; it is not the original Tang timber pagoda.
Form: An octagonal five-story pavilion-style pagoda whose stone columns, bracket sets, balcony platforms and eaves imitate timber architecture; reliefs of Buddhist figures are set into the walls.
Separate entries: The plate shows only the east pagoda; Renshou Pagoda to the west and the Mahavira Hall each keep their own entries.

baziqiao.name: Bazi Bridge
baziqiao.sub: Three streets, three rivers · Ancient stone-beam bridge
baziqiao.yearNote: 1256 is the rebuilding year recorded in local gazetteers, and there was a further repair in 1783; what is seen today includes repairs from many periods, and not every stone member is an original of 1256.
baziqiao.lede: Stone steps rise along the riverbanks and meet above the waterway. With a single stone-beam span and flights of steps running in several directions, Bazi Bridge gathers up the crisscrossing streets and rivers of old Shaoxing.
facts: Baoyou rebuilding: The bridge was first built before the Jiatai era of the Southern Song, rebuilt in the winter of the 4th year of Baoyou (1256), and repaired again in the 48th year of Qianlong in the Qing.

Stone beams over the river: The main bridge spans the waterway with stone beams laid side by side, with a clear span of about 4.5 m at the main opening; its rectangular beam opening differs from the form of a round arch bridge.

Three streets, three rivers: The bridge stands where three streets and three rivers cross; its stone steps connect to the banks in different directions, and its name comes from a layout splayed like the Chinese character ba, “eight.”
captions: Bazi Bridge · South stone-beam span and riverside steps
Southern Song · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Baoyou (1256)

geyuan.name: Geyuan Temple, Laiyuan
geyuan.lede: In the county town of Laiyuan, the Manjushri Hall of Geyuan Temple retains the bearing of Liao timber architecture with its broad three-bay facade and low, gently pitched hip-and-gable roof. Massive bracket sets under the eaves meet ancient latticed windows; beyond the timber frame, even the small door and window fittings carry on a craft a thousand years old.
facts: The Manjushri Hall is a Liao timber structure, usually dated in museum and heritage sources to the 16th year of Yingli in the Liao (966); it was repaired in the Yuan and Ming.
It is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the interior uses the reduced-column method, with only two interior columns.
Geyuan Temple was listed in 1996 in the fourth batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level; the Manjushri Hall preserves some Liao latticed doors and windows.

dule.name: Dule Temple, Tianjin
dule.lede: In the old town of Jizhou, the Guanyin Pavilion spreads its facade with two deep tiers of eaves and a balcony platform. A concealed mezzanine inside ties beams and columns together, and the space of the pavilion unfolds around a towering Guanyin statue.
facts: The surviving Guanyin Pavilion was rebuilt in the 2nd year of Tonghe in the Liao (984) and, together with the Main Gate, preserves the forms of Liao timber construction.
The Guanyin Pavilion is five bays wide and four bays deep; it appears two-storied from outside but has three levels inside, including a concealed mezzanine.
The upper level has inner and outer balcony galleries, and beams, tie-beams and bracket sets bind the two rings of columns into a single whole.
captions: Front of the Guanyin Pavilion, Dule Temple · Redrawn from photographs of the site
Rebuilt in the 2nd year of Tonghe, Liao (984) · Five bays wide; two stories outside, three levels inside

jl_nongan.name: Nong'an Liao Pagoda
jl_nongan.yearNote: 1000 is only a sorting point. Jilin local gazetteer sources give a range of 983–1030; the 1023 date, which has problems with mixed-up reign names, is not taken as the exact year of construction.
jl_nongan.place: Jilin · Nong'an · Ancient City of Huanglong Prefecture
jl_nongan.lede: In the town of Nong'an, the Liao pagoda tapers upward with a plain brick shaft and closely spaced bands of eaves. It is both a Liao survival and a present appearance left by modern repairs, and both are recorded in the source notes for the same drawing.
facts: An octagonal thirteen-story multi-eaved brick pagoda; the plate keeps its relatively plain shaft and does not transplant the wall-covering Buddha figures of the Liaoyang White Pagoda.
Local gazetteers adopt a Liao construction range; its position on the timeline is approximate, not a precise completion date.
Its present appearance has been shaped by modern repairs; full-view, eave and aerial photographs were used respectively to check proportions and details.

kaishan.name: Kaishan Temple, Gaobeidian
kaishan.lede: One of the eight surviving Liao timber buildings. It is not large, yet it uses the full range of Liao techniques: reduced and shifted columns leave only four columns inside the hall, and the massive bracket sets reach nearly one-third of the column height.
facts: Five bays wide (25.8 m), three bays deep (14.5 m) and 12.08 m high, with a single-eaved hipped roof.

Thirty bracket sets run around the eave columns: twelve on column heads, fourteen intercolumnar and four at the corners; the bracket sets are 1.41 m tall overall, a ratio of 1 : 3.41 to the column height.
The interior uses the reduced-column and shifted-column methods, with only four columns standing, which leaves the space open.

fengguo.name: Fengguo Temple, Yi County
fengguo.place: Liaoning · Jinzhou · Old town of Yi County
fengguo.lede: In the old town of Yi County, the Mahavira Hall of Fengguo Temple spreads its nine-bay facade beneath a single expansive hipped roof. Seven Liao painted clay Buddha statues sit side by side inside, facing the flying apsaras painted on the beam frame; timber structure, sculpture and painting together preserve the building practice of the eleventh century.
facts: Fengguo Temple was founded in the 9th year of Kaitai in the Liao (1020); its main surviving structure, the Mahavira Hall, is a Liao building.
The Mahavira Hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep, with a single-eaved hipped roof; doors open in the central seven bays of the front.

It was listed in 1961 in the first batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level; the hall preserves seven Liao painted clay Buddha statues and Liao paintings on the beam frame.

zhuozhou.name: Liao Twin Pagodas of Zhuozhou
zhuozhou.sub: Yunju Temple Pagoda · Zhidu Temple Pagoda
zhuozhou.lede: Two Liao pagodas face each other north and south, freezing the columns, windows and bracket sets of timber pavilions in brick. The north pagoda has six stories and the south five, and their differing silhouettes form the landmark of old Zhuozhou.
facts: To the north is the Yunju Temple Pagoda, of six stories; to the south the Zhidu Temple Pagoda, of five. Both are octagonal pavilion-style brick pagodas imitating timber construction.

The Zhidu Temple Pagoda was built in the 11th year of Taiping in the Liao (1031) and is 44 m tall; each cardinal face has an arched doorway, and each diagonal face a false window with vertical mullions.

Studies differ on the date of the Yunju Temple Pagoda, proposing the Chongxi era, the 8th year of Da'an and others; this entry keeps the general label of the 11th century and does not present a disputed year as settled.
captions: Yunju Temple Pagoda · Zhidu Temple Pagoda

huayan.name: Huayan Temple
huayan.sub: Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall · Mahavira Hall
huayan.lede: The Khitans worshipped the sun, so the whole monastery faces east. The Liao Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall houses wall-mounted sutra cabinets and a celestial palace pavilion, while the Mahavira Hall, rebuilt under the Jin, is the largest of the surviving Liao and Jin Buddhist halls.
facts: The Mahavira Hall (rebuilt in the 3rd year of Tianjuan in the Jin, 1140) is nine bays and fifty-three meters wide and stands on a 4 m high platform; the ridge-end ornaments on its main ridge are 4.5 m tall, the largest in historic Chinese architecture.

The Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall (7th year of Chongxi in the Liao, 1038) holds thirty-eight bays of wall-mounted sutra cabinets, with a “celestial palace pavilion” at the center joined by an arched bridge, which Liang Sicheng praised as “the only one of its kind in the land.”
The Liao clay bodhisattva in the hall, with palms joined and teeth showing, was called the “Venus of the East” by Zheng Zhenduo.

qingzhou.name: Qingzhou White Pagoda
qingzhou.sub: Liao city of Qingzhou · Sakyamuni Buddha Relic Pagoda
qingzhou.lede: The White Pagoda of the Liao city of Qingzhou stands on the grassland, its seven-story body imitating timber in brick. Doors and windows, reliefs of heavenly kings and tier upon tier of bracket sets interweave, preserving the refined and ornate appearance of a Khitan Buddhist pagoda.
facts: Begun in the 16th year of Chongxi (1047) and completed in the 18th year of Chongxi (1049).
An octagonal seven-story pavilion-style pagoda; carved brick bracket sets support timber eave rafters.
It stands in the northwest of the site of the Liao city of Qingzhou and is also called the Sakyamuni Buddha Relic Pagoda.
captions: Liao Qingzhou White Pagoda
Octagonal, seven stories; north elevation

huanghuatan.name: Huanghuatan Pagoda
huanghuatan.lede: Huanghuatan Pagoda stands on Xita Hill beside the Daling River, facing the site of the Liao city of Jianzhou across the fields. Its octagonal body carries thirteen tiers of close-set eaves, and the flower baskets and flying apsaras above the arched doorways still show the delicacy of Liao brick carving.
facts: The pagoda is in Dapingfang Town, Longcheng District, Chaoyang, Liaoning; its main body is Liao, and the exact year of construction is undetermined.
The octagonal brick pagoda consists of a high platform, a double Sumeru plinth, the shaft and thirteen tiers of close-set eaves.
Repairs were completed and the finial re-erected in 2012; this plate depicts the present, post-repair appearance from 2023 photographs of the site.

yingxian.name: Yingxian Wooden Pagoda
yingxian.lede: Sixty-seven meters, all timber, nine hundred seventy years. It is the tallest and oldest surviving wooden pagoda in the world; it has come through repeated earthquakes and shelling and still stands beside the Sanggan River.
facts: Octagonal, with five stories and six eaves; five visible stories and four concealed mezzanines make nine levels in all, and a peripheral aisle surrounds the ground floor, giving six tiers of eaves outside.
The pagoda uses fifty-four kinds of bracket sets and has been called a “museum of bracket sets”; the stories are joined by balcony platforms and taper level by level.
The seated Sakyamuni on the ground floor is eleven meters tall; in 1974 a Liao Buddha-tooth relic and sutra scrolls were found inside Buddha statues in the pagoda.
It stands 67.31 m tall overall and is ranked with the Leaning Tower of Pisa in Italy and the Eiffel Tower in France as one of the “three wondrous towers of the world.”

hb_nanansi.name: Nan'an Temple Pagoda
hb_nanansi.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau presumes a Liao date from its form; 1100 serves only as an approximate Liao value for sorting. 1706 marks the Qing encasing of the base and repairs, and in 1986 eave corners partly damaged by shelling were repaired.
hb_nanansi.lede: Nan'an Temple Pagoda rises among the rooftops of the old town of Yuzhou. A tall first story stands on an upturned-lotus base, thirteen close-set eaves taper gently, and an iron finial extends the silhouette into the sky.
facts: Dating: The surviving octagonal multi-eaved brick pagoda is dated to the Liao by its form; the exact year of founding is unknown, and this guide uses an approximate value.

Thirteen eaves: The pagoda is solid; its first story is relatively tall, with false doors on the four cardinal faces and blind windows on the four diagonal faces, and above it thirteen brick eaves are closely stacked.
Layers of repair: The present base was encased in the 45th year of Kangxi in the Qing (1706), and parts of the eave corners on the east side damaged by shelling were repaired in 1986.

tj_jizhou_baita.name: White Pagoda of Jixian, Tianjin
tj_jizhou_baita.yearNote: The national listing dates it to the Liao through Qing. 1100 is only an approximate timeline placement for the Liao form and does not represent the exact year of founding, rebuilding or making of all surviving members; the plate shows the present appearance after repairs over the centuries.
tj_jizhou_baita.lede: An octagonal lower section and three low tiers of eaves support a rounded inverted-bowl body, and a finial of tapering rings extends the silhouette above. Traces of pale plaster remain between the gray bricks, and this White Pagoda preserves a meeting of two forms, the pavilion and the stupa.
facts: The Tianjin register of national protected sites records the date of the Jixian White Pagoda as Liao to Qing; its present appearance includes later repairs, and no single early date sums up the whole pagoda.

The plate keeps the octagonal lower section, three low tiers of eaves, inverted-bowl body and ringed finial, distinguishing it from an ordinary multi-eaved pagoda or a purely Tibetan-style white stupa.
The colored plate keeps the gray brick, mottled pale-gray plaster, dark red wooden doors and darker finial, rather than repainting it as an all-white new pagoda.

ln_liaoyang.name: Liaoyang White Pagoda
ln_liaoyang.yearNote: 1100 is only a sorting position for the traditional Liao dating, not an exact construction year; neither the founding legends nor the competing Liao and Jin theories are used to force a completion year.
ln_liaoyang.lede: Thirteen tiers of close-set eaves taper step by step, and the broad first story of the shaft is filled with Buddhist niches and figures. The name White Pagoda is not an instruction to paint the masonry pure white; the colored plate keeps the gray-brown weathered surface of its present state.
facts: Octagonal with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves; the first story of the shaft has Buddhist reliefs and imitation-timber decoration.
Liaoyang Museum sources adopt a Liao date; the exact year of construction is unknown, and this entry does not use disputed precise dates.
The lower part in the reference photographs is screened by plants, so the plate gives only a conservative low platform and does not invent an unverified massive stepped terrace.

ln_chongxing.name: Twin Pagodas of Chongxing Temple
ln_chongxing.sub: West and east pagodas · Thirteen eaves each
ln_chongxing.yearNote: 1100 is an approximate sorting point for the late Liao; heritage sources conjecture the reigns of Emperors Daozong to Tianzuo, and this does not mean it was definitely built in 1100.
ln_chongxing.lede: Two octagonal brick pagodas stand side by side, each with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves, yet they are not copy-and-paste replicas of one pagoda. The west pagoda is slightly lower, and the reliefs and remaining color on each shaft follow two separate site photographs.
facts: Both pagodas are octagonal with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves; the first story of each shaft is decorated with Buddhist niches, attendant figures, flying apsaras and more.
Heritage sources conjecture construction in the late Liao; the present appearance of both the east and west pagodas also reflects later repairs.
The plate arranges photographs of the two individual pagodas as a side-by-side comparison and is not a basis for their actual spacing on site or measured proportions.

tianning.name: Tianning Temple Pagoda, Beijing
tianning.lede: Built in the 9th to 10th years of Tianqing in the Liao (1119–1120), octagonal with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves and 57.8 m tall overall, it is the oldest above-ground structure in Beijing. Above the Sumeru plinth, three tiers of upturned lotus petals support the tall shaft, and higher still thirteen eaves press one upon another, drawing ever tighter.
facts: The eight faces of the shaft: arched doorways on the four cardinal faces, flanked by brick-carved vajra guardians and bodhisattvas; windows with vertical mullions on the four diagonal faces.
All thirteen tiers of close-set eaves rest on brick bracket sets imitating timber, and the spacing between eaves shortens level by level; Liang Sicheng said it had “a rich musical rhythm.”
A solid brick pagoda that cannot be climbed; it is the only Liao building within the Liao Southern Capital to survive to the present.

huilong.name: Huilong Temple
huilong.sub: Main hall · South bank of the Zhuozhang River
huilong.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
huilong.lede: In Houbi Village on the south bank of the Zhuozhang River, all that remains of Huilong Temple is a three-bay main hall. Two octagonal stone columns stand in the front porch, and a low, gently pitched overhanging gable roof reaches out to either side; with no tall pagoda or multistory halls, the weight of early timber construction rests among the few bracket sets beneath the eaves.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and four rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; two octagonal stone columns stand in the central bay of the front eave, the supports at either side are enclosed in the walls, and behind are one door and two windows.
No plate beam (pupaifang) is laid over the column heads, and the architraves do not project beyond the corner columns, preserving archaic structural features.

The national listing gives the date as Jin; other accounts, citing form and scientific dating, give the late Northern Song to early Jin. There is as yet no exact construction date, and the timeline gives only an approximate placement at the Song–Jin transition.

shanhua.name: Shanhua Temple
shanhua.sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of the Three Sages · Puxian Pavilion
shanhua.lede: The Liao Mahavira Hall and the Jin Hall of the Three Sages, Main Gate and Puxian Pavilion line up intact along a single central axis; this is the largest and most completely laid-out Liao–Jin monastery to survive.
facts: The Mahavira Hall is a Liao structure, seven bays wide; inside are thirty-three Liao and Jin painted clay statues, with the Buddhas of the Five Directions seated at the center and the Twenty-Four Devas ranged on both sides.

The Hall of the Three Sages (6th year of Tianhui to 3rd year of Huangtong in the Jin, 1128–1143) uses reduced-column construction, and its huge diagonal brackets open layer upon layer like a blossoming flower.
The Puxian Pavilion is a two-story Jin pavilion with a balcony platform, balustrade and hip-and-gable roof, one of the few examples for the study of Liao–Jin pavilions.

sx_xixi_erxian.name: Erxian Temple of Xixi, Lingchuan
sx_xixi_erxian.sub: Rear hall · Cult of the Two Immortals
sx_xixi_erxian.yearNote: 1142 is the year a stele records for the start of rebuilding, not the precise completion year of the rear hall; the surviving main structure is dated by its Jin style.
sx_xixi_erxian.place: Shanxi · Lingchuan · West of Lingchang Village, Chongwen Town
sx_xixi_erxian.lede: The rear hall of the Xixi Erxian Temple carries its broad eaves on a three-bay front porch, with bracket sets running continuously beneath. The main hall and the dressing towers on either side retain Jin forms and also bear the architectural imprint of the cult of the Two Immortals in southeastern Shanxi.
facts: Jin rear hall: A stele records that rebuilding began in 1142; the surviving main hall and dressing towers retain a Jin style, while most of the temple's other buildings are Ming and Qing.
Three bays, six rafters: The rear hall sits on a stone platform, three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and keeps a front porch before its doors.

Cult of the Two Immortals: The temple is dedicated to the Two Immortals, and two-story, triple-eaved dressing towers stand on either side of the main hall; this plate redraws only the front of the rear hall.

sx_chongfu.name: Chongfu Temple, Shuozhou
sx_chongfu.yearNote: The construction date of the surviving Amitabha Hall is used; the paintings and statues inside the hall and the later repairs belong to separate phases.
sx_chongfu.lede: A broad, gently pitched roof rests on a seven-bay grid of columns, with widely spaced yet massive bracket sets beneath the eaves. The Amitabha Hall of Chongfu Temple preserves Jin timber construction together with painted sculpture and murals in a single space.
facts: The Amitabha Hall was built in the 3rd year of Huangtong in the Jin (1143); the plate is dated by the surviving hall.
Seven bays wide and four bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; eight columns across the front define a clear column grid.
This plate shows the front of the Amitabha Hall, leaving out the offering vessels and vegetation in the courtyard; the painted sculpture and murals inside are not drawn.

sx_macun.name: Macun Brick-Carved Tombs
sx_macun.sub: Tomb No. 1 · Woman opening the door
sx_macun.yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate sorting point for the early Jin, not the exact burial year of any tomb; the cemetery as a whole spans the late Northern Song to the Jin.
sx_macun.place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
sx_macun.lede: Inside brick-built tomb chambers, bracket sets, doors, windows and balustrades form an underground mansion. In Tomb No. 1 a young maid leans out from behind a half-closed door, and the narrative reliefs beside her preserve Song–Jin life on small brick surfaces.
facts: Underground mansion: The tomb chambers imitate a timber-framed residence in carved brick, with columns, bracket sets, doors, windows and platforms together forming an architectural space.
Woman opening the door: In Tomb No. 1 the central door leaf stands half open and a maid leans out from behind it; reliefs of narrative scenes with figures survive on both sides.
Song–Jin cemetery: The cemetery as a whole dates from the late Northern Song to the Jin; this plate shows a detail of the early Jin Tomb No. 1 and does not represent all the tomb chambers.

yuanjue.name: Yuanjue Temple, Hunyuan
yuanjue.place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Shiqiao North Lane
yuanjue.lede: In the old town of Hunyuan, Yuanjue Temple has left a Jin brick pagoda. A tall first story carries nine tiers of close-set eaves that taper step by step; carved brick imitates timber bracket sets, and a slender iron finial traces a distinctive outline at the top.
facts: According to the Hunyuan Prefecture Gazetteer, the surviving brick pagoda was built in the 3rd year of Zhenglong in the Jin (1158) and was repaired many times in the Ming and Qing.
The pagoda is an octagonal, nine-story multi-eaved pagoda about 30 m tall; its shaft and base use carved brick to represent imitation-timber bracket sets and ornament.
The pagoda of Yuanjue Temple in Hunyuan was listed in 2013 in the seventh batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level.

chunhua.name: Chunhua Temple, Pingshun
chunhua.era: Before the 9th year of Dading, Jin
chunhua.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Yanggao Village
chunhua.lede: Of this old temple founded in the Northern Qi, only a Jin main hall remains. Before the hall stand two stone dharani pillars of the 3rd year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (970), carved with the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra and the Diamond Sutra, two hundred years older than the hall itself.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and an exposed roof frame with no ceiling.
The bracket sets are four-puzuo with a single projecting arm, and the cantilevers are cut in the split-bamboo style, a practice of the Song–Jin transition.
According to a stele, it dates from before the 9th year of Dading in the Jin (1169).

huata.name: Hua Pagoda of Guanghui Temple
huata.era: Founded in the Tang · Restored in the Dading era, Jin
huata.lede: The most ornate of China's surviving flower pagodas: the lower three stories form an octagonal pavilion, each of its four corners embracing a small hexagonal pagoda, and the top story gathers into a “bouquet,” with lions, elephants, bodhisattvas and guardian warriors clustered tier upon tier around the finial.
facts: Founded in the Tang and restored in the Dading era of the Jin; 40.5 m tall overall (another account gives 33.35 m), with four stories of brick imitating timber.

At the four corners of the first story, hexagonal annex chambers connect to the main pagoda, each with an arched doorway and an inverted-bowl top; this combination of “one main and four subsidiary” pagodas is seen nowhere else.

The bouquet-shaped body of the fourth story: its eight faces are modeled with lions, elephants, Buddhist niches and guardian warriors in staggered rows, eight tiers in all, which give the Flower Pagoda its name.
Together with the Xumi Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, the Lingxiao Pagoda of Tianning Temple and the Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple, it is known as one of the “Four Pagodas of Zhengding.”

sx_pingyaowenmiao.name: Pingyao Confucian Temple
sx_pingyaowenmiao.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
sx_pingyaowenmiao.lede: Diagonal brackets spread from the column heads to either side, holding up the deep eaves of the five-bay hall. The Jin date of the Dacheng Hall of the Pingyao Confucian Temple lies hidden in an inscription on its beam frame.
facts: The Dacheng Hall is dated by a rebuilding inscription of the 3rd year of Dading in the Jin (1163); the temple's other buildings belong to separate construction phases.
Five bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; column-head bracket sets and diagonal brackets project in overlapping layers.
The plate keeps the five bays and six columns, along with the stone balustrade and side steps before the hall; later buildings in the courtyard are not counted as Jin structures.

yanshan.name: Yanshan Temple, Fanshi
yanshan.lede: In Tianyan Village, the Manjushri Hall stills the noise of its courtyard amid the mountains. Within its broad plain walls and gently sloping eaves, Jin murals set the life of the Buddha and scenes of worldly town life on the same wall.
facts: The surviving Manjushri Hall is a Jin structure; an inscription beneath a beam records a restoration in the 2nd year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1315).
The Manjushri Hall is five bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and four-puzuo bracket sets.
The Jin murals inside the hall were completed in the 7th year of Dading (1167) and are the work of the painter Wang Kui and others.
captions: Front of the Manjushri Hall, Yanshan Temple · Redrawn from photographs of the site

hn_baima.name: Qiyun Pagoda of White Horse Temple
hn_baima.sub: White Horse Temple · Jin brick pagoda
hn_baima.yearNote: A Jin rebuilding stele states 1175 explicitly; this is not 68, the year White Horse Temple was founded.
hn_baima.place: Henan · Luoyang · East Pagoda Court of White Horse Temple
hn_baima.lede: East of White Horse Temple, Qiyun Pagoda draws a soft curve with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves. Its square shaft steps inward level by level, preserving the form of the brick pagoda rebuilt in the Jin, with a lineage distinct from the temple's Eastern Han founding.
facts: Rebuilding date: The Jin stele beside the pagoda, the Record of the Rebuilding of the Sakyamuni Relic Pagoda of the East White Horse Temple on the Left Street of Henan Prefecture, records its rebuilding in the 15th year of Dading (1175).
Form: A square multi-eaved brick pagoda of thirteen stories, stepping inward level by level from the sixth story up, and topped by a vase-shaped finial.
Temple and pagoda: The Qiyun Pagoda Court lies southeast of White Horse Temple; the history of the present pagoda and the later, newly built halls of the pagoda court are recorded separately.

hn_baolun.name: Baolun Temple Pagoda
hn_baolun.sub: Thirteen eaves drawn into a slender silhouette
hn_baolun.yearNote: Entered according to the surviving pagoda rebuilt in the Jin; the founding date of the old Tang temple is not substituted for the date of the pagoda.
hn_baolun.lede: In the 17th year of Dading in the Jin, the monk Zhixiu rebuilt the Baolun Temple Pagoda. Its square shaft tapers level by level, and thirteen close-set eaves trace a slender outline within the old city of Shanzhou.
facts: Jin rebuilding: The surviving pagoda was built in 1177; the history of the Tang temple and pagoda is recorded separately from this Jin pagoda.
Thirteen close-set eaves: The pagoda is 26.5 m tall; its brick eaves project with saw-tooth courses and corbelling, and at the bottom there is a separate platform and base.
Interior passage: Inside are a central chamber and stairways; its echo effect has earned it the popular name Toad Pagoda.

wangbao.name: Erlang Temple of Wangbao, Gaoping
wangbao.sub: Jin opera stage · Gable facing forward
wangbao.lede: With its gable facing forward, a small one-bay stage carries a spreading hip-and-gable roof. The Erlang Temple at Wangbao preserves a Jin performance space at the south end of its courtyard, and the Dading date on its platform can still be traced.
facts: Jin stage: An inscription on the Sumeru-plinth platform records the 23rd year of Dading (1183), so the date of the surviving stage is clear; most of the temple's other buildings have been restored in the Ming and Qing.

Gable facing forward: The stage, one bay square, turns the gable of its hip-and-gable roof toward the audience; four round columns and stout bracket sets carry the roof, a form that is quite distinctive.
Surviving early stage: Official descriptions call it the earliest surviving stage in China; it sits at the south facing north and bears witness to early village temple fairs and performance spaces.

jingtusi.name: Jingtu Temple, Ying County
jingtusi.lede: In a small temple east of the Wooden Pagoda, a three-bay Jin Buddhist hall holds finely made celestial palace pavilions and caisson ceilings; widely spaced bracket sets beneath the eaves carry a gently undulating, spreading roof.
facts: The Mahavira Hall is an original Jin structure, restored in the 24th year of Dading in the Jin (1184).
The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
Inside, the caisson ceilings are set within a ceiling fully covered with coffered panels, and together with the celestial palace pavilions along the walls they form rare Jin fine joinery.

hn_fengxian.name: Fengxian Temple, Jiyuan
hn_fengxian.yearNote: The Jin date of the surviving Sanqing Hall is used, not the founding of the temple in the 1st year of Chuigong in the Tang.
hn_fengxian.lede: The Sanqing Hall of Fengxian Temple holds its broad overhanging gable roof on six stone columns along the front eave. Massive bracket sets and a clear five-bay column grid make the structure of this Jin hall legible from the front.
facts: Date: The Sanqing Hall was built in the 24th year of Dading in the Jin (1184); this is recorded separately from the history of the temple's Tang founding.
Form: Five bays wide and seven rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; the front column grid and stout bracket sets preserve Jin architectural features.
Layout: The temple also retains a Qing main gate and a Ming Jade Emperor Hall; this plate shows only the surviving Jin Sanqing Hall.

hb_linji.name: Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple
hb_linji.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hb_linji.lede: Close-set eaves draw inward level by level, and between the lotus base and the finial a slender, upright outline emerges. Chengling Pagoda preserves the form of the brick pagoda after its major Jin repair and also marks the ancestral temple of the Linji school.
facts: The present appearance follows the form after the major repair of the 25th year of Dading in the Jin (1185); the earlier history of a pagoda built for the founding patriarch must not stand in for the date of the present structure.
The octagonal nine-story multi-eaved body rests on a carved base and lotus petals.
The finial was reinstalled in 1985; the plate depicts the present state, and the repaired parts and the Jin main body are described separately.

bj_lugou.name: Lugou Bridge, Beijing
bj_lugou.era: Completed in the Jin · Ming–Qing repairs
bj_lugou.lede: Eleven stone arches extend beneath the low, gently sloping deck, and lion-topped balusters join into a long, slender edge. The plate views the bridge from a shallow oblique angle, keeping every arch open, and does not draw the shadows beneath the bridge as solid mass.
facts: Lugou Bridge was completed in 1192 under the Jin and later repaired in the Ming and Qing; the timeline uses the completion date and records the later repairs separately.

The bridge has eleven stone arches; this plate shows the abutments at both ends, the piers and the continuous stone-lion balustrade in full, distinguishing it from the single great arch of the Zhaozhou Bridge.

The colored plate follows the present appearance, with gray stone and lighter balustrade panels; all eleven arches are truly open, and the carved details of the stone lions are artistically simplified.

hongfu.name: Hongfu Temple, Dingxiang
hongfu.lede: On a high platform in Beishe Village, this Jin main hall, with its low, gently pitched overhanging gable roof, widely spaced five-bay doors and windows, and painted clay statues inside, keeps the atmosphere of an old temple at the southern foot of Mount Wutai.
facts: The surviving Mahavira Hall is a Jin structure; its exact year of construction has not been confirmed by any inscription.
The main hall is five bays wide, seven purlins and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof.
The hall preserves nine clay statues; Hongfu Temple was listed in 2001 as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level.

yanqing.name: Yanqing Temple, Wutai
yanqing.lede: In Shanwen Village, the Great Buddha Hall spreads its broad projecting eaves beyond a three-bay body; two beast masks beside the doors guard the central bay, and here the Jin beam frame meets later decoration.
facts: The surviving Great Buddha Hall is a Jin structure; its exact year of construction is unknown.
The hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and deep eave overhangs.
The interior column heads keep Qing beast-mask decoration; the temple also preserves a Song stone dharani pillar.

sx_taifu.name: Taifu Temple, Fenyang
sx_taifu.era: Jin · Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor
sx_taifu.yearNote: 1200 is an approximate sorting point for the period indicated by the altar record of the 5th year of Cheng'an; the main hall is dated to the Jin from its architecture and heritage sources, and the altar date is not forced on the hall as a precise completion year.
sx_taifu.lede: The three-bay Haotian Hall stands on a terrace, its stout bracket sets holding up a single-eaved roof. The Jin timber structure of the main hall, the gilded melon-shaped studs on its doors and the later paintings and sculptures inside record the continuing building history of Taifu Temple.
facts: Jin main hall: The surviving Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor is a Jin structure; a stele of the 5th year of Cheng'an records the founding of a ritual altar in the temple.
Three-bay plan: The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the central plank door is flanked by windows with vertical mullions.

Paintings and sculptures through the ages: The statues in the hall and the other buildings in the courtyard have mostly gone through Ming and Qing construction and refurbishment; the date of the main subject drawn is judged from the timber structure of the main hall.

yongle.name: Yongle Palace, Ruicheng
yongle.lede: The long eaves of the Sanqing Hall lift gently at both sides, and huge glazed dragon ridge-end ornaments guard either end of the main ridge. Inside, the mural Homage to the Primordial (Chaoyuan Tu) arrays hundreds of deities in a grand procession, so that Yuan timber architecture and murals reflect each other within a single space.
facts: Seven-bay hipped hall: The Sanqing Hall, also called the Wuji Hall, is the main hall of Yongle Palace, seven bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof, and is dated to the 3rd year of Zhongtong (1262).
Chaoyuan Tu: The murals in the hall were completed in 1325 and are recorded separately from the construction date of the building.
Relocation for protection: For the Sanmenxia Reservoir project, the palace buildings and murals were moved to their present site in the 1960s, preserving the original halls and murals.

hn_guanxing.name: Dengfeng Observatory
hn_guanxing.sub: Front of the platform and stone scale
hn_guanxing.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hn_guanxing.lede: The brick-and-stone platform is divided into two chambers, with a narrow slit aligned with the stone scale that extends along the ground. The Dengfeng Observatory organizes the height, orientation and graduations needed to measure shadows into a clearly legible building.
facts: The observatory was built in the 13th year of Zhiyuan in the Yuan (1276) and is associated with the large-scale astronomical survey directed by Guo Shoujing.
A slit for measuring shadows is left between the two chambers on top of the platform, the stone scale is laid out on the north side, and twin stairways beside the platform lead to the top.
The plate shows only the observatory itself and the stone scale; the nearby Duke of Zhou's Shadow Measurement Platform is not split off as a separate entry.

bj_miaoying.name: White Pagoda of Miaoying Temple, Beijing
bj_miaoying.era: Built from the 8th to the 16th year of Zhiyuan
bj_miaoying.lede: Inside Fuchengmen, the White Pagoda raises its rounded body on a broad base. The thirteen spire rings, bronze canopy and finial close the silhouette tier by tier, leaving a vivid example of the Yuan Tibetan-style stupa in the capital.
facts: The White Pagoda was built in 1271–1279 and is linked to the history of Araniko's part in Yuan construction; the temple's later halls and repairs have dates of their own.
The plate shows the whole of the surviving White Pagoda, keeping the base, inverted-bowl body, spire rings and bronze canopy, and does not merge the halls in front into the main subject.
The colored plate follows the present appearance, distinguishing the grayish-white body, gray brick base, bronze canopy and metal finial, and does not restore the whole pagoda in gold.

fenghuangsi.name: Prayer Hall of the Phoenix Mosque
fenghuangsi.sub: Hangzhou · Yuan hall of brick vaults and domes
fenghuangsi.era: Rebuilt in the Yuan · Repaired over the centuries
fenghuangsi.lede: The prayer hall of the Phoenix Mosque forms a three-part interior of brick arches and domes, covered outside by three connected pyramidal roofs. The plate takes the group of roofs visible in site photographs, the double-eaved center rising high with lower roofs on either side, presenting the distinctive silhouette of this old Hangzhou mosque.
facts: The surviving core prayer hall derives from a Yuan rebuilding funded by Ala al-Din, and was repaired many times in the Ming, the Qing and the modern period.
Inside, brick arches link three domed spaces; outside, three connected pyramidal roofs cover them, the central one higher and double-eaved, the two side ones lower.

This plate shows only the roofs and upper walls of the prayer hall that can be verified on site; it does not reconstruct the lower facade hidden by later additions, nor does it draw the modern entrance hall.

sx_jishi.name: Ji Family Residence, Gaoping
sx_jishi.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Zhongzhuang Village, Chenqu Town
sx_jishi.lede: The three-bay main house of the Ji Family Residence guards its doorway with stone columns and a shallow porch. An inscription of the 31st year of Zhiyuan on a door pier gives this Yuan dwelling a clearly legible point in time.
facts: Zhiyuan inscription: A bluestone door pier is inscribed with the 31st year of Zhiyuan of the Great Yuan, that is, 1294, providing the basis for dating the dwelling.

Three bays, shallow porch: The main house is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with an overhanging gable roof; the central entrance is set back to form a shallow porch, and the whole is low and plain.
Present doors and windows: The timber structure retains Yuan features, while the square-lattice windows are later alterations; the plate depicts the present state and distinguishes the periods.

hn_yuzhoutianning.name: Tianning Wanshou Temple, Yuzhou
hn_yuzhoutianning.sub: Three-bay Yuan Buddhist hall preserved on a school campus
hn_yuzhoutianning.yearNote: The date of the hall's rebuilding is used; it was later restored in the Ming and Qing and was dismantled and repaired in 2013. The main gate is Ming in style and is not the subject of this plate.
hn_yuzhoutianning.lede: The main hall of Tianning Wanshou Temple is tucked among old school buildings in Yuzhou. A three-bay hip-and-gable roof covers thick brick walls, and the bracket sets under the eaves and the naturally curved timbers inside bear the marks of Yuan construction.
facts: Yuan rebuilding: After the warfare at the end of the Jin, it was rebuilt in the 3rd year of Dade in the Yuan (1299) and repaired many times in the Ming and Qing.

Three-bay Buddhist hall: The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of gray tiles; under the eaves are four-puzuo bracket sets with a single descending cantilever.
Present conservation: Two buildings survive, the main gate and the main hall, inside the grounds of the former Yuzhou No. 1 High School; the hall underwent a major dismantling repair in 2013.

jiutian.name: Temple of the Holy Mother of the Nine Heavens
jiutian.era: Restored in the 1st year of Jianzhong Jingguo, Song · Yuan offering hall
jiutian.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Donghe Village
jiutian.lede: The temple was founded in the Tang, its Holy Mother Hall was rebuilt in the early Northern Song, and the whole temple was restored in the 1st year of Jianzhong Jingguo (1101). The Yuan offering hall before the main hall is the most unusual: it is five bays deep, longer than its three-bay width, its main ridge runs along the depth, and its roof is the highest-ranking hipped type. From the front, in the courtyard, one sees its end face, so the drawing here shows its long side, where the main ridge and both ridge-end ornaments appear.
facts: The offering hall is a Yuan structure, three bays wide and five bays deep, with sixteen chamfered square sandstone columns all around and open on all four sides; its bracket sets are four-puzuo with a single projecting arm, and it stands on a bluestone platform one meter high.
The corner eaves of the three roofs, those of the offering hall, the main hall and the dance pavilion, interlock, which locals call “hooked hearts and fighting horns” (gouxin doujiao).
The Holy Mother Hall is a Song structure, three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; in one village temple, timber buildings of the Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing follow one after another.

hn_huishan.name: Huishan Temple, Dengfeng
hn_huishan.sub: Front of the Yuan main hall
hn_huishan.yearNote: The main subject drawn is dated to the Yuan; the numeric year is only an approximate sorting value.
hn_huishan.lede: At the southern foot of Mount Song, Huishan Temple has left a five-bay Yuan main hall. A broad roof, exposed bracket sets and three central doors give the temple's long history a visible form in a single timber building.
facts: The temple was founded long before the present hall; the hall drawn is entered by its surviving Yuan timber structure.
Five bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the central three bays have doors and the bays on either side have windows.
The plate shows only the front of the surviving hall; the roof and the details of doors and windows bear traces of successive repairs.
captions: Huishan Temple, Dengfeng · Front of the Yuan main hall

hb_shijia.name: Sakyamuni Temple
hb_shijia.yearNote: Dated by the structure of the Yuan hall; the temple's other, Ming halls are not mixed into the main subject.
hb_shijia.lede: A low, spreading single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a wide central bay outline the Yuan layout of the middle hall of Sakyamuni Temple in Yuzhou.
facts: Main subject: The hall drawn is the temple's middle hall, usually called the Mahavira Hall, the earliest surviving and largest building here, dating from the Yuan.
Form: The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; under the eaves are four-puzuo bracket sets with a single projecting arm.

History: The temple was enlarged in the Hongwu era of the Ming and repeatedly repaired afterward; the ridge and ridge ornaments of the middle hall include later replacements, and the ceiling inside is also a later addition.

sx_jiangzhou_datang.name: Jiangzhou Great Hall
sx_jiangzhou_datang.sub: Main hall of the prefectural office · Seven bays, overhanging gable roof
sx_jiangzhou_datang.era: Yuan · Main hall of the prefectural office
sx_jiangzhou_datang.yearNote: 1300 is only an approximate timeline placement for a surviving Yuan structure, not an exact completion year.
sx_jiangzhou_datang.place: Shanxi · Xinjiang County · Jiangzhou Prefectural Office
sx_jiangzhou_datang.lede: The Jiangzhou Great Hall commands its seven-bay facade with a single, spreading overhanging-gable ridge. Thick timber columns, long architraves and bays of unequal width leave the plain and open space of a Yuan prefectural main hall.
facts: Yuan prefectural office: The main body of the surviving hall is a Yuan structure, a rare example of the main hall of a local government office, repaired many times in later periods.

Seven bays, overhanging gable roof: The hall is seven bays wide and eight rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; both ends are walled, and the open center has a column grid of unequal bays.

Reduced columns, long architraves: Seventeen bracket sets along the front eave carry the overhang, and reduced columns and long architraves create a broad space; the original front porch has been destroyed.
captions: Jiangzhou Great Hall · Main hall of the prefectural office
