sx_fusheng.name: Fusheng Temple, Xinjiang County
sx_fusheng.yearNote: 1300 serves only as an approximate sorting point for a surviving Yuan structure and does not claim completion in that year.
sx_fusheng.place: Shanxi · Xinjiang County · Guang Village, Zezhang Town
sx_fusheng.lede: Fusheng Temple in Guang Village unfolds tier upon tier with the terrain, and the Amitabha Hall organizes its inner and outer spaces with double eaves and a surrounding gallery. Its Yuan timber structure and the painted sculptures inside depend on each other, and the north elevation shows the layers of eaves, rear wall and gallery columns more clearly.
facts: Yuan hall: The Amitabha Hall preserves a Yuan timber structure and was restored in the Hongzhi era of the Ming; the temple's founding history cannot directly stand in for the date of the surviving hall.

Double eaves and gallery: The Amitabha Hall is five bays square, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a gallery all around; the ground level differs between the high platform to the south and the rear courtyard to the north.

Surviving painted sculpture: The hall preserves painted sculptures of Amitabha Buddha, attendant bodhisattvas, Guanyin Crossing the Sea and others, which have undergone various later repairs; this plate shows the north side of the hall.
captions: Fusheng Temple · North elevation of the Amitabha Hall
Surviving Yuan structure · Ming repairs

sx_zezhou_yuhuang.name: Jade Emperor Temple, Zezhou
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.sub: Fucheng · Painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.era: Yuan · Painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.yearNote: 1300 is only an approximate sorting point for the Yuan painted sculptures. Official sources give no exact date of making for the single figure selected; 1076 relates to the rebuilding of the temple and cannot substitute for the date of the sculptures.
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.place: Shanxi · Zezhou · Fucheng Village, Jincun Town
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.lede: The Jade Emperor Temple at Fucheng renders the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions of the sky as figures with personalities. Xu Ri Shu, the Rat of the Emptiness Mansion, wears layered robes and a quiet expression, and the pairing of a small rat with a human figure gives ancient astronomical belief a visible face.
facts: Mansions in human form: The painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions combine lunar mansions, animals and human figures, each with its own pose and expression.

Yuan painted sculpture: This plate uses the Xu Ri Shu figure dated to the Yuan in the official catalogue, and does not substitute the year of the temple's Northern Song rebuilding for the date of the sculpture.

One figure as representative: The plate redraws only Xu Ri Shu from among the Twenty-Eight Mansions, omitting the painted patterns and the hall background while keeping the hand gesture, robes and animal features.
captions: Jade Emperor Temple, Zezhou · Xu Ri Shu
Yuan · Representative painted sculpture of the Twenty-Eight Mansions

hb_ciyunge.name: Ciyun Pavilion
hb_ciyunge.yearNote: Of the original Dabei Pavilion complex only this pavilion survives; it was rebuilt in the 10th year of Dade in the Yuan.
hb_ciyunge.lede: In the old town of Dingxing, the Ciyun Pavilion raises spreading double eaves on a two-story timber frame, and inside and out it still keeps the features of Yuan framing. Most of the original temple buildings have vanished, and this small pavilion alone records the old name of the Dabei Pavilion.
facts: Date: The present pavilion was rebuilt in the 10th year of Dade in the Yuan (1306) and is a surviving Yuan timber structure.
Layout: Three bays wide and three bays deep, nearly square in plan, in the form of a two-story pavilion.
Frame: The beam frame combines hanging columns, diagonal corner beams and other devices, preserving Yuan structural and workmanship methods.
captions: Dingxing · Ciyun Pavilion

yongan.name: Yong'an Chan Temple, Hunyuan
yongan.sub: Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma
yongan.place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan
yongan.lede: The Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma at Yong'an Chan Temple holds down its five-bay facade with a broad hipped roof, its ridge ornaments answering the deep eaves. Inside this hall built in the 2nd year of Yanyou in the Yuan, water-and-land ritual murals gather Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist figures; timber structure and painting together form a precious survival in the old town of Hunyuan.
facts: Yong'an Temple was founded in the Jin; the surviving Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma was built with funds donated by Gao Pu in the 2nd year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1315).
The main hall is five bays wide, with a single-eaved hipped roof; the central three bays have doors, and the solid walls at both ends retain large calligraphic inscriptions.

Yong'an Temple was listed in 2001 in the fifth batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level; the Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma preserves water-and-land ritual murals.

yanfu.name: Yanfu Temple, Wuyi
yanfu.sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in Jiangnan
yanfu.era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Yanyou
yanfu.lede: Upper and lower tiers of flying eaves spread out the body of the hall, and a broad central bay flanked by lattice windows resolves into a clean, simple front. The Yuan main hall of Yanfu Temple in Wuyi still preserves memories of earlier timber construction.
facts: Yuan rebuilding: The rebuilding of the surviving main hall began in the 4th year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1317), with funds raised by the monks Huaifa and Dehuan.
Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof: Timber bracket sets show between the two tiers of eaves, and a broad central bay with narrower side bays sets the rhythm of the facade.
Song and Yuan joined: The hall retains Song members, and together with the Yuan rebuilding its visible forms leave construction traces that span periods.
captions: Yanfu Temple · Main hall
4th year of Yanyou, Yuan · Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof

jinhuatianning.name: Tianning Temple, Jinhua
jinhuatianning.lede: A single tier of long eaves lifts high, with light, upturned corners drawn in at either side. Using a scale of only three bays, the main hall of Tianning Temple in Jinhua arranges its wide central bay, lattice windows and the bracket sets beneath its eaves into a front both upright and expansive.
facts: Ink-written date: An ink inscription on a beam records a rebuilding in the 5th year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1318), the direct clue for dating the surviving hall.
Three bays, single eaves: The hall is three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the wide central bay and the window lattices of the side bays form clear layers.

Yuan structure under national protection: The main hall of Tianning Temple was listed in 1988 in the third batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level and is an important Yuan survival in the old city of Jinhua.

5th year of Yanyou, Yuan · Single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

sh_zhenru.name: Main Hall of Zhenru Temple
sh_zhenru.sub: Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Yuan timber structure
sh_zhenru.yearNote: 1320 corresponds to the construction inscription on the hall's timber frame; the present appearance was restored through repairs including those of 1963, which removed a later lower eave. The temple's other buildings and the new pagoda behind the hall are not included in this plate of the Yuan structure.
sh_zhenru.lede: A broad gray-tiled roof rests on the three-bay timber hall, with ridge-end ornaments curling skyward at both ends. The main hall of Zhenru Temple preserves Yuan Jiangnan timber construction within today's city, and an inscription among its beams still records its construction in the 7th year of Yanyou.
facts: An inscription on an interior architrave records that the hall was erected in the 7th year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1320); the hall retains Yuan timber members and is an important Yuan architectural survival in Shanghai.
Three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; four columns across the front frame central lattice doors with windows at the sides, and ridge-end ornaments stand at both ends of the roof.

Repairs in 1963 removed a lower eave added later, restoring its single-eaved appearance. The plate shows only the main hall; the new pagoda behind it and the later buildings on either side have dates of their own.
captions: Front elevation of the main hall · Three bays wide
Yuan · 7th year of Yanyou (1320)

xiayu.name: Xia Yu Shrine
xiayu.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
xiayu.lede: A small temple to Yu the Great in the Zhuozhang River valley, built in the 2nd year of Zhiyuan in the Yuan (1336). A single courtyard: a stage sits reversed on top of the gate, the three-bay main hall is Yuan, and the east and west side halls were added in the Ming and Qing — the complete layout of a village temple.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof, and is a Yuan structure; its timbers are roughly worked and the beam frame uses many naturally curved members, a local Yuan practice.
The gate is a Ming building, and the stage on its upper level faces back toward the main hall.
It is popularly called the King Yu Temple; the Zhuozhang River often flooded, and Yu was worshipped to subdue it.
captions: Line drawing of the main hall · Three bays wide
Single-eaved overhanging gable roof · Yuan

duanliang.name: Second Gate of Tiger Hill
duanliang.sub: Suzhou · Duanliang Hall of Tiger Hill
duanliang.era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan
duanliang.lede: The Second Gate of Tiger Hill covers its three-bay body with a broad, horizontal hip-and-gable roof, and a central round arch with round windows on either side forms a spare front. The name “Duanliang,” or “broken beam,” comes from the ridge purlin, which is joined from separate sections.
facts: According to the Suzhou Municipal Administration of Landscaping and Greening, the surviving Second Gate was rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan in the Yuan (1338).
The gate is three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; a central round-arched doorway and round windows to left and right form the openings of the front.
“Broken beam” refers to the ridge purlin made of two round logs joined end to end; it does not mean that the hall has no beams, nor that a beam has broken and hangs in midair.
captions: Second Gate of Tiger Hill · Front of the Duanliang Hall

protection.note: The first-batch listing of the Yunyan Temple Pagoda in Suzhou notes that it includes other buildings of Yunyan Temple; this entry depicts the Second Gate of Tiger Hill.

sx_doudafu.name: Shrine of Grand Master Dou, Taiyuan
sx_doudafu.sub: Offering pavilion and main hall · Shanglan Village
sx_doudafu.era: Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng
sx_doudafu.yearNote: Placed by the Yuan rebuilding date, the 3rd year of Zhizheng, of the surviving offering pavilion and main hall; neither the Spring and Autumn date of the person venerated nor the earlier history of the shrine is used as the date of the timber structures.
sx_doudafu.lede: Stout timber columns hold up deep eaves, and the offering pavilion joins the main hall behind it. Among the gray-brown old timbers, dark green glazed tiles outline the ridges and eave-tile ends; the Shrine of Grand Master Dou gathers its ritual space into a tight group of timber buildings.
facts: The shrine is dedicated to Dou Chou, a grand master of the state of Jin, and is also called the Lieshi Shrine and the Yingji Shrine; the early history of the shrine and the dates of the surviving buildings are described separately.

The surviving gate, offering pavilion and main hall were rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1343). The plate selects the offering pavilion and main hall and does not count the Qing side buildings as Yuan structures.

The hip-and-gable roof of the offering pavilion links with the overhanging gable roof of the main hall behind, and thick columns and massive bracket sets create a striking contrast of scale; the colored plate follows the surviving old timber, gray tiles and glazed tiles, and is not a reconstruction of historical painted decoration.
captions: Shrine of Grand Master Dou, Taiyuan · Front of the offering pavilion and main hall
Yuan · Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng (1343)

bj_juyong_yuntai.name: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass, Beijing
bj_juyong_yuntai.sub: Yuan base of a street-spanning stupa · Half-hexagonal arched passage
bj_juyong_yuntai.era: Built from the 2nd to the 5th year of Zhizheng
bj_juyong_yuntai.lede: A high white stone platform straddles the old passage, its body tapering upward and its top rail running flat. The half-hexagonal arched passage and the reliefs on its door frame remain from the stone base of a Yuan street-spanning stupa; the vanished stupa halls on the platform are not reconstructed.
facts: The Cloud Platform is the base of a Yuan street-spanning stupa, built in 1342–1345; the original stupa halls no longer stand on the platform today.

The inner opening of the central passage is half-hexagonal, and the door frame and passage walls bear reliefs and sutras carved in several scripts; the plate only suggests the carving with sparse lines.
The present-state drawing keeps the empty platform, stone balustrade, tapering body and arched passage, removes modern barriers and surroundings, and does not add the three historical stupas.
captions: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass · Surviving base of the street-spanning stupa

hb_beiyue.name: Beiyue Temple
hb_beiyue.sub: Front elevation of the Dening Hall (with gallery and platform)
hb_beiyue.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau lists the present hall under the 7th year of Zhizheng (1347); the county gazetteer records completion in the 7th year of Zhiyuan (1270), so both construction phases need to be recorded.
hb_beiyue.lede: The Dening Hall of Beiyue Temple sits on a high platform, its two tiers of hipped eaves stretching horizontally. Once the place where the court made sacrifices from afar to the Northern Peak, Mount Heng, it preserves the memory of this ancient peak temple through its Yuan timber structure, murals and the steles of sacrifices from many dynasties.
facts: Date: The present hall is Yuan; sources record completion in 1270 and rebuilding in 1347 respectively, and the timeline enters it with an approximate Yuan value.
Hall: A double-eaved hipped roof with a surrounding gallery, nine bays wide and six bays deep overall; a central stairway climbs the high platform.
Sacrifices: Beiyue Temple was originally a temple for sacrifices to Mount Heng from afar; the hall preserves Yuan murals, and steles of many dynasties are gathered in the courtyard.
captions: Quyang · Dening Hall of Beiyue Temple

xuanyuan.name: Main Hall of Xuanyuan Palace
xuanyuan.lede: The main hall of Xuanyuan Palace at Yangwan on Dongshan covers its three-bay body with deep hip-and-gable eaves, its window lattices set within undulating cusped (kunmen) outlines on either side. Yuan framing features and traces of Ming and Qing building remain together on this small hall.
facts: The national listing dates it to the Yuan; the surviving main hall has undergone Ming and Qing rebuilding and repair, and its overall present appearance must not be taken as an unaltered Yuan original.
The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; four central columns help form a grid-shaped beam frame.
This was originally the Xuwang Temple, dedicated to Wu Zixu; in the Republican period it was rededicated to the Yellow Emperor and called Xuanyuan Palace.

shisi.name: Shisi Temple, Jingning
shisi.sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in a mountain village
shisi.lede: Between two tiers of flying eaves, deep bracket sets line up against white walls. With its light timber frame and low stone steps, the main hall of Shisi Temple lies hidden in an old temple in the mountain village of Daji.
facts: Yuan main hall: The hall was built in the 16th year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1356) and still retains many Yuan members.

Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof: The upper and lower eaves spread wide, the bracket sets of the upper eave show their full layering, and a central doorway with windows on either side forms a simple facade.
Several periods side by side: The temple's bell tower, Sanqing Hall and Mei clan ancestral hall form a complex spanning the Yuan, Ming and Qing; the plate takes only the Yuan main hall.

jijian.name: Stone Halls of Jijian Temple
jijian.lede: The Xitian Temple stone hall of Jijian Temple stands hard against the mountain rock, imitating a timber hall with stone columns, stone tie-beams and large stone slabs. A shallow, gently sloping roof and three-bay openings make this Yuan stone hall look low and compact.
facts: The Xitian Temple stone hall was built in the 17th year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1357); it stands as a separate structure from the small stone houses of Doushuai Palace and Jile Garden beside it.
The main hall is three bays wide (about 7.64 m) and two bays deep (about 5.52 m), with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a plan with a projecting central section.
Apart from the lattice doors used for entry, the main members are carved from stone in imitation of timber, and the rear abuts the natural rock of the mountain.

sx_jishan_qinglong.name: Qinglong Temple, Jishan
sx_jishan_qinglong.era: Late Yuan–early Ming · Middle hall murals
sx_jishan_qinglong.yearNote: The subject drawn is the middle hall murals, using the dating range of Sun Bo cited by the Yuncheng Museum; 1360 is only a sorting coordinate. It is not 1289, the completion year of the timber structure, and scholarly opinions on the dating of the murals still differ.
sx_jishan_qinglong.place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
sx_jishan_qinglong.lede: The middle hall of Qinglong Temple at Macun brings Buddhist, Daoist and secular figures together in a single water-and-land painting. In the upper part of the west wall, the Buddhas of the Three Ages sit enthroned among clouds, and the fine lines of their robes and lotus thrones still reveal the hand of painters at the turn of the Yuan and Ming.
facts: Water-and-land rite of the three teachings: The middle hall murals combine Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian-related figures to form a water-and-land assembly, with the Buddhas of the Three Ages above on the west wall and the hosts of deities ranged in tiers below.

Keeping dates distinct: The timber structure of the middle hall has a record of rebuilding in 1289; the murals have been painted and retouched, scholars propose dates such as late Yuan–early Ming, and the timber date cannot be applied to all of them.

Detail redrawn: This plate redraws the upper part of the west wall of the middle hall from site photographs published by the heritage conservation center, keeping the group of the Buddhas of the Three Ages with attendants; it does not represent the murals or painted sculptures of the whole hall.
captions: Qinglong Temple · Buddhas of the Three Ages on the west wall of the middle hall (detail)

sx_pingyaowall.name: Pingyao City Wall
sx_pingyaowall.sub: Yingxun Gate and adjoining wall sections
sx_pingyaowall.yearNote: 1370 is used for sorting by the phase of the wall's expansion; the gate tower and surviving wall faces include later repairs.
sx_pingyaowall.lede: Yingxun Gate opens the outline of the old city on the south, its arched passage, gate platform and gate tower stacked one above another. The wall stretching along the crenellations divides the streets and lanes within the city from the fields outside.
facts: The wall was expanded and faced with brick in the 3rd year of Hongwu in the Ming (1370); its present appearance reflects repairs in the Ming, the Qing and the modern period.
The plate selects the south gate, Yingxun Gate, and the adjoining wall sections to either side, keeping the gate passage and the double-eaved gate tower above.

The Ancient City of Pingyao is inscribed as a World Heritage Site together with Shuanglin Temple and Zhenguo Temple; this entry records only the city wall and does not count the temples a second time.

sn_hancheng.name: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple
sn_hancheng.era: Rebuilt in the Hongwu era, maintained over the centuries
sn_hancheng.yearNote: 1371 is the recorded rebuilding of the Confucian Temple on its Yuan site; the Dacheng Hall retains Yuan building methods and has been maintained over the centuries, so not every surviving member can be assigned to 1371.
sn_hancheng.place: Shaanxi · Weinan · Old town of Hancheng
sn_hancheng.lede: Beneath a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, a broad front porch fronts the five-bay hall. The Hancheng Confucian Temple was rebuilt on its Yuan site, and between columns and architraves the continuation of earlier timber methods can still be seen.
facts: Rebuilding: The local gazetteer records rebuilding on the Yuan site in 1371, followed by repeated maintenance.
Main structure: The Dacheng Hall is five bays wide, its front porch spans three large bays, and it has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
Dating: It retains Yuan building methods; neither the whole temple nor all of its members are equated with a single year.
captions: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple, whole hall · Line drawing
Ming · Rebuilt 1371 · Later maintenance

yuhuang.name: Jade Emperor Pavilion of Yuzhou
yuhuang.era: Founded in the 10th year of Hongwu
yuhuang.place: Hebei · Yu County · North city wall
yuhuang.lede: On the north wall of the old city of Yuzhou, Jingbian Tower spreads three tiers of eaves yet has only two stories. A gallery runs around the upper story, and here a defensive tower and the cult of the Jade Emperor overlap.
facts: Built in the 10th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1377) and also called Jingbian Tower, it is the landmark pavilion on the northern rampart of the old city of Yuzhou.
The main hall is five bays wide, with three tiers of eaves on two stories and a glazed-tile hip-and-gable roof; a waist eave gives the two-story pavilion the appearance of three eaves.
The upper story has a timber gallery around the building, and the lower story a surrounding colonnade; the surviving building preserves the historical layers of many Ming and Qing repairs.

xianwall.name: Xi'an City Wall
xianwall.sub: Arrow tower of Anding Gate · Ming rampart
xianwall.lede: A massive wall platform carries a broad arrow tower, four rows of arrow windows stretch across it, and a single gate passage pierces the defenses. The layout of the west gate preserved at Anding Gate makes the scale and defensive purpose of the Xi'an City Wall clearly legible.
facts: Ming rampart: The main body of the surviving wall was built in the 7th to 11th years of Hongwu (1374–1378), extended from an earlier city site, and later gradually faced with brick and reinforced.

Anding Gate section: The plate takes the arrow tower of the main west gate and its single central arched passage; the broad tower has four rows of arrow windows, and the thick walls and gate tower together form a defensive space.

Repairs through the ages: Anding Gate has been repaired many times in the Ming, the Qing and the modern period and still preserves a defensive layout in which arrow tower, gate tower and barbican are linked.

Ming rampart · Ming, Qing and modern repairs

xianzhonggu.name: Bell Tower and Drum Tower of Xi'an
xianzhonggu.era: Founded in the Hongwu era · Moved in the Wanli era
xianzhonggu.place: Shaanxi · Xi'an · Center of the prefectural city
xianzhonggu.lede: The Bell Tower stands with its pyramidal roof where streets meet, and the long ridge of the Drum Tower stretches across the south end of Beiyuanmen. These two Ming towers once announced the hours of the city with the sound of bell and drum.
facts: The Drum Tower was founded in 1380 and the Bell Tower in 1384; the Bell Tower was moved to its present site in 1582 on a newly built base, so the platform at the present site cannot be equated with the original founding date.

The Bell Tower is a triple-eaved pavilion with a four-sided pyramidal roof on a square platform; the Drum Tower stands on a rectangular platform, its body seven bays wide with a surrounding gallery and a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof on the upper story.

The plate sets near-frontal views of the Bell Tower and the Drum Tower side by side, keeping each one's complete outline; this is a composite of two subjects, not a view of the two towers actually standing next to each other.

linggu.name: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple
linggu.lede: The Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple carries its roof on massive brick walls and continuous vaults, and three arched doorways pierce the broad wall of its front. Above two shallow tiers of eaves, three pagoda-shaped ridge ornaments mark the outline of this Ming brick hall.
facts: The surviving Beamless Hall is a Ming building; Linggu Temple was moved here in the 14th year of Hongwu (1381).

The hall uses no timber beams, and masonry vaults bear the structure; two homophonous names are used side by side, Wuliang Hall meaning “Hall of the Immeasurable” and Wuliang Hall meaning “Beamless Hall.”
According to the scenic area, the hall is about 50 m wide and about 34 m deep, and three pagoda-shaped ridge ornaments stand on its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
captions: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple · Front of the brick-vaulted hall

protection.note: In 1933 the Beamless Hall was converted into the memorial hall of the Cemetery of the Fallen Soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army; in the fifth batch the cemetery was incorporated into the first-batch listing of the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum. It is not a separately listed national protected site under the name “Linggu Temple.”

sx_chongshan.name: Chongshan Temple, Taiyuan
sx_chongshan.sub: Hall of Great Compassion · Early Ming official-style timber structure
sx_chongshan.era: Hongwu era, Ming · Hall of Great Compassion
sx_chongshan.yearNote: 1385 is only an approximate timeline placement within the Hongwu reign, not a precise completion year. Neither the temple's history nor its Qing main gate replaces the date of the Ming main subject drawn.
sx_chongshan.lede: The seven-bay Hall of Great Compassion stretches across the courtyard, its double eaves still preserving the scale of an early Ming official-style Buddhist hall. Having come through fire and changes in the temple's layout, the surviving hall has become an important physical record for understanding Hongwu architecture.
facts: Hongwu survival: The surviving Hall of Great Compassion is a high-ranking official-style Buddhist hall of the Hongwu reign of the Ming; both its timber structure and the statues inside are of great research value.
Seven bays, double eaves: The hall is seven bays wide and four bays deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof; the plate emphasizes the two tiers of eaves and the seven-bay column grid.

Survivor of fire: The Hall of Great Compassion survived the great fire of the 3rd year of Tongzhi in the Qing; the main gate and bell and drum towers rebuilt later are registered separately from the original Ming hall.

fj_chongwu.name: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City
fj_chongwu.sub: Granite gate platform · South gate wall section
fj_chongwu.era: City built in the 20th year of Hongwu, later repaired
fj_chongwu.yearNote: 1387 is the founding date of the Chongwu stone city and an approximate timeline placement; the surviving south gate section has undergone later repairs, and the upper gate tower seen in photographs is not labeled as original 1387 fabric.
fj_chongwu.lede: Sea wind sweeps over gray-brown stone walls, and the arched gate lies beneath a low gate platform. Chongwu was built of granite as a coastal defensive barrier, and its south gate section still keeps the massive scale of a seaside stone city.
facts: History: The Chongwu battalion garrison city was first built in 1387 as part of the Ming coastal defense system; the surviving walls have been maintained over the centuries.
Scope of the drawing: The arched passage of the south gate, the building above the gate and a short adjoining stretch of wall; not the whole ancient city or a collection of its four gates.

Materials and date: The gate platform is built of granite; the upper gate tower is drawn as it stands today, and the founding year of the city cannot be used to assert that all of it is original early Ming fabric.

sx_jiulongbi.name: Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong
sx_jiulongbi.sub: Glazed spirit screen of the Prince of Dai's mansion · Nine-dragon relief
sx_jiulongbi.yearNote: The date given by the Palace Museum, the 25th year of Hongwu (1392), is used; the plate depicts only the surviving Nine-Dragon Screen and not the present-day reconstruction of the Prince of Dai's mansion.
sx_jiulongbi.place: Shanxi · Datong · Heyang Street, Old city
sx_jiulongbi.lede: Nine dragons twist among blue-green glazed tiles, with clouds and waves spreading along the long screen. The Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong contains its dense relief between a low coping and a layered Sumeru plinth, leaving behind the screen of an early Ming princely mansion.
facts: The Nine-Dragon Screen was originally the glazed spirit screen in front of the mansion of Zhu Gui, Prince of Dai. The Palace Museum records it as built in the 25th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1392), and it is assigned to the Ming according to the main body of the screen drawn.
The screen is about 45.5 m long and about 8 m high, with nine principal dragons arrayed along its continuous body; the hipped coping and the glazed Sumeru plinth form its upper and lower borders.

A spirit screen serves as a barrier and decoration in front of a building and is not a city wall or fortification. The plate removes the railings, trees and reflecting pool and simplifies the details of the cloud-and-dragon relief, while keeping the multicolored distribution of the actual glazes.
captions: Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong · Front of the glazed nine-dragon spirit screen
Ming · 25th year of Hongwu (1392)

shuanglin.name: Shuanglin Temple, Pingyao
shuanglin.sub: Hall of Heavenly Kings · Painted sculpture
shuanglin.era: Restored in the 2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi · Rebuilt in the early Ming
shuanglin.lede: Zhongdu Temple, founded in the Northern Wei, was restored in the 2nd year of Wuping in the Northern Qi (571), and most of its surviving halls were rebuilt in the early Ming. It is famous for its painted sculpture: more than two thousand Ming painted statues in ten halls, called the “Gallery of Oriental Painted Sculpture.”
facts: The temple's outer walls were built in the Ming and look like a fortress; within are three courtyards and ten halls.

Four vajra guardians stand in the front porch of the Hall of Heavenly Kings, each more than three meters tall; the statue of Weituo in the Thousand Buddha Hall, twisting his body with a hand on his sword, is a masterpiece of Ming painted sculpture.
The temple holds 2,052 painted statues in all, of which 1,566 are intact; the largest are more than ten Chinese feet tall, the smallest about one Chinese foot.

hb_zixiao.name: Zixiao Palace
hb_zixiao.era: Built in the Yongle era, Ming
hb_zixiao.yearNote: The Zixiao Hall is placed by its construction in the Yongle era of the Ming; 1413 is a sorting reference for this phase of the palace's construction and is not presented as the hall's exact completion year. It was later repaired, and the drawing shows the present state seen in research photographs. The Song founding history is kept separate from the Ming hall drawn.
hb_zixiao.lede: Green double eaves cover a red hall, and tiers of stone terraces raise the main hall high. Keeping only the hall and its steps is enough to show how Wudang architecture unfolds with the mountain terrain.
facts: Main subject: The Zixiao Hall of Zixiao Palace and its front platform.

Date: The Zixiao Hall is placed by its construction in the Yongle era of the Ming; 1413 is a sorting reference for this phase of the palace's construction and is not presented as the hall's exact completion year. It was later repaired, and the drawing shows the present state seen in research photographs. The Song founding history is kept separate from the Ming hall drawn.

Scope of the plate: The five-bay Zixiao Hall, its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, the three-tiered stone terrace in front and the central stairway; the side halls to left and right and the distant mountains are not drawn, and steles, incense burners and visitors are removed.

hb_jindian.name: Golden Hall of Wudang Mountains
hb_jindian.sub: Cast bronze, gilded · Double-eaved hipped roof
hb_jindian.yearNote: The drawing shows the surviving Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, placed at the 14th year of Yongle (1416); it is not to be confused with the ancient Yuan bronze hall moved into the Zhuanyun Hall. The formal national listing includes both the Yuan and Ming bronze halls; this plate shows only the Ming hall.
hb_jindian.lede: The tile ridges, beams, columns and bracket sets are not wood but cast bronze members. Its double roof still looks like that of a small timber hall, and its quiet gold rests on the highest point of Wudang.
facts: Main subject: The Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, Wudang Mountains.

Date: The drawing shows the surviving Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, placed at the 14th year of Yongle (1416); it is not to be confused with the ancient Yuan bronze hall moved into the Zhuanyun Hall. The formal national listing includes both the Yuan and Ming bronze halls; this plate shows only the Ming hall.

Scope of the plate: The complete Ming Golden Hall, with its two tiers of eaves, three-bay facade, and cast-bronze imitation-timber bracket sets and door leaves; the bronze cranes to either side, incense burner, prayer cushions and surrounding temple buildings are not drawn, and it is not the single-eaved ancient Yuan bronze hall.

tiantan.name: Temple of Heaven, Beijing
tiantan.sub: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests
tiantan.era: Founded in the 18th year of Yongle · Rebuilt in the 22nd year of Guangxu
tiantan.lede: The Hall of Great Sacrifice was built in the 18th year of Yongle in the Ming (1420); in the Jiajing era it became a round, triple-eaved hall, and under Qianlong it received blue tiles and was renamed the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. Struck by lightning and burned in the 15th year of Guangxu (1889), it was rebuilt to the original design six years later — what we see today is timber of 1896.
facts: Round, triple-eaved and conical, with blue glazed tiles and a gilded finial; 32.72 m in diameter and 38 m tall overall, it stands on a three-tiered round terrace of white marble.
Twenty-eight columns stand inside: four Dragon Well Columns represent the four seasons, twelve golden columns the twelve months, and twelve eave columns the twelve two-hour periods of the day.
The hall has no great beams; columns, tie-beams and bracket sets support the conical roof layer by layer, the pinnacle of Ming–Qing official-style timber construction.
captions: Line drawing of the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests · Round, triple-eaved
Conical roof · Three-tiered round terrace

hb_jimingyi.name: Jimingyi Post Town
hb_jimingyi.sub: East gate platform and flanking old city walls
hb_jimingyi.yearNote: 1420 is the founding year of the Ming post town recognized by the provincial cultural heritage bureau, with further construction in the Ming and Qing; this plate includes a gate tower restored in modern times, and its timber roof is not claimed as Ming original.
hb_jimingyi.lede: The brick platform of Jimingyi's east gate and the walls on either side preserve the depth of the post town's entrance. What it connects is not just a town but a whole Ming–Qing system of postal relay and military courier roads.
facts: Town site: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau records that Jimingyi Post Town was built in the 18th year of Yongle in the Ming (1420), with further construction in both the Ming and Qing.
Walls: Brick-faced with rammed-earth cores, with one gate each on the east and west; this plate selects the east gate platform and the adjoining wall sections.
Distinguishing restorations: The gate tower in the drawing is based on present-day site photographs, and the dates of the modern restored timber roof and the Ming walls are given separately.

bj_changling.name: Ling'en Hall of Changling, Beijing
bj_changling.sub: Nine-bay nanmu hall · Double-eaved hipped roof
bj_changling.era: Built from Yongle to Xuande · Repaired over the centuries
bj_changling.yearNote: Palace Museum sources record that the sacrificial hall was completed in 1416 and the halls of the mausoleum precinct finished in 1427, while other accounts adopt 1427 as the completion of the hall. 1420 is only an approximate sorting point within the early Ming construction history of the hall drawn; the initial construction of the mausoleum in 1409 is not used as the hall's completion year.
bj_changling.lede: The nine-bay hall spreads beneath a long, broad double-eaved hipped roof, its grid of nanmu columns carrying the roof, while the stone terrace and imperial steps join tier upon tier in front. This plate depicts the Ling'en Hall and does not substitute the initial construction date of the whole Changling precinct for the date of the hall.
facts: The Ling'en Hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep, the core building of Changling's ritual space; the plate selects the surviving hall and its platform.

The Palace Museum's account records that the sacrificial hall was completed in 1416 and the halls of the mausoleum precinct finished in 1427; the construction history and later repairs are marked separately.

Yellow glazed tiles, dark red timberwork, blue-green painted decoration under the eaves and a pale stone platform are zoned according to the present appearance; the nanmu inside the hall is not uniformly drawn as gold.

baoen.name: Pagoda of Great Bao'en Temple, Nanjing
baoen.era: Begun in the 10th year of Yongle · Completed in the 3rd year of Xuande
baoen.lede: Begun in the 10th year of Yongle in the Ming (1412) and completed in the 3rd year of Xuande (1428), it was octagonal with nine stories and 78.2 m tall, clad entirely in white porcelain bricks and five-colored glazed tiles, and more than a hundred lamps on the pagoda burned every night — Europeans called it the “Porcelain Tower of Nanjing” and counted it among the Seven Wonders of the medieval world. It was destroyed in 1856 in the Taiping war, and a glass reconstruction now stands on the original site.
facts: The glazed pagoda had nine stories and eight faces, with a balcony platform and balustrade on every story and bells hanging from the eave corners; 78.2 m tall overall, it was the tallest building in Ming Nanjing.
The body was faced with white porcelain bricks, and the arched doorways were pieced together in five-colored glaze with lions, elephants, flying goats and garudas.

After its destruction, an underground crypt and a Seven-Treasure Ashoka Stupa were excavated at the original site; the reconstruction completed in 2015 uses light steel and glass, taking only the outline and not recreating the brick body.
captions: Nine stories, eight faces · Drawn from the Tushanwan model of the old pagoda
Original pagoda destroyed · Not the modern glass tower

bj_zhihua.name: Zhihua Temple, Beijing
bj_zhihua.sub: Tathagata Hall · Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion
bj_zhihua.era: Founded in the Zhengtong era · Surviving Ming halls
bj_zhihua.yearNote: Official descriptions give 1443 and 1444 respectively as the founding year of Zhihua Temple. 1444 is used for approximate sorting; the temple's founding year cannot be taken directly as the precise date of making of every surviving member.
bj_zhihua.lede: Black-gray glazed tiles cover the upper and lower roofs, and dark red colonnades and blue-green painted decoration are tucked beneath deep eaves. The five-bay Tathagata Hall below and the three-bay Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion above form a compact and clear layering of hall and pavilion.
facts: This plate shows only the south side of the Tathagata Hall and the Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion above it, and does not fold other buildings such as the Zhihua Hall in under the temple's general name.
The lower story is five bays wide and the upper story three; the black glazed tile roofs and the painted decoration under the eaves each keep the colors of their surviving materials.
Zhihua Temple was founded in the Zhengtong era of the Ming; official sources give two founding dates, 1443 and 1444, and the timeline keeps this explanation rather than inventing a precise date.
captions: Zhihua Temple, Beijing · Tathagata Hall and Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion
Ming · Founded 1443–1444

hunyuanwenmiao.name: Hunyuan Confucian Temple
hunyuanwenmiao.place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Yong'an West Street
hunyuanwenmiao.lede: The Dacheng Hall of the Hunyuan Confucian Temple carries a broad roof on its five-bay facade, its central lattice doors with vertical mullions meeting brick walls at either side. The surviving hall is a Ming structure that still retains early building methods; the dragon-carved stone of the imperial path and the inscription “Loyalty, Filial Piety, Chastity, Righteousness” behind the hall record the ritual functions of this prefectural school.
facts: Official sources record that the Confucian Temple was rebuilt on a large scale in the 8th year of Chenghua in the Ming (1472); the surviving buildings are Ming and Qing structures, and the precise completion year of the Dacheng Hall has not been determined.
The Dacheng Hall is five bays wide, with a single-eaved hipped roof; the central three bays of the front eave have lattice doors, and the two ends are brick walls.
The Hunyuan Confucian Temple was listed in 2013 in the seventh batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level.

bj_zhenjue.name: Diamond Throne Pagoda of Zhenjue Temple, Beijing
bj_zhenjue.era: Completed in the 9th year of Chenghua
bj_zhenjue.lede: Five small multi-eaved pagodas stand on a stone throne. Five rows of Buddha figures on the front, animal and floral patterns at the base and an arched entrance are layered one upon another, forming the most striking carved stone silhouette of Beijing's Five Pagoda Temple.
facts: The diamond throne was completed in the 9th year of Chenghua in the Ming (1473); the five pagodas and the throne form a single stone structure, not five separate brick pagodas.

The facade of the throne has five tiers of Buddhist niches, with additional bands of animals and floral patterns at the bottom. In the frontal view the two rear pagodas are hidden, and the five pagodas are not forcibly spread out in a row.

The pagoda eaves and niche figures are carved stone, and the present appearance is mainly gray-beige stone; the glazed members of the small pavilion over the stair to the top are colored separately from the stone pagoda eaves.

hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.name: Qingyuan Tower, Xuanhua
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.sub: Triple-eaved bell tower with cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, and brick platform
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.yearNote: Only one Xuanhua city tower is selected as representative; Zhenshuo Tower and the Five-Dragon Screen are not added.
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.lede: Cross-shaped hip-and-gable roofs overlap tier upon tier, and the bell tower stands on a tall brick platform at the heart of old Xuanhua's streets, its north and south arched passages letting the street run through the tower.
facts: Date: Qingyuan Tower was built in the 18th year of Chenghua in the Ming (1482) and has been repaired through the ages; the surviving main body follows the Ming form.
Structure: The tower has three stories and a triple-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, with the central and wing roofs interpenetrating front and back to form a complex yet clear outline.
City tower: An arched passage runs through the center of the huge brick platform; this entry uses Qingyuan Tower to represent the towers of Xuanhua and does not split off neighboring buildings.

yn_jianshui.name: Jianshui Confucian Temple
yn_jianshui.sub: Hall of the First Teacher · Dacheng Hall
yn_jianshui.yearNote: 1495 is only an approximate sorting point within the Hongzhi era (1488–1505); dating follows the Hall of the First Teacher drawn, and the temple's founding date of 1285 is not substituted for it.
yn_jianshui.place: Yunnan · Jianshui · Old city of Lin'an
yn_jianshui.lede: Beyond the Sea of Learning pond and the successive courtyards, the Hall of the First Teacher faces the old city with a single, spreading roof. The Confucian Temple dates back to the Yuan, while this single-eaved hip-and-gable main hall belongs to the Hongzhi era of the Ming; its stone columns and lattice doors preserve Yunnan craft details in Confucian architecture.
facts: Main subject drawn: The Hall of the First Teacher, that is, the Dacheng Hall, five bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
Date: The hall was built in the Hongzhi era of the Ming (1488–1505); 1285 is the date of the Confucian Temple's original founding.

sx_yuci_chenghuang.name: City God Temple of Yuci
sx_yuci_chenghuang.sub: Xuanjian Tower · Music tower and stage
sx_yuci_chenghuang.era: Ming · Xuanjian Tower and music tower

zhaoling.name: Zhaoling Palace, Xianyou
zhaoling.era: Ming · Exact date to be determined
zhaoling.place: Fujian · Putian · Dingdonghu Village, Xiyuan Township, Xianyou
zhaoling.lede: The hip-and-gable roof spreads low, and slanting wooden rain boards run along the gallery beneath the eaves. Wooden railings and curved-back railing seats enclose the light hall, and a stone platform holds this small temple on the hillside of Dingdonghu Village.

sn_yanan.lede: The octagonal nine-story brick pagoda stands on Baota Hill, its outline now the emblem of Yan'an. The pagoda's Tang–Song history and its layers of Ming restoration coexist, and the plate is drawn according to the form seen today.

gs_jiayuguan.name: Jiayu Pass
gs_jiayuguan.era: Built in the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns, Ming
gs_jiayuguan.yearNote: The drawing shows the Jiayuguan Tower on the west side and its gate platform. The tower was built during the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns of the Ming and repaired continuously in later periods; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point and does not equal a completion year, nor is the establishment of the pass in 1372 used in place of the tower's date.
gs_jiayuguan.lede: A three-story gate tower stands on a massive gate platform, with an arched passage cutting through the loess-colored wall. Only the west tower is shown; the Guanghua and Rouyuan towers are not combined into the same drawing.

gongzhu.name: Gongzhu Temple, Fanshi
gongzhu.lede: Deep in a courtyard in Gongzhu Village, the Mahavira Hall closes the court with plain walls and simple beams. Ming-dynasty Water-and-Land murals are kept inside the three-bay hall, gathering deities from every quarter into a single ritual assembly.
facts: The surviving Mahavira Hall is a Ming-dynasty structure bearing a restoration date of the 16th year of Hongzhi (1503); it was repaired again during the Kangxi reign of the Qing.
The Mahavira Hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof and no bracket sets beneath the eaves.
The hall preserves Ming Water-and-Land murals, in which Buddhist and Daoist deities together form a layered and orderly image of a ritual assembly.

hb_xtkaiyuan.sub: Bodhisattva Hall of the old Kaiyuan Temple (third hall / Sakyamuni Hall), full facade and four coiling-dragon stone columns
hb_xtkaiyuan.yearNote: The Vairocana Hall burned in 1988 and was rebuilt in 1997, so it was not chosen. It must be distinguished from the new temple of 2013 on the east side.
hb_xtkaiyuan.lede: The Bodhisattva Hall of the old Kaiyuan Temple carries its front eaves on four coiling-dragon stone columns; beneath the broad flush gable roof, the layers of the Ming restoration can still be read.
facts: Surviving subject: the drawing shows the Bodhisattva Hall, the third hall of the old temple, also called the Sakyamuni Hall; it was restored in the 13th year of Zhengde in the Ming (1518).
Four columns: the hall is five bays wide; the four coiling-dragon stone columns of the front eaves carry inscriptions dated 1518 and are the key identifying feature of this drawing.
Old and new: neither the Vairocana Hall, rebuilt after the 1988 fire, nor the buildings of the new temple on the east side are taken to represent original Ming fabric.

sx_jiexiu_houtu.name: Houtu Temple, Jiexiu
sx_jiexiu_houtu.sub: Sanqing Tower · Hall and stage combined
sx_jiexiu_houtu.yearNote: The construction of the Sanqing Tower and the Offering Tower in about the Zhengde period is used as the sorting point; the dates 1516 and 1519 in stele records and sources each refer to different things, and 1519 is not forced to stand as the completion year of every component drawn.
sx_jiexiu_houtu.lede: The rear of the Sanqing Tower doubles as the opera stage of the Houtu Temple, a raised platform set between two splayed screen walls. Tiered eaves and glazed ridge ornaments closely join the space for worshipping the deities with the space for performing opera in their honor.
facts: Hall and stage combined: the Sanqing Tower unites hall, tower and stage in one building; the stage on the north side projects as a front annex (baosha) and, with the splayed screen walls on either side, forms an enclosure.

Ming–Qing construction: the present layout took shape mainly in the Ming and Qing; records of the founding of a Sanqing Daoist temple in the Yuan do not mean that the stage in the drawing is entirely Yuan fabric.
Glazed decoration: the ridges and screen walls are lavishly faced with colored glazed tiles; the line drawing keeps the main outlines and the placement of the patterns in fine lines.

tiefo.name: Iron Buddha Temple, Gaoping
tiefo.era: Restored in the 1st year of Jiajing
tiefo.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mishan Town · Mixi Village
tiefo.lede: In the lanes of Mixi Village, the three-bay main hall of the Iron Buddha Temple is finished with an overhanging gable roof and glazed ridge ornaments. Step inside and the Twenty-Four Devas unfold along the walls — glaring, smiling, eyes lowered — their beards, hair and streamers held out on iron wire, giving the clay figures expressions on the verge of movement.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof. The front-eave bracket sets are five-tiered (wucai) with double cantilevers (ang), and a glazed ornament of a lion bearing a treasure vase stands at the center of the ridge.

The Ming painted clay figures of the Twenty-Four Devas inside the hall are modeled in clay over wooden armatures; their beards, hair, headdresses and streamers are shaped with iron wire, making the details light yet full of tension.

The founding date is unknown. In the 7th year of Dading in the Jin (1167) an iron Buddha was cast and the temple restored; it was repaired again in the 1st year of Jiajing (1522) and the 3rd year of Wanli (1575) in the Ming, and in the Qing. The surviving buildings show a Ming–Qing style.

feihong.name: Feihong Pagoda of Guangsheng Temple
feihong.era: Begun in the 10th year of Zhengde · Completed in the 6th year of Jiajing
feihong.lede: Work began in the 10th year of Zhengde in the Ming (1515) and was completed in the 6th year of Jiajing (1527). Octagonal with thirteen stories and 47.31 m tall overall, the pagoda is faced entirely in polychrome glazed tile — red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue and purple. In sunlight it looks like a rainbow, hence the name Feihong, “Flying Rainbow.”
facts: The largest and most complete surviving glazed pagoda in China; a timber gallery surrounds the first story, and the body tapers sharply from story to story.
Beneath the eaves of each story, glazed imitation-timber bracket sets, Buddha niches, guardian figures and coiling dragons have kept their colors to this day.
The “Tang Monk Sweeps the Pagoda” episode of the 1986 television series Journey to the West was filmed here; the Yuan-dynasty murals of the Lower Temple were dispersed overseas long ago.

hb_xianling.sub: Lingxing Gate · Dragon and Phoenix Gate
hb_xianling.yearNote: The surviving Lingxing Gate belongs to the Ming stone remains of the Xianling; 1540 is only a broad sorting point within the Jiajing period, not the exact completion year of this stone archway. Only the stone archway and its linked glazed screen walls are drawn; the stele tower (minglou) restored in 1990 is not drawn, and the founding year of the imperial tomb is not applied to all of its buildings.
hb_xianling.lede: Stone columns raise three gateways, with yellow-glazed screen walls filling the spaces between them. The roof-like stone tops step back to either side, and the central gate opens onto the spirit way, leaving the clearest outline of the mausoleum.
facts: Subject: the stone archway of the Lingxing Gate of the Ming Xianling Mausoleum and its linked glazed screen walls.

Dating: the surviving Lingxing Gate belongs to the Ming stone remains of the Xianling; 1540 is only a broad sorting point within the Jiajing period, not the exact completion year of this stone archway. Only the stone archway and its linked glazed screen walls are drawn; the stele tower (minglou) restored in 1990 is not drawn, and the founding year of the imperial tomb is not applied to all of its buildings.

Plate scope: the Lingxing Gate with three openings, six columns and four roofed tops; the stone columns rising above the gate at the center and sides, with hou beasts and jewels; and the linked yellow-glazed screen walls. taimiao.name: Imperial Ancestral Temple, Beijing
taimiao.lede: The Sacrificial Hall of the Imperial Ancestral Temple spreads its eleven-bay eaves over a three-tier white stone base. Here the emperors once performed rites to their ancestors; massive nanmu columns and a double-eaved hipped roof together hold up this solemn ancestral space.
facts: The Imperial Ancestral Temple was first built in the 18th year of Yongle (1420); this entry follows the date of the Sacrificial Hall's rebuilding in the 24th year of Jiajing (1545).
The Sacrificial Hall is eleven bays wide and six bays deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof of yellow glazed tiles.
The hall stands on a three-tier white marble Sumeru plinth, and its interior preserves sixty-eight columns, each made from a single nanmu trunk.

fuzhoubaita.name: White Pagoda, Fuzhou
fuzhoubaita.lede: At the western foot of Mount Yu, the White Pagoda rises in seven plain white, tapering stories, facing the Black Pagoda on Mount Wu across the city. Shallow eaves, slender pilasters and a small gourd-shaped finial give this city landmark a clear, restrained look.
facts: The White Pagoda's formal name is Baoen Dingguang Duobao Pagoda; it was first built by Wang Shenzhi in the 1st year of Tianyou in the Tang (904).
The surviving pagoda body was rebuilt in the 27th year of Jiajing in the Ming (1548); this entry is classified by the date of this surviving main structure.
It is a seven-story octagonal brick pagoda with a gourd-shaped finial; in 1991 it was listed as a cultural relics protection site at the Fujian provincial level.

sx_haihui.name: Twin Pagodas of Haihui Temple, Yangcheng
sx_haihui.sub: Hexagonal brick pagoda · Octagonal glazed pagoda
sx_haihui.yearNote: 1565 is only a sorting point for the construction period of the large Ming pagoda; sources give either 1561 or 1565–1568. The small pagoda was founded in the Five Dynasties and altered in the Song; the two pagodas were not built in the same year.
sx_haihui.place: Shanxi · Yangcheng · Pagoda courtyard of Haihui Temple, Daqiao Village
sx_haihui.lede: The two brick pagodas of Haihui Temple, one tall and one short, stand side by side like two stretches of history. The small pagoda is covered in Buddha niches; the large one projects a glazed hanging pavilion high up, and its castle-like base gives it an especially solid outline.
facts: Small pagoda, ten stories: the small hexagonal brick pagoda was founded in the Five Dynasties and altered in the Song; its body is densely covered with small niches, and its form differs from that of the large pagoda.

Large pagoda, thirteen stories: the Ming glazed pagoda is octagonal with thirteen stories; its bottom three stories are enclosed by a crenellated outer wall, so the number of exposed eaves cannot be taken directly as the total number of stories.
Pavilion in the air: the tenth story cantilevers out a glazed balcony platform with railings, with three more stories above it — the most distinctive identifying feature of the Haihui twin pagodas.

gx_zhenwu.yearNote: 1573 is taken as the construction date of the Zhenwu Pavilion; the earlier history of the Jinglue Terrace is listed separately from the surviving pavilion, and later repairs do not amount to rebuilding the whole pavilion.

guanyintang.name: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi
guanyintang.lede: Guanyin sits leaning on one knee, a miniature heavenly palace unfolding tier upon tier behind her, with scrolling clouds and crowds of figures suspended toward the beams. The Guanyin Hall of Changzhi sets a dense world of belief inside a small three-bay hall.
facts: Surviving Ming sculpture: the Guanyin Hall was built in the Wanli reign of the Ming, and its surviving painted sculptures and wall sculptures retain Ming craftsmanship; the plate takes the central Guanyin and part of the heavenly palace.

Freestanding and suspended sculpture: the main figure and the lower groups are mostly freestanding, while small figures higher up cling to the walls, beams and the tops of doors and windows, forming a layered space.
Three teachings combined: about five hundred figures in the small hall gather Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist themes in varied sizes, reflecting the composite beliefs of a popular temple.

xuankong.name: Hanging Temple, Hunyuan
xuankong.sub: Pavilions on a sheer cliff · Unity of the Three Teachings
xuankong.place: Shanxi · Hunyuan · Jinlong Gorge, Mount Heng
xuankong.lede: Two three-story flying towers climb the sheer cliff face, the halls strung together by narrow plank walkways. Slender posts and frames driven into the rock together form the Hanging Temple's light yet precarious silhouette.
facts: Ming–Qing structures: the temple's recorded history traces its founding to the Northern Wei, but the surviving buildings are Ming–Qing structures after successive restorations. The plate is dated by the surviving main structures.
North and south towers: two three-story towers, north and south, stand at staggered heights, linked by plank walkways clinging to the cliff; to the left are lower temple buildings.

Three teachings in one hall: the Hall of the Three Teachings at the highest point enshrines Sakyamuni, Laozi and Confucius together, reflecting a temple layout in which Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism coexist.

hn_bigan.sub: Memorial to loyal remonstrance, with temple and tomb joined

The expansion in the 7th year of Hongzhi in the Ming (1494) belongs to the history of the temple complex and is not taken directly as the construction year of every component of the front of the Sacrificial Hall drawn here.
hn_bigan.lede: The Temple of Bi Gan commemorates the loyal Shang-dynasty minister Bi Gan in a layout that joins temple and tomb. The surviving buildings took shape mainly in the Ming and Qing, and the front of the Sacrificial Hall spreads its five-bay facade among ancient cypresses.

Temple in front, tomb behind: the central axis runs from the gate through the stele gallery and the Sacrificial Hall to the burial mound at the rear, forming a layout that combines temple and tomb.

hb_wahuang.sub: Front of the cliff-hugging Wahuang Pavilion
hb_wahuang.yearNote: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau lists the Wahuang Pavilion and other buildings on the mountain as Ming–Qing remains; Handan cultural tourism sources record that a three-story timber pavilion was added on the stone vault in the Ming. 1600 is used only as an approximate sorting value for the Ming–Qing pavilion, and the pavilion is not dated by the year of the Northern Qi carved sutras.
hb_wahuang.lede: The Wahuang Pavilion stands against the cliff of Mount Fenghuang in She County. A three-story timber pavilion is stacked on a grotto and stone vault, its tiers of eaves hugging the slope of the mountain; Northern Qi carved sutras and Ming–Qing architecture lie side by side here.
facts: Surviving date: the pavilion in the drawing is recorded as a Ming–Qing structure; the Northern Qi cliff-carved sutras around it are earlier, and the two are not merged into a single construction date.

Four levels: at the bottom a stone vault fronts a natural cave, with a three-story timber pavilion set above, forming a four-level main structure; the plate shows the visible pavilion facade and the front gallery of the lower level.

Composition: based on 2025 photographs, the drawing shows the cliff-hugging front and the terrace just before it, omits the neighboring pavilions that block the view, and does not reconstruct the unseen rear or a section through the high platform.

im_dazhao.lede: In the old city of Hohhot, Da Zhao joins a Tibetan Buddhist assembly hall and Chinese-style halls into a single whole. sx_yongzuo.name: Twin Pagodas of Yongzuo Temple, Taiyuan
sx_yongzuo.yearNote: 1612 is only an approximate sorting point for the period in which the twin pagodas took shape; the two were built one after the other, and this year is not given as the founding year of both.
sx_yongzuo.lede: Two thirteen-story brick pagodas stand in southeastern Taiyuan, their finials and brick details differing from each other. Side by side, the Wenfeng and Xuanwen pagodas make the twin pagodas an outline by which the city is recognized.
facts: The twin pagodas were built in separate phases during the Wanli reign of the Ming; the Wenfeng Pagoda is earlier, and the Xuanwen Pagoda was completed late in the Wanli reign.

hn_luwang.short: Tomb of the Prince of Lu

rulong.name: Rulong Bridge
rulong.yearNote: According to the county gazetteer it was built in 1625; later repairs do not mean that every component of the bridge is original Ming fabric.
rulong.lede: A long gallery spans the stream, a tall tower lifts its ridge at the bridgehead, and the timber arch traces a broad angular line beneath the board siding. Rulong Bridge joins the road across the stream with a gallery where people can linger; it is the Ming timber-arch covered bridge of Yueshan Village.
facts: Built in the Tianqi reign: the county gazetteer records that Rulong Bridge was built in the 5th year of Tianqi in the Ming (1625); it is one of the surviving Ming timber-arch covered bridges in Qingyuan.

Timber arch structure: the bridge spans the stream on a timber arch frame, its ends resting on masonry abutments; protective boards shield the arch frame, and the gallery shelters travelers from wind and rain.

Staggered heights: the bell tower at the north end, with a triple-eaved hip-and-gable roof, rises high and, together with the central roof and the south entrance, forms a layered outline along the long bridge.

ln_dazheng.name: Dazheng Hall, Shenyang Imperial Palace
ln_dazheng.sub: Octagonal hall with double-eaved pyramidal roof
ln_dazheng.yearNote: 1625 is an approximate sorting point for the early Qing construction; the construction span of the whole palace complex is not taken as the exact completion year of this single hall.
ln_dazheng.lede: An octagonal hall body and a two-tier pyramidal roof gather an early Qing court space for deliberating state affairs beneath yellow tiles. The coiling-dragon columns and red doors and windows on the front are drawn as they look today, without shrinking the whole palace into a single-hall drawing.
facts: The plate's subject is the Dazheng Hall; its octagonal plan, double-eaved pyramidal roof and the coiling-dragon columns on the front are the key identifying features.
Entered as a surviving early Qing hall; the construction history of the Shenyang Imperial Palace complex and the date of this single hall are understood separately.
The roof today has yellow-orange glazed tiles with green edging, and the door columns are dark red; the old colors of the beams are kept as photographed, not historically restored.

quanzhoukaiyuan.name: Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
quanzhoukaiyuan.sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of a Hundred Columns
quanzhoukaiyuan.era: Ming · Restored in the 10th year of Chongzhen
quanzhoukaiyuan.lede: Long double eaves run across the nine-bay hall, and the small pagoda and twin dragons on the main ridge line up against the sky. The Mahavira Hall of Kaiyuan Temple, in the form of its Ming restoration, carries on the daily worship of Quanzhou's thousand-year-old Buddhist temple.
facts: Ming restoration: the Mahavira Hall was restored to its present form in the 10th year of Chongzhen in the Ming (1637); the plate is dated by the surviving main structure.

Nine bays, a hundred columns: the hall is nine bays wide and commonly called the Hall of a Hundred Columns; in fact, through column reduction it retains 86 columns, enlarging the space for worship inside.

Flying apsara musicians: where the beam frame meets the stone columns there are 24 carved wooden flying apsaras playing music, serving both as structural supports and as decoration — a testimony to Quanzhou's multicultural heritage.

xiaoxitian.name: Xiaoxitian, Xi County
xiaoxitian.sub: Hall filled with suspended sculpture · Thousand Buddha Hermitage
xiaoxitian.lede: The main Buddha sits upright as heavenly palaces unfold tier upon tier above his head. Suspended pavilions, crowds of figures and draperies turn a hall of less than 170 square meters into a three-dimensional Buddha land.
facts: Clay over wooden armatures: the figure groups in the Mahavira Hall are suspended sculptures of clay over wooden armatures, gilded and painted, with figures, pavilions and ornament layered one over another.

A Buddha land in a small space: the hall covers about 169.6 square meters yet holds nearly two thousand painted sculptures; figures large and small and the architecture of the heavenly palaces together create depth.

Late Ming–early Qing: the temple was founded in the Ming, and the surviving suspended sculptures belong to the late Ming–early Qing phase of work. The plate takes the central main niche and part of the heavenly-palace pavilions.

tj_wenmiao.sub: Dacheng Hall of the prefectural temple · Central facade and ceremonial stair
tj_wenmiao.era: Founded in the 1st year of Zhengtong · Present form from Ming–Qing repairs
tj_wenmiao.yearNote: 1436 is the year the Confucian Temple was founded and is not used directly as the date of manufacture of all the surviving components of the Dacheng Hall drawn here. 1650 is only an approximate sorting point for the present form shaped by Ming–Qing repairs, not the exact completion year of the Dacheng Hall.

tj_wenmiao.lede: Beneath orange-yellow glazed tiles, blue-green painted decoration and dark red doors and windows frame the entrance to the Dacheng Hall. The plate focuses on the central facade, the incense burner and the stone ceremonial stair; it is explicitly a detail and does not use close-up photographs to invent the unseen full hall.
facts: The Tianjin Confucian Temple was founded in 1436 and preserves a layout in which the prefectural temple, the county temple and the school stand side by side; this drawing takes the central part of the prefectural temple's Dacheng Hall.

The plate shows the three central bays of the facade beneath the eaves, the incense burner and the ceremonial stair; it does not represent the hall's full number of bays or the layout of the whole temple.

The colors of the present yellow glazed tiles, blue-green painted decoration, dark red timberwork and light gray stone terrace are taken from photographs; modern repairs and the original founding are described separately.

xianshen.name: Xianshen Tower, Jiexiu
xianshen.sub: Street-spanning tower and music tower · Composite pavilion
xianshen.era: Qing · Late Shunzhi to early Kangxi
xianshen.lede: The street passes beneath the tower, and a stage opens out above the gateway. Xianshen Tower stacks different uses into linked pavilions; glazed double eaves and gable ends interlock, tracing a singular skyline in the city of Jiexiu.
facts: Early Qing rebuilding: the surviving tower was rebuilt between the late Shunzhi and early Kangxi reigns and later repaired; the tower's name and the history of early Xian (Zoroastrian) worship do not equal the date of the surviving timberwork.

Three in one: a street-spanning tower, a temple gate and a music tower form a building with a projecting, convex plan; the front serves for passage, the rear leads into the temple, and the upper level doubles as a stage.

Interlocking double eaves: the joined hip-and-gable roofs, projecting gable ends and tiers of overhanging eaves form a composite outline, with the glazed ridge ornaments and timber bracket sets (puzuo) setting each other off.

gz_wenchang.name: Wenchang Pavilion, Guiyang
gz_wenchang.sub: East of the old city · Three stories, three eaves
gz_wenchang.era: Rebuilt in the 8th year of Kangxi
gz_wenchang.yearNote: First built in 1609; the entry is placed according to the surviving pavilion formed by the 1669 rebuilding and later repairs, as given in official Guiyang municipal sources, and the founding year is not substituted for the surviving main structure.
gz_wenchang.lede: The Wenchang Pavilion rises from the eastern part of Guiyang's old city, yet its three-story, triple-eaved roof is neither the usual four-cornered nor eight-cornered form. Its nine-cornered outline is its identifying feature; the Ming founding, the Qing rebuilding and repeated repairs together shaped the pavilion seen today.
facts: Dates: first built in the 37th year of Wanli in the Ming (1609), rebuilt in the 8th year of Kangxi in the Qing (1669), and repaired many times since.
Form: three stories, triple eaves and a nine-cornered roof; the plate does not mix the adjacent city gate tower into the Wenchang Pavilion.
Dating: this guide places it by the surviving rebuilding phase, with the founding date explained separately.

yn_jindian.name: Golden Hall, Kunming
yn_jindian.era: Recast in the 10th year of Kangxi
yn_jindian.yearNote: The surviving bronze hall drawn here was rebuilt by Wu Sangui in 1671; the bronze hall first built in 1602 and its relocation are recorded separately, and the Golden Hall of the Wudang Mountains is not mistakenly used as a reference.
yn_jindian.lede: From afar it looks like a timber hall; only up close does one find that the roof, columns, beams, doors and windows are all cast in bronze. The surviving Golden Hall on Mount Mingfeng was built in the 10th year of Kangxi; the bronze has darkened through wind and rain, yet the metal structure still keeps the details of a traditional hall.
facts: Surviving subject: the bronze hall rebuilt by Wu Sangui in the 10th year of Kangxi in the Qing (1671).

Distinguishing its history: the bronze hall first built in the 30th year of Wanli in the Ming (1602) was later moved away, and its date is not taken as the construction year of the bronze hall seen today.

hb_qingdongling.name: Eastern Qing Tombs
hb_qingdongling.sub: Stone memorial archway on the Xiaoling spirit way
hb_qingdongling.yearNote: The date 1672 is adopted for the stone archway drawn here: Wang Qiheng, on the basis of the Xiaoling drawings and the archives on the transport of stone, established that the components were transported at the end of 1671 and the archway completed in early 1672. The early main works of the Xiaoling in 1663–1664 and the traditionally recorded ancillary works of 1668 are not used as the date of this stone archway.
hb_qingdongling.lede: The five-bay, six-column, eleven-roof stone memorial archway stands at the southern end of the Xiaoling spirit way, opening the ceremonial sequence of the Eastern Qing Tombs with a run of stone roofs at staggered heights.
facts: Construction: the architectural historian Wang Qiheng established from archival records that the stone archway was completed early in the 11th year of Kangxi (1672).
Form: five bays, six stone columns and eleven roofed tops at staggered heights make up a complete stone archway imitating timber construction.

Scope of the entry: the whole Eastern Qing Tombs area forms a single record; this drawing takes the stone archway on the Xiaoling spirit way as representative and does not split the entry into the individual imperial tombs.

sd_mengmiao.name: Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple, Zoucheng
sd_mengmiao.sub: Seven bays, double-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Green glazed tiles
sd_mengmiao.era: Rebuilt in the 12th year of Kangxi, later repaired
sd_mengmiao.yearNote: The surviving hall is placed at 1673, when it was rebuilt five years after the earthquake damage of 1668; the comprehensive repair of 1736 and modern renovations are described separately. It is not the original fabric of the hall first built in the Northern Song.
sd_mengmiao.lede: Double green eaves spread over the seven-bay hall, and stone columns alternate with vermilion doors beneath them. Rebuilt in the Qing after an earthquake, the Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple remains the center of the worship of Mencius in Zoucheng.
facts: History: an earthquake in 1668 damaged the main hall, which was rebuilt five years later; it underwent a comprehensive repair in 1736, and its present state also reflects modern renovation.
Form: seven bays wide, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof covered in green glazed tiles; stone columns on the outer eaves and timberwork on the inner eaves together support the hall.

Identifying the subject: the drawing shows the Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple, not the main hall of the adjoining Mencius Family Mansion, and it is not to be confused with the Dacheng Hall of the Temple of Confucius in Qufu.

daimiao.name: Tiankuang Hall of the Dai Temple
daimiao.lede: At the foot of Mount Tai, the Tiankuang Hall spreads two broad tiers of eaves to the scale of the rites to the sacred mountain. From its founding in the Song to its Qing restoration, its beam frame, doors, windows and murals layer the memories of different periods.
facts: The Tiankuang Hall is the main hall of the Dai Temple, dedicated to the god of Mount Tai; founded in the Song, it has been repaired many times since.
The hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof covered in yellow glazed tiles.
The proportions and construction methods of the surviving timber frame show Qing characteristics, and the murals inside the hall were repainted in the early Qing.

A Kangxi-era stele records that the restoration was completed in 1677, keeping the usable beams and columns of the hall and replacing damaged members; the timeline places it approximately on this basis, with later repairs counted separately.

gugong.name: Forbidden City, Beijing
gugong.lede: The Hall of Supreme Harmony stands on a three-tier white marble base, commanding the Outer Court with its eleven-bay width and double-eaved hipped roof. Broad ceremonial stairs lift the hall on high; its present form comes from the rebuilding of the Kangxi reign.
facts: Work on the surviving Hall of Supreme Harmony began in the 34th year of Kangxi (1695) and was completed in the 36th year (1697).
Eleven bays wide and five bays deep, it is the foremost of the three great halls of the Outer Court of the Forbidden City.

The roof is a double-eaved hipped roof, with the number of ridge beasts on the eave corners increased to ten; important ceremonies such as enthronements and imperial weddings were once held in the hall.

mimi.place: Shanxi · Fanshi · Yantou Township · Mimo Cliff
mimi.lede: Beneath Mimo Cliff, the Manjushri Hall faces the valley with a broad, plain front gallery. Timber columns, lattice doors and painted panels under the eaves make up its five-bay facade, and its Qing painting preserves the Manjushri worship of this area.
facts: Five bays, flush gable roof: the plate takes the Manjushri Hall, five bays wide, with a timber gallery in front and central steps leading up to the raised hall base.
Qing painting: the panel paintings of the front gallery and the murals inside the hall present the beliefs of Mount Wutai; it is classified by its surviving Qing main structure.
National protected site: Mimi Temple was listed in 2006 in the sixth batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level.

hn_kangbaiwan.name: Kang Baiwan Manor
hn_kangbaiwan.era: Late Ming–early Qing · Extended over generations

hn_kangbaiwan.lede: The facade of a storied cave dwelling and the buildings on either side enclose a long, deep inner courtyard. Kang Baiwan Manor combines caves dug into the cliff with siheyuan courtyard houses, preserving the living spaces of a merchant family of the Heluo region.
facts: Date of the manor: the Zhengzhou Municipal Bureau of Cultural Heritage dates the manor to the late Ming–early Qing; it was built up over many generations of the Kang family, and the surviving courtyards were not completed in the same year.
Local form: the manor has cave dwellings dug against the cliff and storied buildings along the street, with residential courtyards laid out as siheyuan, combining timber, brick and stone elements.

Plate scope: based on photographs of the inner courtyard, it shows the front of the storied cave dwelling with arched openings above and below and the inward-facing houses on either side; the incomplete surrounding walls are left blank at the edges, and hidden exterior views are not added.

gx_gongcheng.lede: The Dacheng Hall stands on a high platform, its double eaves and ceramic-sculpture ridges drawing the eye upward. The plate takes only the main hall of the Confucian temple and does not include the incense-burner pavilion, the side halls or the adjacent Martial Temple.

hu_zhanggu.era: Built over generations in the Ming–Qing

hu_zhanggu.lede: Gray-tiled ridges run into one another, with skywells and gable walls hidden among the layers of roofs. What is drawn here is one corner of the old village, not more than a thousand rooms compressed into a single house.
facts: Subject: part of the roofscape of the Ming–Qing dwellings of Zhangguying Village.

yn_jingzhen.yearNote: 1701 is the year the Octagonal Pavilion was founded; later repairs, such as those of 1978 and 1993, are recorded separately, and the other, now destroyed buildings of Jingzhen Temple are not invented in the drawing.
yn_jingzhen.lede: The Octagonal Pavilion is not a small garden pavilion for enjoying the view but the ordination hall of a Dai Theravada Buddhist temple. Tiered roofs spread out in eight directions and close lightly into a spire; most of the original Jingzhen Temple no longer survives, and the ordination hall built in 1701 has lasted to the present through repeated repairs.
facts: Use: the ordination hall of a Theravada Buddhist temple, and also an important surviving historic building of Jingzhen Temple.

fj_chengqi.lede: A ring of yellow-brown rammed-earth wall gathers in hundreds of rooms, its tiled eaves projecting lightly along the circumference. With a four-story outer ring and layer upon layer of inner courtyards, Chengqi Lou has housed a shared life in the mountains of Yongding.
