Space: the outer ring has four stories, with several concentric ring-shaped courtyards inside and an ancestral hall at the center; this drawing shows only the complete exterior and makes no hypothetical cutaway.

hn_wuhou.sub: Honoring a worthy beneath the eaves
hn_wuhou.era: Qing structure · Repaired over the centuries
hn_wuhou.yearNote: 1711 — the comprehensive restoration of the whole shrine in the 50th year of Kangxi in the Qing, as officially recorded — is taken as an approximate sorting point, without asserting on this basis that the surviving Great Worship Hall was built entirely in that year. hn_wuhou.lede: Deep among the columns and beams of the Great Worship Hall, tiers of inscribed plaques surround the ritual space. The Wuhou Shrine of Nanyang has been built up and repaired many times, and the space beneath its eaves still keeps the traces of generations commemorating Zhuge Liang.
facts: Surviving date: Nanyang's official list of protected sites classifies the Wuhou Shrine as Qing; local government records note the construction of the main hall in the Ming and the comprehensive restoration of the whole shrine in 1711, with many repairs since.

sx_jiezhou_guandi.sub: Chongning Hall · Ancestral temple of Guandi
sx_jiezhou_guandi.yearLabel: Qing · Rebuilt after the Kangxi-era fire
sx_jiezhou_guandi.yearNote: 1725 is only an approximate sorting point for the rebuilding phase in the early 18th century, not the exact completion year of the Chongning Hall; 1702 is the year of the temple fire.
sx_jiezhou_guandi.lede: With its seven-bay hall and surrounding stone colonnade, the Chongning Hall anchors the central axis of the ancestral temple; beneath its double eaves, dragon columns, stone balustrades and plaques from successive periods together display the ritual space of the worship of Guan Yu.

hb_qingxiling.name: Western Qing Tombs
hb_qingxiling.sub: Front elevation of the Long'en Hall of the Tailing
hb_qingxiling.yearNote: The whole tomb complex forms one entry, represented by the Long'en Hall of the Tailing; the Palace Museum gives 1736 as the completion date, which is recorded separately from the burial in 1737.
hb_qingxiling.lede: With its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and high stone base, the Long'en Hall of the Tailing forms the ceremonial center of the earliest imperial tomb of the Western Qing Tombs. The plate chooses this hall to represent the entire tomb area.
facts: Dating: work on the Tailing began in 1730 and was completed in 1736; the burial in 1737 is a separate milestone.
Hall form: the Long'en Hall is five bays wide and three bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof; in front of the platform the imperial ramp lies alongside flights of steps on either side.
Tomb area: the Western Qing Tombs are recorded as a single tomb complex; this drawing shows only the Long'en Hall of the Tailing and does not stand for the layout of the whole site.

feiyun.name: Dongyue Temple, Wanrong
feiyun.era: Restored in the 11th year of Qianlong
feiyun.lede: The eave corners of the Feiyun Tower project tier upon tier in all four directions, with bracket sets clustered like clouds around the body of the tower. Looking up from below, the three-story tower, interlocking front annexes and cross-shaped hip-and-gable roofs join into a light yet intricate timber silhouette.
facts: The tower's founding date is unknown, and its present appearance results from Ming and Qing restorations; this entry is displayed under the date of the Qianlong restoration of 1746.

The ground floor is five bays wide and five bays deep; the tower has three stories visible outside and five levels within, with cross-shaped hip-and-gable roofs in three stories and four tiers of eaves.
The whole tower is 23.19 m tall; through-columns and layered bracket sets support its body, while small drip eaves and front annexes enrich its outline.

hu_tianhou.name: Tianhou Temple, Zhijiang
hu_tianhou.sub: Gate of the Tianhou Temple · Bluestone relief
hu_tianhou.yearNote: Placed by the construction date, 1748, of the surviving bluestone gate archway; the history of the Fujian Guild Hall from 1684 is listed separately. The drawing shows the stone archway and the steps immediately adjoining it, not the whole compound of the Tianhou Temple.
hu_tianhou.place: Hunan · Zhijiang · West bank of the Wushui River
hu_tianhou.lede: On the bluestone of a single gate archway, figures, birds and beasts, flowers and trees unfold layer upon layer. The raised center and lower eaves on either side give even the carving an architectural rhythm.
facts: Subject: the complete facade of the stone archway of the Tianhou Temple, Zhijiang.

Dating: placed by the construction date, 1748, of the surviving bluestone gate archway; the history of the Fujian Guild Hall from 1684 is listed separately. The drawing shows the stone archway and the steps immediately adjoining it, not the whole compound of the Tianhou Temple.

Plate scope: the stone gate archway, high in the center and lower at the sides, with its carved stone panels and central doorway; the fish-shaped ridge ornaments at the top are complete, and the stone drums at the base and the stone lions near the gate on either side are kept, without extending the full length of the enclosing wall.
captions: Complete facade of the stone archway, Tianhou Temple, Zhijiang · Line drawing

hn_zhongyue.name: Zhongyue Temple, Mount Song
hn_zhongyue.sub: Central facade of the Junji Hall (detail)
hn_zhongyue.yearNote: 1750 is an approximate sorting point for the Qing appearance, not the exact rebuilding year of the Junji Hall; the hall underwent a major repair in 1986.
hn_zhongyue.lede: With its double-eaved hipped roof and high platform with stone steps, the Junji Hall forms the center of the Zhongyue Temple. The central facade, glimpsed among ancient trees, keeps legible the scale and ritual order of the buildings for the worship of the Five Sacred Mountains.
facts: The full Junji Hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep; its present appearance is mainly the result of Qing construction and later repairs.
Ancient trees in front hide the wings, so this drawing takes only the central five bays and the stone steps, with the eaves fading out to either side to indicate a detail.
The history of the Zhongyue Temple can be traced back to early mountain worship, but the dates in the temple's history cannot be taken directly as the date of the surviving Junji Hall.

sx_jiexiu_chenghuang.name: City God Temple, Jiexiu
sx_jiexiu_chenghuang.yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate timeline position for the Qing building, not the exact completion year of the stage; the founding of the temple and the surviving Ming main hall have their own dates.
sx_jiexiu_chenghuang.lede: A round-ridge flush gable roof and a hip-and-gable front annex projecting into the courtyard combine to form the inward-facing opera stage of the City God Temple; carved corbel brackets (queti) and glazed ridge ornaments link the spaces of worship, temple fairs and opera performance.
facts: Five-bay stage: the stage as a whole is five bays wide; at the front, the central and flanking bays project outward as a hip-and-gable front annex, forming a three-bay open stage front.
Distinguishing dates: the temple originated in the Hongwu reign of the Ming, and the surviving main hall is a Ming structure; the stage in the drawing is registered as Qing, with later repairs.
Combined roofs: a round-ridge flush gable roof sits beside the projecting hip-and-gable roof in front; the glazed ridges and wood-carved decoration are important identifying features of the building.
captions: City God Temple, Jiexiu · Inward-facing opera stage

hb_bishushanzhuang.name: Chengde Mountain Resort
hb_bishushanzhuang.sub: Front elevation of the Danbo Jingcheng Hall
hb_bishushanzhuang.yearNote: The whole resort forms one entry; the founding of the hall in 1711 and the rebuilding of the present main structure in 1754 are kept separate.
hb_bishushanzhuang.lede: The Danbo Jingcheng Hall is the main hall of the Main Palace of the Mountain Resort. Its round-ridge hip-and-gable roof spreads broad and open, and its nanmu frame, without heavy painted decoration, conveys the plain taste of the resort's palaces.
facts: Surviving date: founded in the 50th year of Kangxi (1711) and rebuilt in nanmu in the 19th year of Qianlong (1754); this guide places it at 1754, the date of the surviving main structure.
Form: seven bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved round-ridge hip-and-gable roof, and a broad terrace and steps in front of the hall.

Scope of the entry: the entire Mountain Resort is recorded as a single entry; this drawing takes only the Danbo Jingcheng Hall of the Main Palace as representative and does not mix in later pavilions.

im_wudang.name: Wudang Monastery
im_wudang.yearNote: The Suguqin Hall is a building of the Qianlong period of the Qing; sources differ between 1755 and 1757, and 1755 serves only as an approximate sorting point. The 1749 expansion of the monastery is not used to fix the completion of the hall drawn here.
im_wudang.lede: In a valley of the Yin Mountains, Wudang Monastery spreads its white-walled, flat-roofed Tibetan-style halls tier by tier along the slope. The Suguqin Hall at the front of the monastery is the space where the whole community gathers to chant sutras; its broad, steady mass contrasts sharply with the curved roofs of the timber halls of the Central Plains.
facts: Subject drawn: the Suguqin Hall, also called the Suguqin Dugong; it is not merged with the whole monastery or with the Nuni Hall rebuilt in 2005 into a single building.
Date: the monastery was expanded in the 14th year of Qianlong (1749); the Suguqin Hall is placed approximately in the Qianlong period, as sources differ on the hall's own construction year.
Form: a Tibetan-style flat roof, white walls, stepped terraces and a dark eave band; Wudang Monastery was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1996.
captions: Suguqin Hall, Wudang Monastery · Line drawing · Pending user review

hb_puning.name: Puning Temple
hb_puning.sub: Complete elevation of the Mahayana Pavilion
hb_puning.yearNote: The Chinese-Tibetan building complex forms a single entry, without a separate entry for the great Buddha statue; the Mahayana Pavilion is the representative.
hb_puning.lede: Within its six tiers of eaves and stepped tapering, the Mahayana Pavilion houses a colossal Thousand-Armed, Thousand-Eyed Guanyin, bringing Chinese and Tibetan Buddhist temple forms together in a single tall pavilion.
facts: Date: Puning Temple was built from the 20th to the 23rd year of Qianlong (1755–1758); the Mahayana Pavilion is the core building at the rear.

Form: the Mahayana Pavilion shows six tiers of eaves on the outside, and its top consists of a central roof and four corner roofs, forming an outline in which the raised center is guarded by the four corners.
Guanyin: the pavilion enshrines a large carved wooden Thousand-Armed, Thousand-Eyed Guanyin; the building's height, its structure between floors and the statue within together organize the space.

sx_dingcun.name: Dingcun Folk Houses
sx_dingcun.sub: Ding Kun Compound · Southern Shanxi courtyard house
sx_dingcun.era: Qianlong period, Qing · Ding Kun Compound
sx_dingcun.yearNote: 1760 is only for approximate sorting within the Qianlong period. The Ding Kun family built over three generations across about 50 years, and no precise completion year is invented for the hall drawn here.
sx_dingcun.lede: On the east bank of the Fen River, Dingcun gathers the life of southern Shanxi families into one courtyard house after another. The three-bay hall of the Ding Kun Compound is notable for its woodcarving and stone column bases, and the side wings on either side enclose a deep, quiet courtyard.
facts: Ming–Qing houses: the surviving courtyards of the Dingcun historic building complex span the Wanli reign of the Ming to the Republic of China; the Ding Kun Compound drawn here was built in the Qianlong period of the Qing.
Three generations of building: Lian Da's field records note that this compound was built successively by three generations — Ding Kun, Ding Jialun and Ding Xilian, grandfather, son and grandson.

Courtyard view: this drawing takes the three-bay hall and part of the side wings, keeping the relationship between the timber gallery columns and the courtyard; it does not represent the complete village plan.

quanzhouwenmiao.name: Quanzhou Prefectural Confucian Temple
quanzhouwenmiao.sub: Dacheng Hall · Qing structure in Song style
quanzhouwenmiao.lede: Broad double eaves press down on the seven-bay hall, and carved stone dragon columns stretch out beneath them. Rebuilt in the Qing, the Dacheng Hall of the Quanzhou Prefectural Confucian Temple still follows the dignified frame of a Song-style hipped hall.
facts: Present Qing hall: the Dacheng Hall was completed in the 26th year of Qianlong in the Qing (1761), retaining the structural features of its rebuilding in the Xianchun reign of the Song.
Seven-bay hipped hall: the Dacheng Hall is seven bays wide and five bays deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof; the carved stone dragon columns in front are a feature of its facade.

Temple and school in one: the Quanzhou Prefectural Confucian Temple served both for the worship of Confucius and as the prefectural school, testifying to the old city's tradition of Confucian education; the plate takes the Dacheng Hall alone.

hb_putuozongcheng.name: Putuo Zongcheng Temple
hb_putuozongcheng.sub: Complete front of the Great Red Terrace and its surviving upper roofs
hb_putuozongcheng.yearNote: An independent temple complex forming one entry; it is not combined with the Xumi Fushou Temple into one entry, nor split into separate courtyards to pad the count.
hb_putuozongcheng.lede: The massive Great Red Terrace rises above tier upon tier of white terraces; its square windows, glazed niches and Chinese-style eaves at the top display the distinctive Chinese-Tibetan synthesis of the Eight Outer Temples of Chengde.
facts: Date: the Putuo Zongcheng Temple was built from the 32nd to the 36th year of Qianlong (1767–1771), with the Potala Palace as its main architectural model.

Subject: the drawing shows the core Great Red Terrace and the white terraces immediately beside it; the square blind windows on the broad wall and the central band of glazed niches are prominent features.

Space: the Great Red Terrace encloses spaces for worship such as the Wanfa Guiyi Hall; the plate takes the south exterior and does not split the panorama of the hillside temple complex into multiple entries.

hn_kfhuiguan.name: Shanxi-Shaanxi-Gansu Guild Hall, Kaifeng
hn_kfhuiguan.sub: Front of the timber memorial archway
hn_kfhuiguan.yearNote: The subject drawn is dated to the Qing; the numerical year is only for approximate sorting.
hn_kfhuiguan.lede: Five roofs at staggered heights rest on two clusters of columns, and woodcarving and stone column bases finely adorn the facade of this merchant guild hall. The wide passage in the middle makes the archway appear both elaborate and open.
facts: The guild hall was built with pooled funds during the Qianlong reign of the Qing; 1776 is a year in the guild hall's founding history and is not taken directly as the exact completion year of the archway.
The archway has three bays, six columns and five roofs; the columns are divided into two groups of supports staggered front to back, rather than six columns in a single row.
The plate draws the timber archway from 2023 frontal photographs; the halls behind and the side galleries are omitted.

sx_xinjiang_longxing.name: Longxing Temple, Xinjiang County
sx_xinjiang_longxing.era: Qing · Qianlong restoration with added stories
sx_xinjiang_longxing.yearNote: This year is the date of the Qing restoration that added stories, producing the surviving thirteen-story exterior; neither the temple's Tang history nor early remains inside the pagoda are equated directly with the date of the exterior.
sx_xinjiang_longxing.lede: The Longxing Pagoda tapers story by story with flat, corbeled brick eaves, its thirteen-story silhouette standing on the high ground in the north of the old Jiangzhou city. The surviving brick-cased exterior and the added stories record the Qing restoration of an earlier pagoda.
facts: Thirteen-story pagoda: the pagoda is octagonal in plan, its thirteen stories gradually diminishing in height, with the body divided by corbeled brick eaves; it is about 42 m tall overall.

Qing additions: sources record that in the restoration of the 49th year of Qianlong (1784) it was cased in gray brick and raised from eight to thirteen stories; the plate is dated by this surviving exterior.
Layers of an old temple: Longxing Temple also preserves a Yuan main hall, painted sculptures and the Biluo Stele, remains of different dates; this drawing shows only the pagoda.

hn_guanlin.name: Guanlin, Luoyang
hn_guanlin.yearNote: The plate takes the Qianqiujian Stage Tower and is dated by its construction in 1791; the history of the Guanlin hall complex from the Wanli reign of the Ming is not used for the coloring of this stage tower.
hn_guanlin.lede: On its high platform, the Qianqiujian Stage Tower faces the main gate of Guanlin. The hip-and-gable front stage overlaps the flush-gable rear stage, leaving a distinct outline of a Qing space for ritual opera.
facts: Stage tower drawn: also called Qianqiujian, the stage tower was built in the 56th year of Qianlong in the Qing (1791) and faces the main gate of Guanlin across a square.

Composite roof: the stage tower has a convex plan, combining a hip-and-gable roof over the front stage with a flush gable roof over the rear stage, giving it the appearance of a double-eaved pavilion.

Layout of Guanlin: Guanlin's shrine halls and burial mound together form courtyards on a central axis, and its surviving buildings include structures from several Ming and Qing phases; this drawing takes only the stage tower and does not split the site into duplicate entries.

hn_shedian.name: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Shedian
hn_shedian.yearNote: 1800 is an approximate sorting point for the Qing construction phase to which the Xuanjian Tower belongs. Officially reproduced material contains the conversion error “1st year of Jiaqing = 1786,” so that figure is not adopted as a precise completion year; 1756–1892 is the construction span of the whole guild hall complex.
hn_shedian.place: Henan · Nanyang · Shedian Town, Sheqi County
hn_shedian.lede: The Xuanjian Tower of the Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall at Shedian raises its stage above the courtyard, its central triple-eaved block joined to pavilions on either side. Opera performed in honor of the gods at this merchants' guild hall is framed by layered roofs and an open stage front.
facts: Guild hall: built with funds raised by merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi, the guild hall served both for gatherings of fellow provincials and for the worship of Guan Yu.

Phases: the guild hall complex was built in phases from 1756 to 1892; the Xuanjian Tower belongs to the earlier works, and the founding year of the whole complex is not taken directly as the date of the opera tower.

Opera tower: the Xuanjian Tower is the guild hall's stage, forming a symmetrical composition with its triple-eaved main block and flanking pavilions; this drawing excludes the separate viewing galleries on either side.

hb_jingjue.name: Jingjue Temple
hb_jingjue.sub: Xiangfu Palace and its projecting round-ridge front annex
hb_jingjue.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau identifies the surviving temple buildings as Qing; 1800 is only an approximate Qing sorting value. No precise construction year has been found for the Xiangfu Palace itself, and the tradition of a Tang founding is not used to date the present structure.
hb_jingjue.lede: The main hall of Jingjue Temple in Yutian, the Xiangfu Palace, has a projecting round-ridge front annex; stone columns, timber framing and the broad roof meet, showing the fine decoration and construction of a temple restored in the Qing.
facts: Dating: the surviving main structures are recorded as Qing remains, with an approximate date; records of the temple's early founding do not equal the construction year of the present hall.

Main hall: the Xiangfu Palace drawn here is a timber main hall with a hip-and-gable roof and a round-ridge front annex, distinct from the Mahavira Hall with double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in the rear courtyard.

Courtyards: the temple's gate, gateway stele tower and bell and drum towers each differ in form; this drawing takes only the main hall and does not mistake the stele tower for a pagoda or the main hall.

gs_fuxi.name: Fuxi Temple, Tianshui
gs_fuxi.era: Enlarged in the 10th year of Jiaqing, Qing
gs_fuxi.yearNote: The Ceremonial Gate was first built in 1523 and changed from three bays to five during the 1805 restoration; the drawing shows the surviving five-bay gate, dated by its 1805 form, and does not take the founding of the whole temple in 1483–1484 as the date of this gate. Repairs to the roofs and eaves, including those of the Ceremonial Gate, were completed in early 2026.
gs_fuxi.lede: The five-bay Ceremonial Gate lies across the central axis, leaving a ceremonial passage between its red columns. It is neither the memorial archway at the very front nor the Xiantian Hall behind.
facts: Subject: the Ceremonial Gate of the Fuxi Temple.

Dating: the Ceremonial Gate was first built in 1523 and changed from three bays to five during the 1805 restoration; the drawing shows the surviving five-bay gate, dated by its 1805 form, and does not take the founding of the whole temple in 1483–1484 as the date of this gate. Repairs to the roofs and eaves, including those of the Ceremonial Gate, were completed in early 2026.

Plate scope: the five-bay, single-eaved Ceremonial Gate and the short steps before it; the red columns and the open central passage. The Xiantian Hall behind, the cypresses and the ancillary buildings to the left and right are not drawn; the plaque is left blank.

hb_dzgongyuan.name: Dingzhou Examination Hall
hb_dzgongyuan.sub: Complete front elevation of the Kui Pavilion and examination cells
hb_dzgongyuan.yearNote: The intention is to use the Qing enlarged form shown by the surviving Kui Pavilion and examination cells; the precise founding year of the individual building needs further verification at the photograph stage.
hb_dzgongyuan.lede: Seven groups of roofs rise tier upon tier like a mountain range, the central Kui Pavilion joined to the examination cells on either side, preserving the architectural memory of local imperial examinations in the Qing.
facts: Imperial examinations: the examination hall was founded in the 3rd year of Qianlong (1738) and enlarged in the 14th year of Daoguang (1834); its present scale was formed mainly by this enlargement.

Form: the drawing shows the front of the Kui Pavilion and examination cells; the central Kui Pavilion rises high, the cells on either side step down in turn, and the seven groups of roofs form a distinctive symmetrical outline.
Remains: the compound preserves buildings such as the examination cells, the Kui Pavilion and the Lansheng Tower — rare surviving remains of a local Qing imperial examination site.

sx_jishan_jiwang.name: Jiwang Temple, Jishan
sx_jishan_jiwang.sub: Offering Hall · Bell and drum towers
sx_jishan_jiwang.yearNote: The Offering Hall, bell and drum towers and Houji Tower drawn here are Qing rebuildings; the Yuan-dynasty Jiangyuan Hall in the temple is not drawn.
sx_jishan_jiwang.place: Shanxi · Jishan · West Street of the county town
sx_jishan_jiwang.lede: The Offering Hall and the bell and drum towers spread a cluster of delicate eaves in the town of Jishan, with the Houji Tower rising behind. Glazed tile, woodcarving and stone carving together tell of the local tradition of worshipping Houji and valuing agriculture.
facts: Qing rebuilding: the surviving Offering Hall, Houji Tower and bell and drum towers are Qing; the 1843 rebuilding and later repairs left a complete group of ritual buildings.
Three crafts together: the Jiwang Temple is renowned for its glazed tile, woodcarving and stone carving; the agricultural carvings on the beams of the Offering Hall depict plowing and harvest.

Distinguishing structures: the Jiangyuan Hall and others in the temple preserve Yuan main structures; this drawing shows the Offering Hall, the bell and drum towers and the upper eaves of the Houji Tower, and is not colored as Yuan.

xitai.name: Ancient Opera Stages of Ninghai
xitai.sub: Hu Clan Ancestral Hall, Aohu · Chongxing Temple · City God Temple
xitai.era: Qing to Republic · Aohu stage, 4th year of Xianfeng
xitai.lede: Ninghai County has 125 surviving old opera stages, ten of them listed as national protected sites, all built inside ancestral halls and temples between the Qing and the Republic. A stage one bay square is raised half a person's height into the air, the upturned corners of its hip-and-gable roof curling like ox horns, and inside a caisson ceiling spirals upward.
facts: Most stages are one bay wide, with the stage floor raised off the ground and a carved balustrade around the stage front; the column heads support the eaves with carved brackets (niutui, “ox legs”) rather than bracket sets.

Caisson ceilings are the specialty of Ninghai's stages: the stage of the Hu Clan Ancestral Hall in Aohu and its linking corridor have three caisson ceilings in a row, one of only three surviving “three linked caisson ceilings” in Zhejiang.

The Hu Clan Ancestral Hall in Aohu was built in the 4th year of Xianfeng in the Qing (1854); the stage connects with viewing galleries on either side, from whose upper floors the audience watched performances.

qiufeng.name: Houtu Shrine, Wanrong
qiufeng.era: Qing · Rebuilt in the 9th year of Tongzhi
qiufeng.place: Shanxi · Wanrong · Ronghe Town · Miaoqian Village
qiufeng.lede: On a high platform, the three-story tower spreads upward with overlapping gable pediments and flying eaves. Qiufeng Tower takes its name from the stele of Emperor Wu of Han's Autumn Wind Ode that it houses; the lightness of the tower answers vividly to the massiveness of its base.
facts: Qing rebuilding: the present tower is dated by its rebuilding in the 9th year of Tongzhi in the Qing (1870); the Han-dynasty poem and Yuan stele inscriptions inside are recorded separately from the building's date.
Three-story tower: about 32.6 m tall, the timber tower stands on a tall base, with gable pediments at the center of each story and layered flying eaves.
Autumn Wind Ode stele: the tower preserves the carved stone of the Autumn Wind Ode, continuing the historical link between the Houtu Shrine and Han-dynasty worship.

tj_shijia.name: Shi Family Compound, Yangliuqing, Tianjin
tj_shijia.era: Large-scale construction in the early Guangxu reign · Later repairs
tj_shijia.yearNote: 1875 is the starting point of the large-scale construction of the Shi family residence; the date of manufacture of the inner-courtyard gate drawn here as a separate element is unconfirmed, and this sorting point is not called the gate's exact completion year.
tj_shijia.lede: Gray-brick gateways recede one behind another along the axis of the nested courtyards, with dark red timber frames and pale drum-shaped stones finishing the entrance. The inner-courtyard gate and the receding gateway courtyards are chosen here; the stone lions and eave ornaments of another, outer gateway are not pieced into the same plate.
facts: The surviving Shi Family Compound is the Zunmei Tang residence; its large-scale construction began early in the Guangxu reign of the Qing (1875), and later conservation repairs have their own dates.

The plate is based on photographs of the inner-courtyard gate, keeping the low tiled roof, gray-brick gate piers, short walls on either side, drum-shaped stones and the gates of the nested courtyards behind.

Gray brick and gray tile, near-black reddish-brown door frames, dark red inset panels and a few ocher-gold edge lines are distinguished as they appear today; no bird's-eye view of the whole residence is drawn, and the outer gateway is not spliced in.

hu_yueyang.name: Yueyang Tower
hu_yueyang.era: Rebuilt in the 6th year of Guangxu, Qing
hu_yueyang.yearNote: Dated by the surviving tower form produced by the rebuilding of the 6th year of Guangxu in the Qing (1880); the 1984 dismantling and major repair continued the old form, and neither the Three Kingdoms legend of a troop-review tower nor the year of the Northern Song restoration is used as the date of this drawing.
hu_yueyang.place: Hunan · Yueyang · Shore of Dongting Lake
hu_yueyang.lede: Three tiers of eaves spread out one above another, and the helmet-shaped roof at the top gathers lightly inward. The tower stands by Dongting Lake; the drawing keeps only this timber tower in its Qing form.
facts: Subject: the three-story main tower of Yueyang Tower.

Dating: dated by the surviving tower form produced by the rebuilding of the 6th year of Guangxu in the Qing (1880); the 1984 dismantling and major repair continued the old form, and neither the Three Kingdoms legend of a troop-review tower nor the year of the Northern Song restoration is used as the date of this drawing.

Plate scope: three stories, triple eaves and a helmet-shaped roof; only the tower body, the short stone base and the railings are drawn, not the city gate below, the stone archways on either side or the ancillary pavilions.

hu_nanyue.era: Rebuilt in the Guangxu reign, Qing

hu_nanyue.lede: A broad double-eaved roof covers the seven-bay main hall, and a long row of stone columns holds open the shadows beneath the eaves. The ritual space of Nanyue is gathered here into a single drawing of a hall.
facts: Subject: the Shengdi Hall of the Nanyue Grand Temple.

Dating: 1882 is taken as the rebuilding date of the surviving main structures of the Nanyue Grand Temple; the Shengdi Hall later underwent changes such as repairs and column replacement. The drawing shows the present state as photographed and does not take the Tang founding of the whole temple as the date of this hall.

Plate scope: the complete Shengdi Hall, its seven-bay facade, double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and outer colonnade of stone columns; present-day photographs govern, with a 1909 photograph used only to fill in building outlines hidden by visitors and trees. The incense-burner pavilion is not drawn.

gd_chen.name: Chen Clan Academy, Guangzhou
gd_chen.sub: Front gate · Lingnan ceramic sculpture and stone carving
gd_chen.yearNote: 1893 is the completion year of the Chen Clan Academy; the plate takes the present state of the central front gate, and components repaired later are not all regarded as original work of that year.
gd_chen.lede: Gray brick, stone columns and the ceramic sculpture on the ridges turn the entrance of a clan ancestral hall into a finely worked display wall of Lingnan craftsmanship. The plate takes only the central front gate and does not piece in the courtyards behind.
facts: Subject: the facade of the central front gate of the Chen Clan Academy.

Dating: 1893 is the completion year of the Chen Clan Academy; the plate takes the present state of the central front gate, and components repaired later are not all regarded as original work of that year.

Plate scope: the visible facade of the central front gate and the roofs adjoining it to the left and right; flush gable pitched roofs, figural ceramic-sculpture ridges, stone columns and stone beams, and the central doorway. The courtyard and rear halls are not reconstructed.

tj_guangdonghuiguan.name: Guangdong Guild Hall, Tianjin
tj_guangdonghuiguan.sub: Stage · Detail of the chicken-cage caisson ceiling
tj_guangdonghuiguan.era: Completed in the 33rd year of Guangxu
tj_guangdonghuiguan.lede: The thrust stage joins two-story side galleries, and within the square canopy the chicken-cage caisson ceiling spirals inward. The plate chooses an interior detail of the stage and caisson ceiling so that the layers of woodcarving, beams and brackets and surviving paintwork can be clearly seen.
facts: The Guangdong Guild Hall was completed in 1907; it is a late Qing guild hall building and today serves as the Tianjin Opera Museum.
The stage is a thrust stage; the chicken-cage caisson ceiling above the canopy is square outside and round inside, and no floor-standing columns block the view in front of the stage.

The plate does not draw the exterior of the whole guild hall; it chooses the stage, the suspended canopy and a short stretch of the two-story side galleries, removing modern light tubes, display screens and audience tables and chairs.

jl_wenmiao.name: Dacheng Hall of the Jilin Confucian Temple
jl_wenmiao.era: Main buildings completed in the 1st year of Xuantong
jl_wenmiao.yearNote: 1909 is the completion year of the surviving main buildings; 1736 is the founding of the Confucian temple, and the repairs of the 1920s and modern times are recorded separately, not merged into one year.
jl_wenmiao.lede: The long eleven-bay facade unfolds across twelve front gallery columns, and two tiers of roof bear down on the red columns and blue-green beams. What is recorded here is the Dacheng Hall built after the late Qing relocation; the founding year of the early temple is not attached to the surviving hall.
facts: The facade is eleven bays wide; the plate checks the twelve front columns one by one and keeps both eave bands.
The main buildings were completed in 1909; later restorations are not hidden on this account, nor is the 1736 founding substituted for the date of the main structure.
The yellow glazed tiles, dark red timberwork and light gray stone balustrades follow the present appearance in 2026 photographs; temporary banners are not drawn.
captions: Jilin Confucian Temple · Eleven-bay Dacheng Hall

gz_jiaxiu.name: Jiaxiu Tower, Guiyang
gz_jiaxiu.sub: Nanming River · Three stories, three eaves
gz_jiaxiu.era: Rebuilt in the 1st year of Xuantong · Later repairs
gz_jiaxiu.yearNote: The present appearance follows the 1909 restoration design and later repairs such as those of 1981; the Ming founding date does not replace the date of the surviving tower's form.
gz_jiaxiu.lede: On a stone platform in the Nanming River, the three-story Jiaxiu Tower stacks red columns and three tiers of eaves into a silhouette of Guiyang. First built in the Ming, it changed through several cycles of destruction and repair; today's plate follows the present appearance formed by the restoration design of the 1st year of Xuantong and later repairs.
facts: Subject drawn: the three-story, triple-eaved tower body, its stone platform and its own stone balustrades; the whole Fuyu Bridge and the riverside annex buildings are not treated as one building with it.
History: founded in the Wanli reign of the Ming and destroyed and repaired many times; the present appearance follows the restoration design of the 1st year of Xuantong in the Qing (1909).
Later repairs: repairs such as those of 1981 are recorded separately; the timeline is not an identification of original Ming fabric, and the plate is not a conservation survey drawing.
captions: Surviving Jiaxiu Tower, Guiyang · Line drawing · Pending user review
Qing · 1909

gx_chengyang.name: Chengyang Yongji Bridge
gx_chengyang.sub: Dong wind-and-rain bridge · Timber gallery with five pavilions
gx_chengyang.yearNote: Following volume 7 of Sanjiang Historical and Literary Materials, completion is taken as 1924; the proposal to build it in 1911 or the start of work in 1912 does not equal the completion year. The bridge has been repaired in later times, and the plate draws the complete bridge with all five pavilions as photographed today.
gx_chengyang.lede: Five pavilion towers line a continuous timber gallery, and stone piers hold the long bridge above the river. It is both a passage and a place to shelter from rain, linger and gather.
facts: Subject: the whole Chengyang Yongji Bridge and its five pavilions.

Dating: following volume 7 of Sanjiang Historical and Literary Materials, completion is taken as 1924; the proposal to build it in 1911 or the start of work in 1912 does not equal the completion year. The bridge has been repaired in later times, and the plate draws the complete bridge with all five pavilions as photographed today.

Plate scope: the five pavilions, the continuous timber gallery and the boat-shaped stone piers — the whole bridge rather than a detail of one end; the pyramidal roof at the center is distinguished from the hip-and-gable roofs at the two ends.

gd_ruishi.name: Ruishi Lou, Kaiping
gd_ruishi.sub: Diaolou of Jinjiangli · Blend of Chinese and Western styles
gd_ruishi.yearNote: 1925 is taken as the completion year of Ruishi Lou, not the date of all the Kaiping diaolou; the national protected site listing falls under “Kaiping Diaolou,” and World Heritage inscription belongs to a separate system.
gd_ruishi.lede: Above a squarish residential block, colonnades, domes and a lookout pavilion rise tier by tier. Village defense and the architectural tastes of an overseas-Chinese home district meet in a single nine-story diaolou.
facts: Subject: the complete tower of Ruishi Lou, Jinjiangli, Kaiping.

Dating: 1925 is taken as the completion year of Ruishi Lou, not the date of all the Kaiping diaolou; the national protected site listing falls under “Kaiping Diaolou,” and World Heritage inscription belongs to a separate system.

Plate scope: the mass of the nine-story diaolou, with the five-story main body distinguished from the upper colonnades, corner pavilions and central lookout pavilion; the slight upward view of the photograph is kept, and it is not turned into a Chinese pagoda.

hlj_sofia.name: Saint Sophia Cathedral, Harbin
hlj_sofia.yearNote: The surviving brick church was begun in 1923 and completed in 1932; the early wooden church of 1907 is not used as the date of the plate's subject.
hlj_sofia.lede: A red-brick bell tower and side towers gather around a huge green metal onion dome. Saint Sophia's early wooden church has a separate history; what is drawn here is the brick structure completed in 1932.
facts: The great dome, the bell tower's conical spire and the side towers are arranged according to photographs of the real building; ice sculptures of the same name were not used as references.
The surviving brick structure was begun in 1923 and completed in 1932; the founding date of 1907 is not substituted for it.

Today it has reddish-brown brick walls and old green metal roofs; pale gold on the small metal domes and crosses is limited to what is visible in photographs, and the modern ticket-office annex is not drawn.

Red-brick walls · Onion dome and bell tower

guanque.name: Stork Tower, Yongji
guanque.sub: On the bank of the Yellow River · Contemporary reconstruction
guanque.place: Shanxi · Yongji · West of the old city of Puzhou
guanque.lede: The famous tower of Wang Zhihuan's poem stands again today on the bank of the Yellow River west of the old city of Puzhou. The present tower was rebuilt and completed in 2002: a high platform raises four tiers of eaves, and tier upon tier of colonnades bring the poetry of climbing high to gaze afar back into reality.
facts: Surviving tower: reconstruction began in December 1997, and the tower was completed and opened on September 26, 2002; this drawing and the timeline both register it under 2002.
Tang-style tower: externally it has four tiers of eaves and three stories, is 73.9 m tall overall and faces north, with Tang-style painted decoration and spreading eaves.

History of the old tower: the original tower was first built in the Northern Zhou, survived through the Tang and Song, and was destroyed by war in the early Yuan; its founding date and the surviving reconstruction are recorded separately.
captions: Front of the Stork Tower · Four eaves, three stories
Tang-style form · Rebuilt 2002

horyuji.name: Hōryū-ji
horyuji.era: Asuka period · Second half of the 7th century
horyuji.lede: Beneath its two tiers of tiled roofs, the Kondō of Hōryū-ji forms a distinctive outline with cloud-shaped bracketing, an upper-story railing and a low pent roof (mokoshi). This Asuka-period timber building faces the five-story pagoda on the west side of the courtyard, preserving clues to the space of early East Asian Buddhist temples.
facts: The temple was founded in 607; the surviving Kondō belongs to the Western Precinct (Sai-in Garan), rebuilt after the fire of 670, and is dated to the second half of the 7th century.
The main structure is five bays across and four bays deep, with a two-tiered irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof; a board-roofed mokoshi surrounds the first story, forming a shallower eave line below.
Cloud-shaped bearing blocks and bracket arms (kumoto and kumohijiki), slightly swelling round columns and the geometric railing of the upper story are important features of the Kondō's exterior.
captions: Hōryū-ji · Front of the Kondō
Asuka period · Two-tiered irimoya roof and mokoshi

toshodaiji.name: Tōshōdai-ji
toshodaiji.era: Nara period · Second half of the 8th century
toshodaiji.lede: Eight round columns carry the broad single-eaved roof of the Kondō of Tōshōdai-ji, and the open portico in front adds a quiet layer of transition between the courtyard and the inner chamber where the Buddha images stand. After Jianzhen (Ganjin) founded the temple, his disciples completed this Kondō in the second half of the 8th century.
facts: Jianzhen (Ganjin) founded Tōshōdai-ji in 759, while the surviving Kondō was built in the second half of the 8th century; the temple's official account links its construction to his disciple Nyohō.
The Kondō is seven bays across the front and four bays deep, with a yosemune (hipped) roof covered in hongawara tiles; the front bay is left open to form a colonnade.

Three-stepped bracket sets (mitesaki kumimono) beneath the eaves carry the deep overhang, and the shibi ridge-end ornaments at both ends of the ridge and the broad single eave together define its exterior.
captions: Tōshōdai-ji · Front of the Kondō
Nara period · Seven-bay yosemune roof

byodoin.name: Byōdō-in
byodoin.lede: Across the Aji Pond, the central hall and its two wing corridors spread like a bird with outstretched wings, and twin phoenixes face each other on the ridge. The Amida Hall built by Fujiwara no Yorimichi in 1053 sets the Heian-period vision of the Pure Land above the waters of Uji.
facts: Heian structure: the Phoenix Hall was built in 1053 by Fujiwara no Yorimichi; the surviving central hall and wing corridors reflect the layout of an Amida hall of the late Heian period.

Twin phoenixes and two wings: the left and right wing corridors enclose the central hall, and a pair of phoenixes stands on the ridge; the name Phoenix Hall gradually came into use in the Edo period, and the phoenixes now on the roof are replacements installed in 1968.

Worship across the pond: the building sits in the west facing east, and worshippers on the east bank of the Aji Pond face west to venerate the Buddha; garden and hall together express the image of the Western Pure Land.
captions: Byōdō-in · Front of the Phoenix Hall and its two wings
Heian period · 1053

todaiji.name: Tōdai-ji
todaiji.lede: With round columns rising straight to the heights and tier upon tier of tie beams passing through them, the Nandaimon shows the structural power of the Daibutsuyō style. Three passages run beneath the broad double eaves, and Niō guardian statues on either side protect the entrance to Tōdai-ji.
facts: The surviving Nandaimon was rebuilt under the direction of Chōgen; its ridgepole was raised in 1199, and it was completed in 1203 together with the Kongō Rikishi statues within the gate.
The gate has an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof, five bays across the front with three central doorways and double eaves; it is an important surviving example of Daibutsuyō architecture.
The gate has 18 great round columns in all, with six columns across the front dividing it into five bays; according to the temple, the gate is 25.46 m tall above the platform.
captions: Tōdai-ji · Front of the Nandaimon
Kamakura period · Rebuilt 1199–1203

kiyomizu.name: Kiyomizu-dera
kiyomizu.lede: The main hall of Kiyomizu-dera lays its broad cypress-bark roof over the slope of Mount Otowa, and the Kiyomizu stage in front of the eaves projects out from the cliff. Beneath the stage, rows of tall timber posts interlace with horizontal tie beams, revealing the support system of Japanese kakezukuri (cliffside) architecture.
facts: The temple was founded in 778; the surviving main hall and stage shown here were rebuilt in 1633 and are registered as Edo period.
The main hall has a yosemune (hipped) roof with cypress-bark roofing; the small gables on both sides of the south face and the stage projecting at the center form its main outline.
The Kiyomizu stage stands nearly 13 m above the ground, supported by 18 zelkova columns linked by horizontal tie beams; it was originally used for performances offered to Kannon.
captions: Kiyomizu-dera · Main hall and Kiyomizu stage
Near-frontal view from the south · Edo period, 10th year of Kan'ei (1633)

toji.name: Tō-ji
toji.lede: The five-story pagoda of Tō-ji tapers story by story beneath five broad tiled eaves, with a slender spire of rings (sōrin) at the top. About 55 m tall, this timber pagoda is a striking historic building in southern Kyoto, its outline following the tiered eaves and railings of Japanese Buddhist pagodas.
facts: The surviving five-story pagoda was rebuilt in 1644 and is the fifth pagoda on the site, after four fires; it is not registered by the founding date of the temple or of the first pagoda.
The pagoda is a five-story square timber structure with hongawara tile roofing; a complete spire of rings stands above the five broad eaves, and the total height is about 55 m.

Inside the first story, the central pillar (shinbashira) running through all the stories symbolizes Dainichi Nyorai and is surrounded by images of Nyorai and Bosatsu, forming an Esoteric Buddhist space.
captions: Tō-ji · Five-story pagoda
Near-frontal view · Edo period, 21st year of Kan'ei (1644)

sd_guangyue.name: Guangyue Tower
sd_guangyue.era: Completed in the 7th year of Hongwu, Ming
sd_guangyue.yearNote: The date corresponds to the surviving Guangyue Tower; repairs over the centuries and its completion in the 7th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1374) are described separately.
sd_guangyue.place: Shandong · Liaocheng · Old city of Dongchang Prefecture
sd_guangyue.lede: The old city's four streets meet beneath a tall brick platform, and the four-story timber tower tapers upward. Guangyue Tower turns the crossing point of the city's traffic into a landmark of tiered eaves.
facts: Guangyue Tower was completed in the 7th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1374) and stands at the center of the old city of Dongchang Prefecture.
The plate draws the whole tower and brick base; the four-story tower body, layered eaves and arched passages through the base form its main outline.
The coloring is based on 2024 photographs, keeping the material distinctions between gray tiles, vermilion timber walls and blue-green painted decoration.
captions: Guangyue Tower · Whole tower and base · Line drawing
Four-story timber tower · 7th year of Hongwu, Ming (1374)

sd_yantai_huiguan.name: Fujian Guild Hall, Yantai
sd_yantai_huiguan.era: Begun in the 10th year of Guangxu · Completed in the 32nd year
sd_yantai_huiguan.yearNote: Begun in 1884 and completed in 1906; the drawing shows the street-front exterior in 2023 photographs, which predate the 2025 repairs.
sd_yantai_huiguan.lede: Fujianese merchants brought the bricks, tiles, timber and stone of Quanzhou, and its craftsmanship, to Yantai. Red walls, fire-break gables and swallowtail ridges give this guild hall in a northern port city a distinctly southern Fujian appearance.
facts: The Fujian Guild Hall was funded by Fujianese merchants; work began in 1884 and it was completed in 1906. It is also called the Tianhou Palace.
Its bricks, tiles, timber and stone were procured and worked in the Quanzhou area, then shipped to Yantai for assembly.
The plate takes the walls, gate and roofs visible from the street and does not show the plan of the whole courtyard group; material colors are based on 2023 photographs.
captions: Fujian Guild Hall, Yantai · Street-front exterior · Line drawing
Southern Fujian guild hall · 32nd year of Guangxu, Qing (1906)

sd_jiuding.name: Nine-Top Pagoda
sd_jiuding.yearNote: 750 is used only to place it approximately in the Tang on the timeline, not as an exact construction year; the surviving pagoda includes later repairs, and the date of the folk-culture park is not counted as the date of the ancient pagoda.
sd_jiuding.lede: The top of this single-story octagonal brick pagoda is not a single finial but nine small pagodas: eight arranged in a ring and one rising high in the center. The pagoda's name comes directly from this rare silhouette.
facts: The Nine-Top Pagoda stands on the site of Jiuta Temple; its surviving main structure is generally identified as a Tang remain, but its exact construction year has not been confirmed in the materials for this batch.
The body is a single octagonal story, with corbeled eaves projecting outward and carrying eight small outer pagodas and one central small pagoda.
The perspective drawing shows only the small pagodas visible from this angle and does not force the back into view; the pagoda was repaired in 1962.
captions: Nine-Top Pagoda · Octagonal brick pagoda · Line drawing

sd_hongjialou.name: Hongjialou Catholic Church
sd_hongjialou.sub: Cathedral of the Sacred Heart of Jesus · Front elevation
sd_hongjialou.era: Completed in the 31st year of Guangxu, Qing
sd_hongjialou.yearNote: The date corresponds to the surviving church completed in 1905, distinguishing it from the earlier old church at Hongjialou and from later repairs.
sd_hongjialou.lede: Two soaring spires flank a rose window, and pointed arches, buttresses and stone ornament extend in continuous succession. The front of Honglou Church gives Jinan's modern religious architecture a face of gray-brown brick and stone.
facts: The surviving church was completed in 1905; it faces west, with its back to the east, and is cruciform in plan.
The plate chooses the front elevation, keeping the twin spires, central rose window and three pointed-arch entrances.
The gray spire tops, gray-brown brick and stone, dark brown doors and reddish-brown louvers are each colored as photographed.

sd_qingdao_catholic.name: Qingdao Catholic Church
sd_qingdao_catholic.yearNote: Begun in 1932 and completed in 1934; the date corresponds to the surviving St. Michael's Church and does not borrow the Qing-era dates of nearby German buildings.
sd_qingdao_catholic.lede: Yellowish-beige walls carry two bell towers with red-tiled spires, and the central rose window and three arched doorways line up tier above tier. The church combines Gothic and Romanesque elements into a striking outline in Qingdao's old town.
facts: The church was completed in 1934; it has a Latin-cross plan, with two bell towers placed symmetrically left and right.
The plate takes the west elevation from a slightly oblique angle, keeping the round rose window, the arched doorways and the stair towers at the sides.
The two red-tiled spires are presented distinctly from the gray spires of Jinan's Honglou Church, and the name is also registered separately from Qingdao's Protestant Church.

sd_qingdao_christ.name: Qingdao Protestant Church
sd_qingdao_christ.sub: Jiangsu Road · Main hall and bell tower
sd_qingdao_christ.yearNote: The date refers to the main hall and bell tower built in 1908–1910; the church is kept separate from the Qingdao Catholic Church, completed in 1934.
sd_qingdao_christ.lede: A bell tower rises on one side, while the main hall on the other ends in a curved gable; the composition is asymmetrical. Red tiles, yellow walls, rusticated stone and a green copper roof each have their own place on this church.
facts: The church was built in 1908–1910 and consists of a main hall and a bell tower, at No. 15 Jiangsu Road.
The bell tower has a large clock face; rusticated granite is used for the wall base and corners, the roofs are covered in red tiles, and the bell tower's spire is green.

As part of the German Building Complex of Qingdao, it was merged in the sixth batch into a national protected site first listed in the fourth batch; the batch in which this building was included and the parent unit's first batch are recorded separately.

sd_yanmiao.name: Yan Temple of Qufu
sd_yanmiao.era: Fusheng Hall rebuilt in the 2nd year of Zhengde, Ming
sd_yanmiao.yearNote: The plate corresponds to the seven-bay Fusheng Hall as rebuilt in 1507, which continued to be repaired in the Ming and Qing and in 1934, 1978 and 2006; neither the date of the Yan Temple's relocation in the Yuan nor the 1509 construction date of the stele pavilion is used to date this hall.
sd_yanmiao.lede: The Yan Temple is dedicated to Yan Hui, and its main hall, Fusheng Hall, spreads across seven bays beneath a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Carved stone dragon columns and the balustrade of the terrace before the hall give concrete form to the ritual order of a Confucian temple through columns, steps and eaves.
facts: Fusheng Hall was originally a five-bay, double-eaved Yuan building; rebuilt in the 2nd year of Zhengde in the Ming (1507), it became seven bays wide and has since been repaired many times.
Four carved stone dragon columns in the front gallery, together with the other octagonal stone columns, carry a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green tiles; a terrace lies in front of the hall.

The Yan Temple is a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level; the plate shows only Fusheng Hall, which has its own card separate from the Dacheng Hall of the Qufu Confucian Temple.
captions: Yan Temple of Qufu · Fusheng Hall · Line drawing
Seven bays, double-eaved · Rebuilt in the 2nd year of Zhengde, Ming (1507)
