sd_chongjue.name: Iron Pagoda of Chongjue Temple
sd_chongjue.era: Seven stories built in the 4th year of Chongning, Song · Two stories added in the 9th year of Wanli, Ming
sd_chongjue.yearNote: 1105 refers to the seven-story cast-iron main body of the Song; two stories and the finial were added in 1581, so the nine stories standing today cannot all be labeled as Song construction. The plate shows only the pagoda body and the upper platform visible in the photograph.
sd_chongjue.lede: Iron is cast into the columns, tie beams, railings and flying eaves of a pavilion, and the nine-story octagonal pagoda tapers story by story. Begun in the Song and completed at the top in the Ming, the Iron Pagoda unites imitation timber construction with the craft of casting.
facts: Seven stories were cast in the 4th year of Chongning in the Northern Song (1105); in the 9th year of Wanli in the Ming (1581), two stories and the finial were added.
The cast-iron body is octagonal with nine stories; each story is divided into body, balcony platform, railing and bracketed eaves, giving it the character of a timber pavilion-style tower.
The reference photograph does not show the lower brick platform in full; the plate keeps the complete pagoda body and the visible upper platform and does not fill in the cropped base.
captions: Iron Pagoda of Chongjue Temple · Body and upper platform · Line drawing
Seven stories built in the Song · Two stories and finial added in the Ming

protection.scope: Body and upper platform of the Iron Pagoda of Chongjue Temple, Jining

sd_xiaotang_shrine.name: Stone Shrine of the Guo Family Tomb on Mount Xiaotang
sd_xiaotang_shrine.sub: Eastern Han stone chamber · Modern shelter excluded
sd_xiaotang_shrine.yearNote: The plate shows the Eastern Han stone shrine itself inside its shelter; “about the 1st century” is an archaeological dating, not an exact construction year.
sd_xiaotang_shrine.lede: A small stone chamber stands inside a later protective building. Its stone slabs imitate the tile ridges and projecting eaves of a Han roof, and the pictorial carvings inside preserve early above-ground architecture and funerary imagery together.
facts: The shrine was built roughly in the early Eastern Han and is one of the earliest surviving above-ground buildings constructed and carved in stone.

The main body is built of bluestone slabs, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof and a front divided into two bays; the plate shows only the shrine and does not treat the red-columned outer shelter as original Han fabric.
“Guo family” is the inherited heritage name; the precise identity of the tomb's occupant is still debated, and legend is not taken as grounds for identifying him as Guo Ju.
captions: Stone Shrine of the Guo Family Tomb on Mount Xiaotang · Line drawing
About 1st century

protection.unitName: Stone Shrine of the Guo Family Tomb on Mount Xiaotang
protection.scope: The Eastern Han stone shrine itself, within the protective shelter

fj_qingjing_gate.name: Qingjing Mosque, Quanzhou
fj_qingjing_gate.era: Founded in the 2nd year of Dazhong Xiangfu
fj_qingjing_gate.yearNote: 1009 is the founding year of Qingjing Mosque; the surviving gatehouse has gone through a restoration in the 3rd year of Zhida in the Yuan (1310) and later repairs. The plate shows its present state and does not claim that every stone is Song work.
fj_qingjing_gate.lede: Pointed arches, recessed layer by layer, lead from the street into the mosque; the stone gatehouse preserves the form of West Asian mosques in the port city of Song and Yuan Quanzhou.
facts: Qingjing Mosque was founded in the 2nd year of Dazhong Xiangfu in the Northern Song (1009) and was restored in the 3rd year of Zhida in the Yuan (1310).
In the surviving gatehouse, the first and second doorways are both pointed arches, topped by half-dome vaults.
The plate shows the gatehouse and the attached stone walls; the prayer hall and later buildings within the mosque are not included in this drawing.
captions: Qingjing Mosque, Quanzhou · Line drawing
Founded 1009, restored 1310

protection.scope: Surviving stone entrance gatehouse and attached stone walls

fj_anping_bridge.name: Anping Bridge
fj_anping_bridge.era: Begun in the 8th year of Shaoxing · Completed about the 22nd year of Shaoxing
fj_anping_bridge.yearNote: Begun in 1138; the Quanzhou Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism records its completion in 1152, while other sources record that it was finished in 1151. The plate shows only one section of the surviving deck and does not let this detail stand for the full length.
fj_anping_bridge.lede: Huge granite slabs lie across stone piers, and the deck stretches on over the old bay. This bridge, five li long, once joined the trade route between Anhai and Shuitou.
facts: Anping Bridge was begun in the 8th year of Shaoxing in the Southern Song (1138); the surviving bridge is about 2.25 km long and is a flat stone beam bridge.
Stone beams rest on the piers, which take different forms according to water flow and terrain; the plate selects a detail of the stone-slab deck, railings and nearby piers.
The present structure has been repaired over many periods; this partial view is not a survey of the whole bridge or an exact count of its piers.
captions: Anping Bridge · Line drawing
Begun 1138, completed 1152

protection.scope: Representative section of the surviving stone-slab deck and piers

bj_yunju_north.name: Pagodas and Stone Sutras of Yunju Temple, Fangshan
bj_yunju_north.era: Founded in the Liao · Repaired in the Ming
bj_yunju_north.yearNote: The North Pagoda was founded in the Liao; its exact construction year has not been verified, and it was later repaired in the Ming and other periods. The start of sutra carving at Yunju Temple in the Sui is not used here as the date of the North Pagoda.
bj_yunju_north.lede: The North Pagoda has stacked pavilion stories below, a round drum in the middle and a tall, tapering bell shape on top; beyond the pagoda, the thousand-year history of carving the Yunju Temple stone sutras continues.
facts: The North Pagoda of Yunju Temple, also called the Arhat Pagoda or the Sarira Pagoda, was founded in the Liao and repaired in the Ming.

A pavilion-like lower section, a drum-shaped middle and a bell-shaped top are stacked together, giving the North Pagoda its rare profile; the plate shows only the North Pagoda and does not substitute the recently rebuilt South Pagoda.
“Pagodas and Stone Sutras of Yunju Temple” is the name of the national protected site; the sutras and the pagodas each have their own chronology and cannot be merged into a single construction date.
captions: Pagodas and Stone Sutras of Yunju Temple, Fangshan · Line drawing
Founded in the Liao, repaired in the Ming

protection.unitName: Pagodas and Stone Sutras of Yunju Temple, Fangshan
protection.scope: Liao North Pagoda of Yunju Temple

xz_jokhang.name: Jokhang Temple
xz_jokhang.sub: Present main facade · Buildings of several phases
xz_jokhang.yearNote: 647 is the traditional record of the temple's founding; the plate shows the surviving main facade, including expansions and repairs from many periods, and does not treat the whole golden roof and outer walls as original 7th-century fabric.
xz_jokhang.lede: Golden roofs and deep-red walls face Barkhor Street. The temple has grown from its Tibetan Empire core to the present day, and the surviving facade layers the building work of many eras.
facts: The Jokhang was founded in the mid-7th century, with official Lhasa sources giving 647 CE; it was expanded in later periods.

The plate takes the present main facade, keeping the central golden roof, the red walls and the outlines of the flanking buildings; it is an exterior built up over several phases, not a reconstruction of the original Tibetan Empire appearance.
The temple is an important site revered by all schools, and Barkhor Street grew up around it.
captions: Jokhang Temple · Line drawing
Founded 647; present form of several phases

protection.scope: Surviving main facade (buildings of several phases)

hb_shanhaiguan.name: Zhendong Tower of Shanhaiguan
hb_shanhaiguan.sub: East Gate arrow tower · Gate platform and short wall sections
hb_shanhaiguan.era: Tower built in the Ming · Modern repairs
hb_shanhaiguan.yearNote: Shanhai Garrison was established in 1381, and the Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau records that the pass fortress was built the following year. This plate shows the surviving Zhendong Tower and its gate platform; 1400 is only an approximate placement within the Ming, not the exact construction year of the timber tower. Repeated modern repairs are described separately.
hb_shanhaiguan.lede: A massive gate platform raises a double-eaved arrow tower, and an arched gateway passes through the fortress. The broad horizontal spread of Zhendong Tower condenses the pass between mountains and sea into its most familiar silhouette.
facts: The plate covers Zhendong Tower of the East Gate, its gate platform and the short wall sections on either side; it does not depict the whole pass fortress or Laolongtou.
The building of the pass fortress and the repairs to the surviving tower are recorded separately, and the timeline places it approximately within the Ming.
The tower and adjoining walls have been repaired continually since 1978, and Zhendong Tower underwent a major overhaul in 1998.
captions: Shanhaiguan · Zhendong Tower and gate platform
Ming arrow tower · Repairs over the centuries and in modern times

protection.scope: Zhendong Tower with its gate platform and the short wall sections on both sides

hb_pule.name: Pule Temple
hb_pule.yearNote: 1766 refers to the construction of Pule Temple and Xuguang Pavilion; this plate shows only the round pavilion and the upper terrace directly supporting it, not the complete mandala platform.
hb_pule.place: Hebei · Chengde · East of the Wulie River
hb_pule.lede: Two tiers of round yellow-tiled roofs draw inward above a stone terrace, the round pavilion and the square platform setting each other off. Xuguang Pavilion adds a distinctive circular silhouette to the temple group of Chengde.
facts: Pule Temple was built in 1766; the halls at the front and the mandala platform at the rear form distinct spaces.
This plate shows Xuguang Pavilion and the upper terrace; the other levels, side pavilions and small pagodas are outside its scope.
The round pavilion has double circular eaves; the yellow glazed tiles, vermilion doors and windows, and blue-green architraves are colored after on-site photographs.
captions: Pule Temple · Xuguang Pavilion and upper terrace
Double circular eaves · 31st year of Qianlong, Qing (1766)

protection.scope: Xuguang Pavilion and upper terrace

hb_anyuan.name: Anyuan Temple
hb_anyuan.yearNote: 1764 refers to the founding of Anyuan Temple and Pudu Hall; the surviving hall includes later repairs. Pudu Hall is also written with a variant character in its name, and that form is kept as a search alias.
hb_anyuan.place: Hebei · Chengde · East of the Wulie River
hb_anyuan.lede: A tall square hall holds its mass down beneath three tiers of eaves, the black-tiled roofs with yellow edging setting off the red timber walls. Anyuan Temple leaves in Chengde an architectural memory connected with Ili.
facts: Anyuan Temple was built in 1764; its design drew on the Gurza Temple in Ili, and it is also called the Ili Temple.
The plate covers the whole of Pudu Hall, taking its square plan, seven bays on each side and triple eaves as the structural basis.
The 2011 repairs to Pudu Hall included the eave columns, floors and roof; the founding date and the repairs are described separately.
captions: Anyuan Temple · Pudu Hall
Square triple-eaved hall · 29th year of Qianlong, Qing (1764)

protection.scope: Pudu Hall, entire hall

hb_zhili.name: Zhili Governor-General's Office
hb_zhili.sub: Main Hall · Five-bay principal hall of the office
hb_zhili.era: Surviving main structure of the Yongzheng reign, Qing
hb_zhili.yearNote: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau dates the surviving main buildings to the Yongzheng reign (1723–1735); 1730 is only a sorting point within that range and is not presented as the exact completion year of the Main Hall.
hb_zhili.lede: Among gray tiles, white walls and dark gallery columns, the Main Hall of the office keeps a restrained scale. Here the governor-general conducted ceremonies and major affairs of government, and the order of the courtyards is more striking than any ornament.
facts: The drawing shows the Main Hall on the central axis, where the front gallery and the five-bay interior hall make up a complete facade.
The office was restored and enlarged through the Ming and Qing; its surviving main buildings date from the Yongzheng reign of the Qing.
The Main Hall served for important government affairs and ceremonies, a different function from the trial halls of prefectural and county yamens.
captions: Zhili Governor-General's Office · Main Hall
Five-bay principal hall · Yongzheng reign, Qing

protection.scope: Main Hall

hb_yongtong.name: Yongtong Bridge
hb_yongtong.sub: Zhao County · Single-span open-spandrel stone arch bridge
hb_yongtong.yearNote: According to the Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau, the bridge was built in the Mingchang reign of the Jin (1190–1195); 1192 is a sorting point within that range, and earlier legends are not used to date the surviving structure.
hb_yongtong.lede: Each shoulder of a single low stone arch opens into two small arches, and the deck rises gently between stone balustrades. At a smaller scale, Zhao County's Little Stone Bridge carries on the structural language of the open-spandrel stone arch.
facts: This plate shows the full side elevation of Yongtong Bridge, including the main arch, the four small spandrel arches and the stone balustrades.
The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau gives the bridge's construction as the Mingchang reign of the Jin (1190–1195).
The official main span is about 26 m; it is entered separately from Anji Bridge to avoid confusing identical names or aliases.
captions: Zhao County · Full side elevation of Yongtong Bridge
Single span, four small arches · Mingchang reign, Jin

protection.scope: Yongtong Bridge, Zhao County, entire bridge

hb_tiangong.name: Pagoda of Tiangong Temple
hb_tiangong.sub: Fengrun · Octagonal thirteen-story multi-eaved brick pagoda
hb_tiangong.era: Founded in the 8th year of Qingning, Liao · Later repairs
hb_tiangong.yearNote: 1062 is the Liao founding date; the surviving pagoda has been repaired in the Ming, Qing and modern times, and this plate registers it according to its preserved Liao form.
hb_tiangong.lede: A tall ground story of carved brick supports thirteen closely set, tapering tiers of eaves. Although Tiangong Temple itself is gone, the coiled-dragon engaged columns and stacked eaves still give this Liao pagoda a fine, close-knit rhythm.
facts: The pagoda stands within the former grounds of Tiangong Temple in Fengrun and was founded in the 8th year of Qingning in the Liao (1062).
The plate shows the whole octagonal thirteen-story multi-eaved pagoda, keeping the Sumeru plinth, the upturned lotus and the coiled-dragon engaged columns.
The ground story imitates timber construction in carved brick, with coiled-dragon engaged columns, arched doorways and bracket sets together decorating the body.
captions: Tiangong Temple Pagoda · Whole pagoda
Octagonal, thirteen stories · Founded in the 8th year of Qingning, Liao (1062)

protection.scope: Pagoda of Tiangong Temple, Fengrun, whole pagoda

hb_shien.name: Shi'en Temple
hb_shien.sub: Main Hall · Qing round-ridge front annex
hb_shien.era: Founded in the 6th year of Chenghua, Ming · Front annex added in the Qing
hb_shien.yearNote: 1470 is the founding year of Shi'en Temple, and the surviving Main Hall retains Ming features; the five-bay round-ridge front annex was added in the Qing, so the whole ensemble is not dated as original 1470 fabric.
hb_shien.lede: The five-bay Main Hall spreads beneath a hipped roof, with a light round-ridge front annex attached before it. Roofs of two periods overlap, forming a steady yet richly layered facade in the old town of Xuanhua.
facts: Shi'en Temple was founded in 1470; its other halls have been destroyed, and the surviving main structure is the Main Hall.
The Main Hall is five bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof; the five-bay round-ridge front annex was added in the Qing.
The plate shows the whole hall with its front annex and platform; the offering vessels, stone elephants and city buildings in the foreground are outside the drawn scope.
captions: Shi'en Temple · Main Hall and round-ridge front annex
Ming hall · Front annex added in the Qing

protection.scope: Main Hall and Qing round-ridge front annex

hb_dajingmen.name: Dajingmen Gate
hb_dajingmen.sub: Zhangjiakou · Arched gate and short wall sections
hb_dajingmen.era: Gate opened and built in the 1st year of Shunzhi, Qing
hb_dajingmen.yearNote: 1644 refers to the opening and building of the Dajingmen gate; the adjoining wall sections are Great Wall remains spanning several eras, and this plate does not attribute the whole stretch of mountain wall to 1644.
hb_dajingmen.lede: A brick arched gate without a timber tower is set directly into the wall, with the battlements raised above the gateway. Dajingmen was both a gateway through the Great Wall and a witness to the trade between Zhangjiakou and the grasslands.
facts: The gate was formally opened and built in the 1st year of Shunzhi in the Qing (1644); the earlier wall and passage have a separate history.
The plate takes one complete arched gate and the short wall sections on either side; it does not show the full line of the Great Wall across the mountains.
In 2013, the seventh batch incorporated Dajingmen into the Great Wall, placing it under the fifth-batch national protected site of the Great Wall.
captions: Zhangjiakou · Dajingmen and short wall sections
Gate built in the 1st year of Shunzhi, Qing (1644)

protection.scope: Arched gate of Dajingmen, Zhangjiakou, Hebei, and adjoining short wall sections
protection.note: The Dajingmen section was incorporated into the Great Wall in the seventh batch and placed under the fifth-batch Great Wall listing; the label is registered by the batch in which this section was included.

ah_xuguo.name: Xu Guo Stone Archway
ah_xuguo.yearNote: The construction year of the stone archway is used; the plate shows only the front elevation of one side of the eight-pillared, four-sided archway.
ah_xuguo.lede: Eight stone pillars enclose a four-sided memorial archway: the Xu Guo Archway turns a flat gateway into a stone space one can walk through. Beams, bracket sets and stone lions are all carved from the same gray stone, and it still stands at a street junction in the old Huizhou town.
facts: Built in the 12th year of Wanli in the Ming (1584) in honor of Grand Secretary Xu Guo, it is also called the Grand Secretary's Archway; it was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1988.

It has four sides and eight pillars: the front and back each have three bays, four pillars and three roofed tiers, and the left and right sides each a single bay, two pillars and three roofed tiers, together enclosing a rectangle; carving covers the stone beams and bracket sets that imitate timber construction.

The plate shows only the front elevation of one side, presenting four front pillars and three passages rather than lining up all eight pillars in a row; inscriptions and the street background are omitted.
captions: Xu Guo Stone Archway · Front elevation of one side
Ming · 1584 · Four-sided, eight-pillared stone archway

ah_zhenfeng.name: Zhenfeng Pagoda, Anqing
ah_zhenfeng.sub: Yingjiang Temple · Seven-story octagonal brick-and-stone pagoda
ah_zhenfeng.yearNote: The pagoda body drawn is dated to the Longqing reign of the Ming and placed at the commonly cited completion year of 1570; local records also give a completion date of 1572. The attached eaves, roofs and finial show the repaired state seen in the photographs.
ah_zhenfeng.lede: Zhenfeng Pagoda stands within Yingjiang Temple on the north bank of the Yangtze, its seven white stories and dark-gray eave bands tapering level by level. Balconies and small arched openings between the stories give the heavy masonry a rhythm that climbs tier by tier.
facts: The surviving pagoda body was built in the Longqing reign of the Ming, with a commonly cited completion date of the 4th year of Longqing (1570); it has been repaired repeatedly since and was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 2006.

It is an octagonal, seven-story pavilion-style brick-and-stone pagoda; beneath the eaves, brick and stone imitations of timber members project outward, and each story has a balcony with railings and arched openings. The attached eave at ground level is not counted as a separate story.

The plate checks the pagoda body and ground-story outline against on-site photographs and takes its colors from more recent ones; the red finial, dark-gray roofs and pale walls are the present state after repairs, not a reconstruction of the Ming original.
captions: Zhenfeng Pagoda · Seven-story octagonal body and ground-level attached eave
Ming · Longqing reign · Present state after later repairs

ah_huaxilou.name: Huaxi Opera Tower, Bozhou
ah_huaxilou.sub: Great Guandi Temple · Courtyard opera stage
ah_huaxilou.yearNote: The year 1676, when the courtyard opera stage was added, is used rather than 1656, the founding year of the Great Guandi Temple; the woodcarving, painted decoration and roof have undergone later restoration.
ah_huaxilou.lede: Red columns support a roof of blue-green glazed tiles, and pale woodcarving hangs tier upon tier beneath the eaves. Huaxi Opera Tower carves opera scenes into its beams and hanging fascia; it is a guild-hall stage left in Bozhou by medicine merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi.
facts: The Great Guandi Temple was founded in the 13th year of Shunzhi in the Qing (1656); merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi added the opera tower in the 15th year of Kangxi (1676), and it was later enlarged and restored several times. Huaxi Opera Tower was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1988.

The stage sits on the south side facing north and projects into the courtyard; the woodcarving and painted decoration beneath its eaves mostly depict opera stories. The carved-brick gate, the iron flagpoles and the stage woodcarving are separate parts.

The plate shows only the central courtyard stage and the passage beneath it, keeping the material colors of the glazed roof, red columns and hanging fascia; the gate archway and the viewing galleries on either side are not merged into the main subject.
captions: Huaxi Opera Tower · Central courtyard stage
Qing · Added 1676 · Later restoration

hn_miaole.name: Pagoda of Miaole Temple
hn_miaole.sub: Rebuilt in the Later Zhou · Square multi-eaved brick pagoda
hn_miaole.era: Later Zhou · Rebuilt in the 2nd year of Xiande
hn_miaole.yearNote: The Later Zhou rebuilding date of the 2nd year of Xiande (955) is used; the pagoda's earlier history is described separately, and legendary dates are not used for placement.
hn_miaole.lede: Thirteen brick eaves taper level by level over the square body, and a ring-shaped finial with fine chains forms a light outline high above. Miaole Temple has lost its former appearance, but the old pagoda keeps the steady scale of Five Dynasties brickwork.
facts: Rebuilding date: The surviving pagoda is registered by its rebuilding in the 2nd year of Xiande in the Later Zhou (955); the earlier history of the temple and pagoda is not taken as an exact completion date for the surviving structure.

Form: A square, hollow brick pagoda with thirteen tiers of corbeled multi-eaves; the small niches on each story of the south face and the brick carving on the lower part form layers of differing density.

Plate scope: Based on on-site photographs from 2026, the plate keeps the body, multi-eaves and finial, omitting the offering table, people and surrounding buildings; the rings of the finial are not counted as stories.
captions: Miaole Temple Pagoda, Wuzhi · Thirteen tiers of multi-eaves
Later Zhou · Rebuilt 955

hn_fawang.name: Pagoda of Fawang Temple
hn_fawang.era: Tang · Exact year of construction undetermined
hn_fawang.yearNote: 750 is only an approximate timeline placement for a Tang survival and does not represent the exact year the pagoda was built; the Eastern Han founding date of the temple is not used. The plate omits the lower body and arched doorway hidden by trees.
hn_fawang.lede: The fifteen multi-eaves of the square brick pagoda project tier upon tier, drawing inward in a soft curve as they rise. The plate takes the upper part of the Tang pagoda at Fawang Temple, keeping the rhythm among the brick eaves, the small round-arched openings and the damaged top.
facts: Subject drawn: The great fifteen-tier square multi-eaved pagoda is chosen from the Fawang Temple pagoda group and registered as a Tang survival; the dates of the nearby Yuan and Qing pagodas are not mixed in.
Curve of the brick eaves: Above the body, fifteen tiers of corbeled multi-eaves taper level by level into an overall parabolic profile; the finial at the top has been destroyed.

Partial view: In the on-site photographs the lower body is hidden by trees, so the plate shows only the upper multi-eaves and the top in its present state, without reconstructing the arched doorway, the platform or a complete ancient finial.
captions: Fawang Temple Pagoda · Fifteen multi-eaves and top, detail
Tang · Exact year of construction undetermined

hn_songling.name: Imperial Tombs of the Northern Song
hn_songling.yearNote: 1063 is the construction date of the Yongzhao Mausoleum, and the subject is an original stone civil official before the tomb; it does not mean that all the Song tombs were built in the same year, nor are the modern reconstructed gate towers counted as Song structures.
hn_songling.lede: Robes falling long and hands holding a tablet of office, the stone civil official stands at attention beside the spirit way of the Yongzhao Mausoleum. Weathering has softened the details but has not erased the solemn, quiet figure of a Northern Song tomb honor guard.
facts: Date of the tomb: The Yongzhao Mausoleum is the tomb of Emperor Renzong of Song, Zhao Zhen, begun in 1063; this entry uses its original stone carvings to represent the Northern Song imperial tombs, without counting the individual tombs separately.

Surviving carvings: The spirit ways of the Song tombs set out a ceremonial order with human and animal statues; the stone carvings are physical evidence for the study of Song sculpture and the imperial funerary system.

Plate scope: The plate shows the first stone civil official from the south in the east row at the Yongzhao Mausoleum; based on on-site photographs from 2025, it keeps the damaged crown, the tablet-holding pose and the stone base, and does not include the modern reconstructed gate towers.
captions: Yongzhao Mausoleum · Stone civil official (east row, first from south)
Northern Song · Tomb built 1063

hn_bixia.name: Bixia Palace, Xun County
hn_bixia.sub: Front of the main hall · Worship hall elevation
hn_bixia.era: Ming · Founded in the 21st year of Jiajing, with later repairs
hn_bixia.yearNote: 1542 is the founding date of the main hall recorded in sources, and repeated restorations in the Ming and Qing produced the present appearance; the plate shows only the front worship hall and does not include the unseen roof of the rear hall.
hn_bixia.place: Henan · Hebi · Mount Fuqiu, Xun County
hn_bixia.lede: A round-ridge roof spreads above woodcarving and painted decoration, and red door columns frame the dark entrance of the hall. With its worship hall joined to the main hall, Bixia Palace on Mount Fuqiu preserves the dense craftsmanship of a popular Ming–Qing temple.
facts: Construction and repairs: Sources record the main hall's founding as the 21st year of Jiajing in the Ming (1542), followed by many repairs and expansions in the Ming and Qing; the present appearance does not mean every member is original to the first construction.

Hall arrangement: A round-ridge hip-and-gable worship hall at the front joins a main hall with an overhanging gable roof behind; the woodcarving of the front eaves, pierced-carved windows and painted decoration make up a rich facade.

View notes: Drawn from a 2024 frontal on-site photograph of the front worship hall, omitting neighboring halls, trees, offering furnishings and text; the platform edge and side steps are generalized, and the hidden carved central imperial way is not reconstructed.
captions: Bixia Palace · Front worship hall elevation of the main hall
Founded in the Ming · Further repairs in the Ming and Qing

nx_xumishan.name: Xumishan Grottoes
nx_xumishan.sub: Cave 5 Maitreya Buddha · Chest and knees, detail
nx_xumishan.era: Tang sculpture · Grottoes begun in the Northern Wei
nx_xumishan.yearNote: 750 is only an approximate timeline placement for the Tang great Buddha of Cave 5, not an exact carving date; the Northern Wei founding of the grottoes is not used in place of the subject drawn.
nx_xumishan.place: Ningxia · Guyuan · Yuanzhou District · Mount Xumi
nx_xumishan.lede: At the northern foot of the Liupan Mountains, the grottoes are spread along the undulating cliffs. The Tang Maitreya Buddha of Cave 5 faces the valley with broad shoulders, long ears and a full, round face, its drapery still falling gently from the chest.
facts: Dating of the subject: The grottoes were first cut in the late Northern Wei and developed through the Western Wei, Northern Zhou, Sui and Tang; this plate shows the Tang Maitreya Buddha of Cave 5 and does not treat the Northern Dynasties caves as Tang.

The great Buddha: A large seated Maitreya. Materials from the Ningxia Department of Culture and Tourism give its height as about 20.6 m, while another introduction gives 20.06 m; the approximate figure is kept here, without claiming measured precision on the basis of descriptive texts.

Detail drawn: Based on a 2017 on-site photograph, the plate shows the head, the drapery folds on the chest and the knees, keeping the weathering damage; it does not invent the unseen hands, feet or lotus seat, nor reconstruct the painted color.
captions: Xumishan Cave 5 · Maitreya Buddha, chest and knees
Tang sculpture · Weathering kept as photographed

nx_xixialing.name: Western Xia Imperial Tombs
nx_xixialing.sub: Tomb No. 3 · Surviving rammed-earth tomb tower
nx_xixialing.yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate sorting point for the Western Xia period, not the exact construction year of Tomb No. 3; Tomb No. 3 is generally considered to be Li Yuanhao's Tailing, but the attribution of its occupant is not treated as a proven conclusion.
nx_xixialing.place: Ningxia · Yinchuan · Xixia District · Eastern foot of the Helan Mountains
nx_xixialing.lede: At the eastern foot of the Helan Mountains, the rammed-earth tomb tower exposes layer upon layer of weathered shoulders. The original architectural cladding is gone, yet the remaining earthen core still gives this imperial necropolis a sharply defined profile.
facts: Period of the necropolis: The Western Xia Imperial Tombs took shape between the 11th and 13th centuries as the burial ground of the Western Xia imperial house; Tomb No. 3 is generally thought to be associated with the founding emperor Li Yuanhao, and the plate does not treat this presumed occupant as established fact.

Form of the remains: This plate shows only the surviving rammed-earth tomb tower of Tomb No. 3, keeping its taper, banding and irregular damage as photographed; it does not follow the museum's reconstruction model or add eaves and a finial.

World Heritage: The Western Xia Imperial Tombs were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025; the property comprises nine imperial tombs, satellite tombs and related buildings, and flood-control remains, and this plate does not represent the whole necropolis.
captions: Western Xia Tomb No. 3 · Surviving rammed-earth tomb tower
Western Xia site · Not a reconstruction of the original

nx_108towers.name: One Hundred and Eight Pagodas of Qingtongxia
nx_108towers.sub: Top three rows of the group · Seven pagodas, detail
nx_108towers.era: Western Xia founding attributed · Later restoration
nx_108towers.yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate placement based on the Qingtongxia municipal government's view that the pagodas were founded in the Western Xia, not an exact construction year. The 1988 national protected site list records the period as Yuan; the founding, later restoration and the surviving brick exterior must be considered separately.
nx_108towers.place: Ningxia · Wuzhong · Qingtongxia · West bank of the Yellow River
nx_108towers.lede: On the west bank of the Yellow River, brick pagodas are ranged row by row down the hillside, spreading from a single pagoda at the top into a triangle. Each pagoda is small, yet together they form an exceptionally striking order within Ningxia's Buddhist architecture.
facts: Twelve rows of pagodas: From top to bottom they are arranged in rows of 1, 3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19, totaling 108; the bases and bodies of individual pagodas differ slightly and cannot be treated as identical copies of a single type.

Dating and repairs: The Qingtongxia municipal government's introduction adopts the view of a Western Xia founding, while the 1988 list of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level records them as Yuan; this entry is classified by the founding view and states the discrepancy in registration explicitly, and it does not regard all of the surviving brick cladding as original Western Xia work.

Scope drawn: The plate takes only the top three rows of seven pagodas and the terrace supporting them, emphasizing the larger top pagoda and the 1, 3, 3 arrangement; this seven-pagoda detail is not passed off as a complete panorama of all 108 pagodas.
captions: 108 Pagodas · Top three rows, seven pagodas, detail
Western Xia founding attributed · Present state after later restoration

jp_kinkaku.name: Kinkaku-ji
jp_kinkaku.yearNote: The timeline uses 1955, the year the surviving Shariden was rebuilt; the original structure from the time of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu burned down in 1950.
jp_kinkaku.lede: Beside the Kyōko-chi pond, the three-story Golden Pavilion stacks floors of differing styles. The Shariden seen today was rebuilt in 1955 according to old records, and its gold-leaf surface has undergone later repairs.
facts: The Shariden of Rokuon-ji, popularly called the Golden Pavilion, was originally associated with Ashikaga Yoshimitsu's Kitayama villa; it was destroyed by fire in 1950, and the present building was rebuilt in 1955.
The first floor is the Hōsui-in, the second the Chōondō and the third the Kukyōchō; the second and third floors are covered in gold leaf, and a phoenix stands on the roof.
The plate focuses on the surviving three-story Shariden and does not record the reconstruction as a Muromachi original untouched by fire.

jp_ginkaku.name: Ginkaku-ji
jp_ginkaku.yearNote: Temple records state that the ridgepole of the Kannon-den was raised in 1489 and that it was still unfinished when Ashikaga Yoshimasa died in 1490; the timeline marks the documented year of the ridgepole raising and does not presume a completion year.
jp_ginkaku.lede: The Silver Pavilion was never covered in silver leaf. Amid the tree shadows and pond water of Higashiyama, the two-story Kannon-den retains its dark timber frame, broad eaves and upper-floor window lattices; it is a surviving pavilion of the Muromachi period.
facts: Construction of Ashikaga Yoshimasa's Higashiyama villa began in 1482, and the ridgepole of the Kannon-den was raised in 1489; Yoshimasa did not live to see it completed.
The Kannon-den is a surviving Muromachi-period pavilion and garden building and has since been repaired; the plate is based on its present state.
“Silver Pavilion” is a popular name; the building is in fact the Kannon-den of Jishō-ji and should not be drawn in silver because of its name.

jp_sensoji.name: Sensō-ji
jp_sensoji.yearNote: The timeline marks the 1958 completion of the reinforced-concrete main hall seen today, rather than the temple's founding legend or the old Edo-period main hall.
jp_sensoji.lede: The broad roof of Sensō-ji's main hall bears down on a deep, long veranda, and worshippers walk from Nakamise toward the Kannon Hall. The surviving main hall is a religious building rebuilt after the war.
facts: The original main hall, a National Treasure, burned in the 1945 air raids on Tokyo, and the present main hall was completed in 1958.
Official temple records state that the present main hall has a reinforced-concrete structure and an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof; the roof was re-covered with titanium tiles in 2010.
The plate shows only the front of the main hall and does not mix in the Kaminarimon, rebuilt in 1960, or the five-story pagoda, rebuilt in 1973.

jp_himeji.name: Himeji Castle
jp_himeji.lede: White plastered walls rise tier upon tier above the stone ramparts, and the gables and dark tiled eaves of the main keep overlap into the silhouette of the “White Heron Castle.” The plate takes the surviving main tower as its subject.
facts: Ikeda Terumasa carried out a large-scale rebuilding of Himeji Castle from 1601, and the five-tiered main keep was completed in 1609.
The castle also has smaller keeps, connecting turrets, gates and baileys; the plate shows only the main keep and the high stone wall supporting it.
The surviving keep has undergone repairs in the Shōwa and Heisei eras; 1609 is the completion year of the main structure, not the age of all its surface materials.
captions: Main keep and high stone walls of Himeji Castle · Line drawing
Drawn from the surviving structure

jp_itsukushima.name: Itsukushima Shrine
jp_itsukushima.sub: Seaside main shrine buildings and corridors
jp_itsukushima.era: Built in the 12th century · Main surviving buildings rebuilt in 1241
jp_itsukushima.yearNote: The UNESCO evaluation records that the main surviving shrine buildings were rebuilt in 1241; the main shrine complex has undergone repeated repairs and additions, and the timeline point indicates only the rebuilding phase of the main surviving structures.
jp_itsukushima.lede: Vermilion shrine buildings and corridors stand over the tide, their roofs unfolding layer upon layer along the shore. The plate chooses the seaside buildings of the main shrine and does not let the great torii in the sea stand in for the shrine buildings.
facts: Taira no Kiyomori promoted the building of Itsukushima's shrine halls over the sea in the 12th century, and today's layout preserves the style of that time.
The main surviving shrine buildings were rebuilt after a fire in 1223, with the work completed by 1241; the individual buildings have since undergone separate repairs.
The plate shows the low shrine buildings, the vermilion colonnades and the corridors from the sea side; its scope is the building complex, not a survey of any single hall.
captions: Seaside main shrine buildings and corridors of Itsukushima Shrine · Line drawing
Drawn from the surviving structure

jp_nikko_toshogu.name: Nikkō Tōshō-gū
jp_nikko_toshogu.lede: White columns, black lacquer, gilt fittings and layered carving come together on the two-story Yōmeimon, the most striking entrance of Nikkō Tōshō-gū.
facts: The main shrine buildings of Tōshō-gū in their present state took shape in the great rebuilding of 1636 directed by Tokugawa Iemitsu.
The Yōmeimon is a two-story gate whose eaves and columns are adorned with dense carving; the plate keeps only the recognizable overall structure and part of the decoration.
The gate's painted decoration and surfaces have been restored over time; the plate reflects the present state and does not treat every layer of color as the 17th-century original.
captions: Front of the Yōmeimon, Nikkō Tōshō-gū, present state · Line drawing
Drawn from the surviving structure

jp_daigoji_tower.name: Five-Story Pagoda of Daigo-ji
jp_daigoji_tower.lede: Five tiers of eaves draw in level by level, and the spire rings at the top point to the sky. The five-story pagoda of Daigo-ji is an important Heian-period timber pagoda surviving in Kyoto.
facts: Daigo-ji records that the five-story pagoda was completed in the 5th year of Tenryaku (951).
The plate focuses on the surviving pagoda body and spire rings, omitting the surrounding precinct and trees.
captions: Daigo-ji · Five-story pagoda
Heian period · 951

jp_sanjusangendo.name: Sanjūsangen-dō
jp_sanjusangendo.lede: A colonnade runs the length of the long eaves, forming the most distinctive exterior of Sanjūsangen-dō. The plate takes the surviving main hall as its subject.
facts: The main hall of Rengeō-in was rebuilt in 1266 after a fire.

“Thirty-three bays” is the traditional name for the intercolumnar spaces inside the hall; the plate shows the building's full-length exterior and does not bring the thousand-armed Kannon statues inside into the exterior view.
captions: Sanjūsangen-dō · Main hall
Kamakura period · Rebuilt 1266

jp_nijo_ninomaru.name: Ninomaru Palace, Nijō Castle
jp_nijo_ninomaru.sub: Kurumayose carriage porch and Tozamurai, exterior
jp_nijo_ninomaru.yearNote: The timeline is placed by the major renovation of the surviving palace complex around 1626; the plate takes the exterior of the Kurumayose and Tozamurai and does not mean that the whole castle was completed in the same year.
jp_nijo_ninomaru.lede: Layered roofs and the ornate front of the carriage porch open the entrance sequence of the Ninomaru Palace. The plate takes only part of the surviving palace.
facts: The Ninomaru Palace of Nijō Castle was built in the time of Tokugawa Ieyasu and later extensively renovated in 1624–26 to receive an imperial visit by Emperor Go-Mizunoo.
The plate takes the exterior of the Kurumayose and Tozamurai as its subject and does not mix in the lost former Honmaru Palace or the castle keep.
captions: Nijō Castle · Carriage porch of the Ninomaru Palace
Edo period · Around 1626

jp_yasaka_honden.name: Main Hall of Yasaka Shrine
jp_yasaka_honden.lede: A huge cypress-bark roof gathers the main sanctuary and the worship hall together, and vermilion columns and white walls mark the distinctive Gion-zukuri style of Yasaka Shrine.
facts: The present main hall was built in the 3rd year of Jōō (1654).
Gion-zukuri places the inner sanctuary and the worship hall under a single great roof; the plate omits the surrounding subsidiary shrine buildings.
captions: Yasaka Shrine · Main hall
Edo period · 1654

jp_yakushiji_east.name: East Pagoda of Yakushi-ji
jp_yakushiji_east.sub: East Pagoda · Three stories, six roofs
jp_yakushiji_east.yearNote: The temple gives the 2nd year of Tenpyō (730) as the completion date of the East Pagoda; the timeline point is an approximate completion date for the surviving structure.
jp_yakushiji_east.lede: Beneath each tier of eaves runs an additional pent roof (mokoshi), giving the three-story pagoda a rhythm of six roofs. The East Pagoda is a Nara-period building preserved at Yakushi-ji.
facts: Yakushi-ji records that the East Pagoda was completed around 730; it has undergone modern repairs.
The East Pagoda is a three-story pagoda whose additional pent roofs make it look like six stories; the plate does not substitute the newer West Pagoda.
captions: Yakushi-ji · East Pagoda
Nara period · About 730

jp_gangoji_gokuraku.name: Main Hall of Gangō-ji Gokurakubō
jp_gangoji_gokuraku.yearNote: The surviving main hall was converted from an old monks' dormitory; its date is placed approximately according to the cultural heritage database's record of the mid-Kamakura period.
jp_gangoji_gokuraku.lede: The low, broad roof and rows of timber columns keep the spatial scale of an old monks' dormitory converted into a Buddha hall. The plate shows only the Gokurakubō main hall.
facts: The Gokurakubō main hall of Gangō-ji was converted from an old monks' dormitory building, and its present form took shape in the Kamakura period.
The adjacent Zenshitsu is a separate cultural property; the plate does not merge the two buildings into one hall.
captions: Gangō-ji · Gokurakubō main hall
Kamakura period · About mid-13th century

jp_kofukuji_hokuen.name: Hokuen-dō of Kōfuku-ji
jp_kofukuji_hokuen.lede: An octagonal roof encloses a compact Buddha hall, and the outline of the Hokuen-dō contrasts sharply with the tall pagoda of Kōfuku-ji.
facts: Kōfuku-ji records that the Hokuen-dō was rebuilt in the Jōgen era, and the present hall is a Kamakura-period building.
The plate shows only the octagonal hall and its platform and does not include the five-story pagoda.
captions: Kōfuku-ji · Hokuen-dō
Kamakura period · About 1210

jp_kasuga_honden.name: Four Main Sanctuaries of Kasuga Taisha
jp_kasuga_honden.sub: Four main sanctuaries in Kasuga-zukuri style
jp_kasuga_honden.lede: Four small Kasuga-zukuri sanctuaries are ranged step by step along the slope, their cypress-bark roofs and vermilion and white walls forming an undulating line.
facts: The main sanctuary of Kasuga Taisha consists of four one-bay Kasuga-zukuri buildings; the present sanctuaries were ritually rebuilt in the 3rd year of Bunkyū (1863).
The plate is a composite illustration based on partial on-site photographs and information on the arrangement, omitting the Chūmon gate, the Onrō corridor and the trees that screen the sanctuaries.
captions: Kasuga Taisha · Four main sanctuaries, illustration
Edo period · Ritually rebuilt 1863

jp_sumiyoshi_honden.name: Four Main Sanctuaries of Sumiyoshi Taisha
jp_sumiyoshi_honden.sub: Four main sanctuaries in Sumiyoshi-zukuri style
jp_sumiyoshi_honden.lede: Three main sanctuaries stand in a line one behind another, and the fourth stands beside the third. The unusual layout of the vermilion shrine buildings resembles a fleet of ships facing the sea.
facts: The four main sanctuaries of Sumiyoshi Taisha are Sumiyoshi-zukuri buildings ritually rebuilt in the 7th year of Bunka (1810).

The First, Second and Third Sanctuaries are arranged in a line, one behind another, and the Fourth Sanctuary lies on the south side of the Third; the plate is a composite illustration showing the layout of the four.
captions: Sumiyoshi Taisha · Four main sanctuaries, illustration
Edo period · 1810

jp_osaka_sengan.name: Sengan Turret of Osaka Castle
jp_osaka_sengan.lede: The white-walled, black-tiled Sengan Turret stands at the corner of a high stone wall, a defensive structure surviving from the Tokugawa period of Osaka Castle.
facts: The Sengan Turret was completed in the 6th year of Genna (1620) and survives to the west of the Ōte entrance of Osaka Castle.
The plate shows the surviving turret and the stone wall that supports it, not the main keep rebuilt in 1931.
captions: Osaka Castle · Sengan Turret and stone wall
Edo period · 1620

jp_jigenin_tahoto.name: Tahōtō of Jigen-in
jp_jigenin_tahoto.lede: A square lower story and a cylindrical upper body carry two cypress-bark roofs. At its compact scale, the tahōtō of Jigen-in preserves a Kamakura-period form.
facts: Cultural property records state that the tahōtō of Jigen-in was built in the 8th year of Bun'ei (1271).
The plate takes the surviving two-tiered pagoda as its subject and does not mistakenly draw it as a five-story pagoda.
captions: Jigen-in · Tahōtō pagoda
Kamakura period · 1271

jp_kanshinji_kondo.name: Kondō of Kanshin-ji
jp_kanshinji_kondo.yearNote: Cultural property records date the Kondō to between 1346 and 1369; 1355 is only an approximate position on the timeline, not an exact completion year.
jp_kanshinji_kondo.lede: The broad Kondō spreads across a seven-bay front, and its deep eaves and kōhai step canopy gather the timber columns, white walls and doors beneath a low, gentle roof.
facts: The surviving Kondō is generally dated to the Nanboku-chō to early Muromachi periods, and cultural property records give a construction range of 1346–1369.
The plate shows the surviving seven-bay front and three-bay kōhai, and does not label this building with the temple's earlier founding date.
captions: Kanshin-ji · Kondō
Early Muromachi · Mid-14th century

jp_tofukuji_sanmon.name: Sanmon of Tōfuku-ji
jp_tofukuji_sanmon.lede: Broad upper and lower tiled eaves shelter tiers of beam framing, and three passages run through the ground level of the gate. The Sanmon of Tōfuku-ji preserves the grand scale of a Muromachi-period Zen temple gate.
facts: The original gate was destroyed by fire in the 14th century, and the present Sanmon was completed in 1425.
The plate shows the surviving two-story gate, five bays wide with three doorways, and does not use the temple's 13th-century founding date as the date of the timber structure.
captions: Tōfuku-ji · Sanmon
Muromachi period · 1425

jp_fushimi_inari_honden.name: Main Hall of Fushimi Inari Taisha
jp_fushimi_inari_honden.lede: Vermilion timberwork and white walls are gathered beneath an undulating cypress-bark roof. This main hall explains the shrine architecture of Fushimi Inari Taisha better than the thousand torii do.
facts: The old shrine buildings burned in the warfare of 1468, and the present main hall was rebuilt in 1499.
The plate focuses on the main hall and does not let the thousand torii along the approach stand in for the main building.
captions: Fushimi Inari Taisha · Main hall
Muromachi period · Rebuilt 1499

jp_kitano_honden.name: Main Hall of Kitano Tenman-gū
jp_kitano_honden.sub: Main hall, ishi-no-ma and worship hall
jp_kitano_honden.lede: The main hall and the worship hall are joined into one by the ishi-no-ma, and tiers of cypress-bark roofs and carved ornament form a grand shrine in the Momoyama style.
facts: The present shrine buildings were built in 1607 by Toyotomi Hideyori and retain the connected yatsumune-zukuri structure of main hall, ishi-no-ma, worship hall and gaku-no-ma.
The plate focuses on the visible exterior of this connected group of shrine buildings and does not include the other subsidiary shrines in the precinct.
captions: Kitano Tenman-gū · Main hall complex
Early Edo period · 1607

jp_ninnaji_kondo.name: Kondō of Ninna-ji
jp_ninnaji_kondo.sub: Former Shishinden of the Imperial Palace, relocated
jp_ninnaji_kondo.era: Original structure 1613 · Relocated in the early Edo period
jp_ninnaji_kondo.yearNote: The timeline uses 1613, the date of the original structure listed in the cultural heritage database; temple records state that it was relocated as the Kondō between 1624 and 1643, and the present roof has also been altered.
jp_ninnaji_kondo.lede: The old seven-bay palace structure became the Kondō of Ninna-ji, and its low, gentle roof and deep eaves still keep the scale of the Shishinden.
facts: The Kondō was relocated from the Shishinden of the Imperial Palace of the Keichō period; 1613 is the registered date of the original structure, and temple records state that it was relocated between 1624 and 1643.
After relocation it was used as a Buddha hall, and its roofing materials differ from those of its palace period; the plate is drawn from the exterior of the present Kondō.
captions: Ninna-ji · Kondō
Momoyama original structure · Relocated in the early Edo period

jp_hongwanji_hiunkaku.name: Hiunkaku of Nishi Hongan-ji
jp_hongwanji_hiunkaku.sub: Three-story pavilion in the Tekisui-en garden
jp_hongwanji_hiunkaku.yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate timeline placement, not an exact construction year; the tradition that it was relocated from the Jurakudai has been handed down but is unproven. The cultural heritage database assigns it to the Momoyama period.
jp_hongwanji_hiunkaku.lede: The three-story pavilion by the pond steps back story by story and shifts to one side, its asymmetrical roofs and slender columns forming a light silhouette.
facts: The Hiunkaku, together with the Golden and Silver Pavilions, is counted among the three famous pavilions of Kyoto; the surviving building stands in the Tekisui-en garden of Nishi Hongan-ji.
The building's exact date is unknown; the plate does not treat the legendary relocation from the Jurakudai as proven history. It is not normally open to visitors.
captions: Nishi Hongan-ji · Hiunkaku
Momoyama period · Date unknown

jp_manpukuji_daiou.name: Daiyūhōden of Manpuku-ji
jp_manpukuji_daiou.sub: Mahavira Hall of the Ōbaku school
jp_manpukuji_daiou.lede: Dark tiled roofs, round windows and peach-shaped door ornaments give this Buddha hall in Uji the look of late Ming architectural design fused with Japanese timber construction.
facts: The Daiyūhōden (Mahavira Hall) was built in 1668 and is the central Buddha hall of the Manpuku-ji complex.
The plate focuses on the surviving Daiyūhōden and does not combine the Tennōden or the Hattō with it as one building.
captions: Manpuku-ji · Daiyūhōden
Edo period · 1668

jp_iwashimizu_honden.name: Main Shrine of Iwashimizu Hachimangū
jp_iwashimizu_honden.sub: Front of the tower gate and corridors, detail
jp_iwashimizu_honden.lede: A vermilion-lacquered tower gate and corridors enclose the main shrine, and cypress-bark roofs and dense woodwork display the splendor of an early Edo Hachiman shrine.
facts: The ten buildings of the present main shrine took shape in the great construction of 1631–1634 and retain a main hall in Hachiman-zukuri style.

The main hall is screened by the surrounding corridor; the plate shows the tower gate and the front of the main shrine visible from outside, and does not invent the unseen front elevation of the inner sanctuary.
captions: Iwashimizu Hachimangū · Front of the main shrine, detail
Edo period · 1634

jp_ishiyamadera_tahoto.name: Tahōtō of Ishiyama-dera
jp_ishiyamadera_tahoto.lede: A square lower story carries a round body, and the two roofs and slender spire rings form a light yet stable silhouette on the rock.
facts: An ink inscription inside the pagoda records its erection in 1194, making it an early tahōtō with a firmly established date.
The plate shows only the surviving tahōtō and does not include the main hall or gate of Ishiyama-dera.
captions: Ishiyama-dera · Tahōtō pagoda
Kamakura period · 1194

jp_ishiyamadera_hondo.name: Main Hall of Ishiyama-dera
jp_ishiyamadera_hondo.era: Inner hall rebuilt 1096 · Worship hall added 1602
jp_ishiyamadera_hondo.yearNote: The timeline uses 1096, the year the surviving inner hall was rebuilt; the worship hall in front was added in 1602, and the roof and exterior seen in the plate belong to both periods.
jp_ishiyamadera_hondo.lede: Built out against the hillside, the main hall joins a Heian-period inner hall to a later worship hall, its eaves and colonnades spreading along the rocky slope.
facts: The inner hall was rebuilt in 1096 and is one of the older timber buildings preserved in Shiga Prefecture.
The worship hall at the front was added in 1602; the plate shows today's joined exterior and does not misrecord the whole hall as a single construction of 1096.
captions: Ishiyama-dera · Main hall
Heian inner hall · Early Edo worship hall

jp_chionin_sanmon.name: Sanmon of Chion-in
jp_chionin_sanmon.lede: The giant two-story gate spreads about 50 m wide, its layered tiled eaves bearing down on tall timber columns; it is one of the most imposing historic silhouettes in the Higashiyama area of Kyoto.
facts: The present Sanmon was erected in 1621; it is five bays wide with three doorways, and the interior of its upper story is not normally open to the public.
The plate shows the surviving early Edo gate and is catalogued separately from the 1425 Zen temple Sanmon of Tōfuku-ji.
captions: Chion-in · Sanmon
Edo period · 1621

jp_nanzenji_sanmon.name: Sanmon of Nanzen-ji
jp_nanzenji_sanmon.lede: Upper and lower tiled eaves span three open passages, and dark timber columns hold up the broad upper story. The Sanmon of Nanzen-ji is a large early Edo Zen temple gate surviving in the Higashiyama area of Kyoto.
facts: The present Sanmon was rebuilt in 1628; the temple's 13th-century founding date is not the construction year of this gate.
The plate shows the front of the Sanmon and does not include the steps in front or the trees on either side.
captions: Nanzen-ji · Sanmon
Edo period · 1628

jp_ujigami_honden.name: Main Hall of Ujigami Shrine
jp_ujigami_honden.sub: Outer sheltering hall of the main sanctuary
jp_ujigami_honden.yearNote: 1100 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; the main hall is generally dated to the late 11th century, and its outer sheltering hall contains three inner sanctuaries.
jp_ujigami_honden.lede: A long outer sheltering hall encloses three inner sanctuaries, and the wooden lattices and deep eaves at the front create the distinctive exterior of the Ujigami Shrine main hall.
facts: The present main hall is thought to have been built in the late Heian period and cannot be dated together with the later worship hall in front of it.
The plate is drawn from the visible outer sheltering hall and does not speculate about the details of the three hidden inner sanctuaries.
captions: Ujigami Shrine · Main hall
Late Heian · About late 11th century

jp_ujigami_haiden.name: Worship Hall of Ujigami Shrine
jp_ujigami_haiden.yearNote: 1210 serves only as an approximate timeline placement, not an exact completion year; the worship hall is generally dated to the early Kamakura period.
jp_ujigami_haiden.lede: The long, narrow worship hall holds down its broad front beneath a gently curving cypress-bark roof, while wooden lattices, white walls and central steps form a quiet axis.
facts: The worship hall and the late Heian main hall are two National Treasure buildings of different dates.
The plate shows the front of the worship hall, with worship fixtures and visitors removed.
captions: Ujigami Shrine · Worship hall
Early Kamakura · About early 13th century

jp_kozanji_sekisuiin.name: Sekisui-in of Kōzan-ji
jp_kozanji_sekisuiin.sub: Interior of the open veranda of Sekisui-in
jp_kozanji_sekisuiin.era: Early Kamakura original · Relocated in the Meiji period
jp_kozanji_sekisuiin.yearNote: 1230 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; Sekisui-in is an early Kamakura building, and its present site is the location to which it was moved in 1889.
jp_kozanji_sekisuiin.lede: The open timber veranda links light posts and beams, railing panels and the mountain scenery. Sekisui-in preserves the spatial scale of Kamakura-period architecture at Kōzan-ji.
facts: Sekisui-in is an early Kamakura National Treasure building preserved at Kōzan-ji and was moved to its present site in the Meiji period.
The available reference photographs show the inside of the veranda; the plate draws only the verifiable open veranda structure and does not fabricate an entire exterior elevation.
captions: Kōzan-ji · Open veranda of Sekisui-in
Early Kamakura · Relocated in the Meiji period

jp_kamigamo_honden.name: Honden and Gonden of Kamigamo Shrine
jp_kamigamo_honden.sub: Front of the honden and gonden
jp_kamigamo_honden.lede: The honden (main sanctuary) and gonden (provisional sanctuary) stand side by side on a raised platform, their long eaves and front steps showing how the principal sanctuaries of Kamigamo Shrine are grouped.
facts: The present honden and gonden were built in 1863; the shrine's much earlier founding date cannot be substituted for this.

The plate draws the visible fronts of the two halls from 1957 architectural record photographs; its coloring uses only restrained natural wood tones and is not a reconstruction of original painted decoration.
captions: Kamigamo Shrine · Honden and gonden
Edo period · 1863

jp_shimogamo_honden.name: East and West Main Sanctuaries of Shimogamo Shrine
jp_shimogamo_honden.sub: Front of the east and west main sanctuaries, illustration
jp_shimogamo_honden.lede: The east and west main sanctuaries stand side by side deep within the shrine precinct, with raised steps and dark timberwork visible between the front corridors.
facts: The present east and west main sanctuaries were built in 1863, each enshrining a different deity.

The exterior of the main sanctuaries is screened by the front corridor; the plate sets side by side the front elements that can be confirmed from two on-site photographs and does not represent a complete building elevation.
captions: Shimogamo Shrine · Front of the east and west main sanctuaries
Edo period · 1863

jp_enryakuji_komponchudo.name: Enryaku-ji Konponchūdō
jp_enryakuji_komponchudo.lede: The great roof rises above the low front corridor, and tiers of deep eaves enclose this central Buddha hall of the Tendai school on Mount Hiei.
facts: The present Konponchūdō was rebuilt in 1640; the 8th-century founding refers to the beginning of the temple.
The plate is drawn from the main roof and front entrance visible in photographs and does not reconstruct the interior.
captions: Enryaku-ji · Konponchūdō
Edo period · Rebuilt 1640

jp_katsura_koshoin.name: Old Shoin of Katsura Imperial Villa
jp_katsura_koshoin.yearNote: 1615 is only an approximate timeline placement; the Imperial Household Agency assigns the Old Shoin to about the early 17th century, and the shoin complex as a whole is not regarded as built all at once in the same year.
jp_katsura_koshoin.lede: A thin, broad roof, white walls, wooden lattices and a raised timber veranda form the low shoin facade, and views of the garden open outward beneath the low eaves.
facts: The shoin of Katsura Imperial Villa consist of parts from several periods, including the Old Shoin, the Middle Shoin and the New Palace.
The plate shows only the visible exterior of the Old Shoin and does not fold the later additions into this building's dating.
captions: Katsura Imperial Villa · Old Shoin
Early Edo period · About early 17th century

jp_joruriji_hondo.name: Main Hall of Jōruri-ji
jp_joruriji_hondo.yearNote: 1150 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; the main hall is a late Heian survival.
jp_joruriji_hondo.lede: The long, narrow Hall of Nine Amida Buddhas stretches along the pond shore, and a row of lattice doors beneath its single-tier tiled roof corresponds to the nine Amida Buddhas inside.
facts: The main hall is a precious timber building that preserves a late Heian devotional space for nine Amida Buddhas.
The plate focuses on the surviving main hall and does not merge the pond or the three-story pagoda on the far bank into the building's outline.
captions: Jōruri-ji · Main hall
Late Heian · About 12th century

jp_joruriji_tower.name: Three-Story Pagoda of Jōruri-ji
jp_joruriji_tower.yearNote: 1150 serves only as an approximate timeline placement, not the exact date of the original structure; 1178 is the year it was moved to its present site, not the year it was built.
jp_joruriji_tower.lede: Three tiers of tiled eaves diminish level by level, and the vermilion timberwork and white walls form a striking vertical marker on the east side of the pond.
facts: The three-story pagoda is a late Heian building, moved from Kyoto to Jōruri-ji in 1178.
The plate shows the complete three-story body and spire rings and does not miswrite the relocation year as the pagoda's founding year.
captions: Jōruri-ji · Three-story pagoda
Late Heian original · Relocated 1178

jp_ryoanji_garden.name: Rock Garden of Ryōan-ji
jp_ryoanji_garden.sub: Dry landscape rock garden of the hōjō
jp_ryoanji_garden.era: Garden made in the Muromachi period · Date unknown
jp_ryoanji_garden.yearNote: 1500 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; the garden's creator and exact date of creation are still disputed, and this sorting point is not treated as an exact date.
jp_ryoanji_garden.lede: Rock groupings in white sand and a low earthen wall form an extremely restrained karesansui (dry landscape) space, where the empty expanse lets the distances between the stones take center stage.
facts: The rock garden of Ryōan-ji lies south of the hōjō and consists of white sand, fifteen stones and an earthen wall.
The plate draws part of the rock garden from one on-site photographic viewpoint and does not replace the visible rock groupings with a fabricated panorama.
captions: Ryōan-ji · Rock garden, detail
Muromachi period · Date unknown

jp_tenryuji_garden.name: Sōgen Pond Garden of Tenryū-ji
jp_tenryuji_garden.era: Garden made in the mid-14th century
jp_tenryuji_garden.yearNote: 1340 is only an approximate timeline placement; the garden was reworked by Musō Soseki around the founding of the temple in 1339, and the present scene shows changes from later maintenance.
jp_tenryuji_garden.lede: Sōgen Pond joins the shoreline rock groupings, garden trees and the borrowed scenery of Arashiyama into one view; the temple buildings at the pond's edge merely lend scale to the landscape.
facts: The Sōgen Pond Garden is closely tied to the founding period of Tenryū-ji and retains the layout of a medieval stroll garden.
The plate takes the pond and rock groupings as its subject and does not use the adjacent halls as evidence for dating the old garden.
captions: Tenryū-ji · Sōgen Pond Garden
Early Muromachi · About mid-14th century

jp_saihoji_garden.name: Garden of Saihō-ji
jp_saihoji_garden.yearNote: 1340 serves only as an approximate timeline placement; Musō Soseki reworked the garden in the mid-14th century, and the moss that now spreads so widely is a landscape that formed gradually later.
jp_saihoji_garden.lede: Moss envelops the irregular pond shores and small rock islands, and its varying shades of green set the lower garden of Saihō-ji apart from the usual dry landscape garden.
facts: The layout of the surviving garden is associated with Musō Soseki's medieval reworking.
The plate shows the water, moss and rock islands of one corner of the Golden Pond and does not equate today's moss cover with the 14th-century original appearance.

jp_hokanji_tower.name: Yasaka Pagoda of Hōkan-ji
jp_hokanji_tower.lede: Five tiers of tiled eaves diminish level by level above the lanes of Higashiyama, and the tall spire rings make the Yasaka Pagoda one of the most striking historic silhouettes in Kyoto.
facts: The present five-story pagoda was rebuilt in the 12th year of Eikyō (1440) and is not a structure surviving from the temple's founding.

jp_gosho_shishinden.name: Shishinden of the Kyoto Imperial Palace
jp_gosho_shishinden.lede: A broad cypress-bark roof bears down on a nine-bay front and raised steps; the Shishinden keeps the solemn scale of the principal hall of the early modern court.
facts: The present Shishinden was built in the 2nd year of Ansei (1855); the date of the old hall of the Heian palace must not be used as the date of this building.

Edo period · 1855

jp_daitokuji_karamon.name: Karamon of Daitoku-ji
jp_daitokuji_karamon.sub: Karamon gate of the main temple

jp_daitokuji_karamon.lede: A curved karahafu gable and dense carving sit above dark doors; it is an ornate Momoyama-period gate preserved at the main temple of Daitoku-ji.
facts: The cultural heritage database assigns the surviving Karamon to the Momoyama period; its exact completion year is unknown.

jp_daitokuji_hojo.name: Hōjō of Daitoku-ji
jp_daitokuji_hojo.yearNote: The cultural heritage database listing gives 1635, while its building description gives 1636; the timeline uses the latter for approximate placement.
jp_daitokuji_hojo.lede: A long single-story building stretches out beneath a gray tiled roof, and its orderly lattice doors and raised veranda show the quiet scale of a Zen temple hōjō (abbot's quarters).
facts: The Hōjō of the main temple is an early Edo survival, recorded in sources as either 1635 or 1636.

jp_jishoji_togudo.name: Tōgu-dō of Jishō-ji
jp_jishoji_togudo.yearNote: The cultural heritage database listing gives 1485, while its description gives 1486; the timeline takes the latter for approximate placement.
jp_jishoji_togudo.lede: A low cypress-bark roof encloses white walls and wooden lattices, and the Tōgu-dō preserves the architectural character of Higashiyama culture, in which a Buddha hall adjoins living space.
facts: The Tōgu-dō is a Muromachi-period building preserved at Jishō-ji, separate from the two-story Kannon-den known as the “Silver Pavilion.”

jp_toji_kondo.name: Kondō of Tō-ji
jp_toji_kondo.lede: A great upper roof overlaps the lower pent roof, and the broad latticed facade gives the Kondō of Tō-ji an outline distinct from the tall pagoda in the precinct.
facts: The present Kondō was rebuilt in the 8th year of Keichō (1603) and is a Momoyama-period temple timber building.
The plate focuses on the Kondō and does not substitute the five-story pagoda or the lecture hall of Tō-ji.
captions: Tō-ji · Kondō
Momoyama period · Rebuilt 1603

jp_daigoji_sanboin.name: Omote Shoin of Sanbō-in, Daigo-ji
jp_daigoji_sanboin.lede: The long shoin facade faces the garden, its tiled roof, lattice doors and veranda preserving the spatial scale of an ornate shoin of the Toyotomi period.
facts: The present Omote Shoin was built in the 3rd year of Keichō (1598) and is a National Treasure building of Sanbō-in.
The plate draws the exterior of the Omote Shoin from the temple's own photographs and does not conflate it with the Karamon of Sanbō-in.
captions: Daigo-ji · Omote Shoin of Sanbō-in
Momoyama period · 1598

jp_hongwanji_goeido.name: Goei-dō of Nishi Hongan-ji
jp_hongwanji_goeido.lede: A huge tiled roof covers the open front veranda and dense rows of timber columns, and the Goei-dō displays the scale of an early Edo head temple of Jōdo Shinshū.
facts: The present Goei-dō was rebuilt in the 13th year of Kan'ei (1636).
The plate shows the Goei-dō of Nishi Hongan-ji and does not confuse it with the Goei-dō of Higashi Hongan-ji or the adjacent Amida-dō.
captions: Nishi Hongan-ji · Goei-dō

jp_chionin_mieido.name: Miei-dō of Chion-in
jp_chionin_mieido.lede: A broad tiled roof and a continuous colonnade carry the main hall; the Miei-dō and the huge Sanmon at the entrance each stand as major buildings of Chion-in.
facts: The present Miei-dō was rebuilt in the 16th year of Kan'ei (1639).

facts: Fan Qin built the Tianyi Pavilion in the Jiajing reign of the Ming; the book collection within the pavilion and the building are both protected.

facts: Qing'an Guild Hall is a survival of the activities of Ningbo's shipping merchant guild and was completed in the Xianfeng reign of the Qing.
