fj_laojun.sub: Seated Lord Lao · Song stone carving
fj_laojun.yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate placement on the Song timeline, not a confirmed carving date for Laojun Rock; the subject is registered under the third-batch listing of the Laojun Rock Statue.
fj_laojun.lede: With flowing hair and a long beard, Lord Lao sits within a huge natural boulder, the stone's original shape merging with the figure's posture.
facts: The Laojun Rock Statue was in the third batch of national protected sites and was later combined with other stone statues on Mount Qingyuan for protection.
The plate shows only the seated Lord Lao and the rock attached to it, and does not borrow the batch of other carvings on the same mountain.
captions: Laojun Rock, Mount Qingyuan · Seated figure
Song stone carving · Third batch, national protected site

protection.scope: Seated Laojun figure at Mount Qingyuan and the connected native rock
protection.note: The Laojun Rock Statue was itself listed in the third batch and later merged into the Mount Qingyuan Stone Statues; it is labeled with the batch in which it was first announced.

fj_fuzhou_wenmiao.name: Fuzhou Confucian Temple
fj_fuzhou_wenmiao.era: Present structure from the Xianfeng reign
fj_fuzhou_wenmiao.yearNote: The Confucian Temple has earlier origins; the Dacheng Hall is placed approximately by its 1851–1854 construction phase, and the plate shows its present state after the 2026 restoration.
fj_fuzhou_wenmiao.lede: The broad Dacheng Hall stretches seven bays across; stone steps and deep eaves frame the core space for Confucian rites and teaching in Fuzhou.
facts: The Fuzhou Confucian Temple was in the sixth batch of national protected sites; its surviving buildings were mainly built in the Xianfeng reign of the Qing.
The plate shows only the front of the Dacheng Hall; its recently restored condition is based on photographs taken in 2026.
captions: Fuzhou Confucian Temple · Dacheng Hall
Xianfeng reign, Qing · Seven bays

protection.scope: Front of the Dacheng Hall of the Fuzhou Confucian Temple

tw_tainan_confucius.name: Dacheng Hall, Tainan Confucian Temple
tw_tainan_confucius.yearNote: 1665 marks the founding of the temple and school, and the Dacheng Hall was enlarged in 1712; the surviving hall was dismantled, restored and rebuilt in 1917, and the timeline is placed by the most recent large-scale restoration of the present main structure.
tw_tainan_confucius.lede: Swallowtail ridges sweep upward, and beneath two tiers of red-tiled eaves stands the Dacheng Hall of the Confucian Temple. The Tainan Confucian Temple dates from 1665; the hall seen today has gone through Qing enlargement and a modern dismantling and restoration.
facts: In 1665 Chen Yonghua oversaw the founding of the Temple of the Former Teacher; during a major rebuilding in 1712, the Dacheng Hall, the Qisheng Shrine and other buildings were enlarged.

In 1917 the Dacheng Hall and other buildings were dismantled and restored. The plate shows the front of the surviving Dacheng Hall and does not take the 1665 founding as the date of all its surviving components.

The two tiers of eaves, the paired dragons and central ornament on the ridge, the vermilion columns of the front veranda and the central stone steps make up the front view; the side corridors to left and right are outside the scope of the plate.
captions: Tainan Confucian Temple · Front of the Dacheng Hall
Temple founded 1665 · Dismantled and restored 1917

tw_lukang_longshan.name: Five-Door Hall, Lukang Longshan Temple
tw_lukang_longshan.yearNote: The temple moved to its present site in 1786, and the 1831 renovation established its scale; the plate shows the present state of the Five-Door Hall after component replacements in the 1960s and later restoration, and does not date every column and beam to the Qing.
tw_lukang_longshan.lede: The Five-Door Hall stretches wide, its raised central red-tiled ridge joining the lower side eaves in an undulating outline. It is the gate hall that follows the front gate on the way into the main courtyard of Lukang Longshan Temple.
facts: Longshan Temple moved to its present site in 1786 and completed a major renovation in 1831; the Five-Door Hall belongs to the spatial sequence leading from the front gate through the inner courtyard to the main hall.

The front has five openings, with two carved dragon stone columns at the center and a round decorative window on each of the left and right walls. The plate shows only the Five-Door Hall, without the front gate before it or the main hall behind it.

Some eave columns and beams of the surviving Five-Door Hall were replaced in the 1960s, followed by later restoration; the colored plate is based on 2013 photographs showing red clay tiles, gray-white ridge ornaments, gray stone and old timber.
captions: Lukang Longshan Temple · Front of the Five-Door Hall
Relocated 1786 · Renovated 1831

tw_taipei_northgate.name: North Gate of Taipei Prefectural City
tw_taipei_northgate.era: Completed in the 10th year of Guangxu (1884)
tw_taipei_northgate.lede: An arched passage pierces a massive gray stone platform, topped by red walls and a tiled roof with upturned corners. Cheng'en Gate is a Qing city gate surviving from Taipei Prefectural City.
facts: The North Gate of Taipei Prefectural City was completed in 1884, its plaque inscribed "Cheng'en Gate"; the surviving gate is one of the original gates of Taipei Prefectural City.

The stone-built lower platform is pierced by a single arched passage, and the red upper walls carry a single-eaved tiled roof; the round window on the front and the narrow windows on the sides are kept in the plate.
The plate takes an oblique view of the surviving gate from the northwest and shows only the gate tower itself; the demolished barbican and connecting city walls are not reconstructed.
captions: North Gate of Taipei Prefectural City · Cheng'en Gate
10th year of Guangxu, Qing (1884)

sc_leshan.name: Leshan Giant Buddha
sc_leshan.yearNote: The timeline is placed by 803, the year the Buddha statue was completed. The plate covers the surviving head down to the chest and abdomen and does not represent the complete 71-meter seated figure.
sc_leshan.lede: Tightly coiled snail-shell curls and long ears emerge from the cliff, and below the broad face fall the folds of the robe. Carved over several decades in the Tang, the Leshan Giant Buddha remains joined to the sandstone of Mount Lingyun.
facts: Carving began in 713 and was completed in 803; the plate depicts the present state of the head down to the chest and abdomen.
The Buddha itself is a cliff carving whose image is shaped by the snail-shell curls, long ears and robe folds; the plate does not add the legs or base that the photographs do not include.

The surviving surface has undergone weathering and repeated maintenance. The colored plate follows the pinkish-brown and grayish-brown of the present sandstone and is not a reconstruction of Tang painted decoration.
captions: Leshan Giant Buddha · Head to chest and abdomen
Begun 713 · Completed 803

protection.scope: Surviving cliff-carved head to chest and abdomen of the Leshan Giant Buddha
protection.note: Its first announcement in the second batch is explicitly confirmed by the State Council's sixth-batch merged list; only the surviving head to chest and abdomen of the Buddha is drawn, not the Lingbao Pagoda that was merged into the listing.

sc_baoen.name: Bao'en Temple, Pingwu
sc_baoen.yearNote: Work on the temple began in 1439, its main buildings had taken shape by 1446, and the whole was completed in 1460. The Mahavira Hall is placed at about 1450 within this construction period; no unconfirmed completion date is given for the single hall.
sc_baoen.lede: Beneath double eaves, densely set bracket sets support blue-green glazed tiles. The Mahavira Hall of Pingwu Bao'en Temple preserves the open front of an early Ming official-style hall.
facts: Wang Xi and his son Wang Jian oversaw the building of Bao'en Temple; work began in 1439, and the whole temple was completed in 1460.

The Mahavira Hall stands in the temple's second courtyard, forming the main worship space together with the Dabei Hall and the Huayan Repository, which face each other; the plate shows only the front of the main hall.

The five-bay width and the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof serve as the structural basis; the colored plate follows photographs in keeping the blue-green tiles, grayish-brown timberwork and red doors and columns.
captions: Pingwu Bao'en Temple · Mahavira Hall
Zhengtong to Tianshun reigns, Ming (1439–1460)

protection.scope: Front of the Mahavira Hall of Pingwu Bao'en Temple

sc_wuliang.name: Wuliang Pagoda
sc_wuliang.yearNote: The State Council's sixth-batch list dates it to the Song. The timeline position of about 1000 is for placement within the dynasty and is not a confirmed completion year; the traditional attribution to the Jianlong reign is not presented as a proven exact date.
sc_wuliang.lede: The White Pagoda beside the Jialing River projects eave after eave, its pale body tapering story by story. Built in brick in imitation of a timber pavilion, Wuliang Pagoda leaves the slender outline of an old pagoda of northern Sichuan.
facts: Wuliang Pagoda, also called the Nanchong White Pagoda, stands on Heming Hill in Gaoping District; the sixth-batch national protected site list records its date as Song.
The pagoda is a square, thirteen-story pavilion-style brick pagoda; its eaves diminish gradually, and its carved brick decoration imitates timber architecture.

Accounts of its construction year differ, and this entry gives only an approximate Song placement; the plate is based on photographs of the surviving pagoda and does not reconstruct historical colors.
captions: Wuliang Pagoda · Thirteen-story brick pagoda
Song · Construction year undetermined

protection.scope: Surviving thirteen-story brick Wuliang Pagoda, Nanchong

sc_zhanghuan.name: Zhang Huanhou Shrine
sc_zhanghuan.yearNote: Diwan Tower belongs to the surviving Ming–Qing shrine complex; about 1600 is only a timeline placement, does not assert that all components were built in the same year, and is certainly not based on the year of Zhang Fei's death.
sc_zhanghuan.lede: A raised small tower meets broad lower eaves, and between red columns stands the Diwan Tower of the Zhang Huanhou Shrine in Langzhong. The shrine commemorating Zhang Fei took its present layout through Ming and Qing restorations.
facts: The Zhang Huanhou Shrine is popularly known as the Zhang Fei Temple; the surviving shrine is a Ming–Qing building complex, and the national protected site list likewise dates it to the Ming and Qing.
Diwan Tower is one of the buildings on the shrine's central axis; the plate takes the tower and its connected front eaves and excludes the main hall, the tomb pavilion and Zhang Fei's tomb.

The upper tower, the broad lower eaves and the doors and windows between the columns are rendered from photographs; the visible components have undergone repairs, and no claim is made that all are original Ming fabric.
captions: Zhang Huanhou Shrine · Diwan Tower
Surviving Ming–Qing buildings · Approximate date

protection.scope: Diwan Tower and connected front eaves of the Zhang Huanhou Shrine, Langzhong

sc_luodai.name: Luodai Guild Halls
sc_luodai.era: First built in the Qing · Rebuilt 1913
sc_luodai.yearNote: Yuwang Palace was first built in the Qianlong period of the Qing and rebuilt in 1913 after a fire in 1912. The timeline uses the rebuilding year of the surviving main structure and does not follow the parent unit's "Qing" label to mark the present gate tower as original Qianlong work.
sc_luodai.lede: Undulating fire walls carry cloud and dragon ornaments, and three arched gateways lead into the Huguang Guild Hall of Luodai. Yuwang Palace is one of the guild halls where migrants who came to repopulate Sichuan kept up hometown bonds far from home.
facts: The Luodai Guild Halls national protected site includes the Guangdong, Huguang, Jiangxi and Northern Sichuan guild halls, among others; the plate shows the gate tower of Yuwang Palace, the Huguang Guild Hall.
The Huguang Guild Hall was first built in the Qianlong period of the Qing and rebuilt the year after a fire in 1912; the date of its present state and its founding date are recorded separately.

Of the gate tower's three arched gateways the central one is taller, and the top of the wall has an undulating outline; the cloud motifs, dragon ornaments and deity figures are simplified from photographs, and the shops along the street are not drawn.
captions: Luodai Guild Halls · Gate tower of Yuwang Palace
First built in the Qing · Rebuilt 1913

protection.scope: Surviving gate tower of Yuwang Palace, Huguang Guild Hall, Luodai

sc_shenque.name: Que of Lord Shen
sc_shenque.era: Eastern Han stone que · Approximate date
sc_shenque.yearNote: The que is an Eastern Han relic; about 150 is a placement within the dynasty on the timeline, not a precise construction date from an inscription. The plate shows only one surviving main que and does not add the lost subsidiary que.
sc_shenque.lede: A single sandstone shaft carries tiers of bracket sets imitating timber, with reliefs of birds and beasts on the stone face. The Que of Lord Shen preserves the image of Han timber construction in the stone carving of Qu County.
facts: The Que of Lord Shen was listed in the first batch of national protected sites in 1961 and later merged with the other Han que of Qu County; this subject is still recorded under the first batch, in which it was first announced.
The surviving east and west que form the remains of a spirit-way entrance; the plate takes one of the main que and does not present a single plate as a reconstruction of the whole group.

The form follows a 1914 photograph, and the coloring also draws on modern photographs of the ocher-brown sandstone and the dark gray weathered stone top; the carved decoration has been artistically simplified.
captions: Que of Lord Shen · One surviving main que
Eastern Han stone que · Approximate date

protection.scope: Near-frontal view of one surviving main que of the Que of Lord Shen, Qu County
protection.note: Announced separately as the Que of Lord Shen in 1961; merged into the Han Que of Qu County after 2001. This subject is labeled with the first batch, in which it was first announced.

cq_shibao.name: Shibaozhai
cq_shibao.era: Founded in the Ming · Enlarged in the Qing
cq_shibao.yearNote: Founded in the Wanli reign of the Ming and enlarged several times from the Kangxi to the Tongzhi reigns of the Qing; about 1800 places the surviving tower within the dynasty. Sources differ on when the top three stories took shape, and the whole present tower is not dated to 1956.
cq_shibao.lede: The vermilion tower climbs against Yuyin Hill, its tiers of upturned eaves narrowing beside the rock face. Shibaozhai binds timber construction tightly to the hill, forming a distinctive vertical silhouette on the bank of the Yangtze.
facts: Shibaozhai was founded in the Ming and enlarged and repaired several times in the Qing; it was listed in the fifth batch of national protected sites in 2001.
The surviving tower consists of nine lower stories and the three-story Kuixing Pavilion above; the timber structure is supported by the hill, with round and square windows alternating.

The plate keeps the surviving twelve stories and the adjoining rock face, omitting the river, the protective embankment and the suspension bridge; an archival photograph of 1909 already shows the upper pavilion, and no enlargement year is forced.
captions: Shibaozhai · Twelve-story fortress tower
Founded in the Ming · Enlarged in the Qing

protection.scope: Surviving twelve-story tower of Shibaozhai and the adjoining rock face

cq_huguang.name: Huguang Guild Hall, Chongqing
cq_huguang.era: Qing guild hall · Enlarged in the Daoguang reign
cq_huguang.yearNote: The guild hall complex took shape in the Qing and was enlarged in the Daoguang reign; about 1846 places the surviving Qing structure, and the plate shows the opera stage as repaired in 2003–2005, without asserting that every beam and column is original 1846 work.
cq_huguang.lede: Carved wooden balustrade panels run across the front of the raised stage, and beneath the flying eaves a three-bay stage opens. The opera stage of the Huguang Guild Hall in Chongqing hosted the public life of migrant gatherings, rituals and theatergoing.
facts: The Huguang Guild Hall of Chongqing, in the Dongshuimen area of Yuzhong District, is a Qing complex of migrant guild halls and is now in the sixth batch of national protected sites.

The guild hall was enlarged in the Daoguang reign, and its present state has also undergone modern conservation repairs; the plate takes the front of one opera stage and does not draw the whole group of courtyards.

The balustrade panels, beams and backstage decoration come from photographs; the colored plate keeps the dark brown carved wood, red backstage and bluish-gray tiles, rather than tinting the Qing building uniformly in a dynasty color.
captions: Huguang Guild Hall, Chongqing · Front of the opera stage
Qing guild hall · Enlarged in the Daoguang reign

protection.scope: Front of the surviving opera stage of the Huguang Guild Hall, Chongqing

cq_diaoyu.name: Diaoyu Fortress Site
cq_diaoyu.era: Fortifications expanded 1243 · Gate tower built later
cq_diaoyu.yearNote: 1243 is a key milestone in the building of the Southern Song defensive system at Diaoyu Fortress, and the timeline is placed by the site. The upper timber gate tower of Huguo Gate was built later, and not all the structure in the photographs is taken as original Song work.
cq_diaoyu.lede: A thick stone wall is pierced by a single arched opening, and stone steps up to the walls cling to the cliff. Huguo Gate condenses the strategic terrain and mountain-fortress defenses of Diaoyu Fortress into a narrow entrance.
facts: Diaoyu Fortress is the site of a Southern Song mountain fortress, expanded in 1243, that endured a long war of siege defense.
The plate takes the stone gateway of Huguo Gate, the later gate tower and the stone steps in front, keeping the passage along the cliff; it does not reconstruct the whole fortress.
The original fourth-batch national protected site list registered it under "Hechuan City, Sichuan Province"; it now lies within Chongqing, and the page uses Chongqing as its region.
captions: Diaoyu Fortress Site · Huguo Gate
Fortifications expanded 1243 · Gate tower built later

protection.scope: Stone gateway of Huguo Gate at Diaoyu Fortress, the later upper gate tower and the stone steps in front
protection.note: The place name originally announced was Hechuan City, Sichuan Province; it now belongs to Hechuan District, Chongqing. The upper gate tower was built later; the national protected site label corresponds to the main structure of Huguo Gate within the site.

cq_tongnan.name: Cliff Carvings of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan
cq_tongnan.era: Head carved in the Tang · Whole statue completed 1151
cq_tongnan.yearNote: The Buddha's head was carved in the Tang and the body continued in the Northern Song, with the whole statue completed in 1151; the surviving gold leaf includes the results of conservation and restoration in the 2010s, and the timeline is not placed by the temple's founding year.
cq_tongnan.lede: Gold leaf covers the broad face and flowing robe folds, and dark snail-shell curls set off the Great Buddha's calm. The head and body of the Tongnan Great Buddha were carved in turn, and the seated figure was completed only after spanning the Tang and Song.
facts: The head was carved first, the body was continued in the Northern Song, and the whole statue was completed in 1151; the plate takes this Great Buddha and does not represent all the cliff niches and figures of the temple.

The surviving seated figure rests its right hand flat before the abdomen and its left hand on the knee, with snail-shell curls on the head and a kasaya draped over the body; the feet hidden by the offering table are not conjecturally completed.

The gilding has been renewed over the centuries and has undergone modern conservation and restoration. The colored plate follows photographs of the gold leaf and dark snail-shell curls, and this artistic rendering is not a reconstruction of the original Song finish.
captions: Cliff Carvings of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan · Surviving gilded Great Buddha
Head carved in the Tang · Whole statue completed 1151

protection.scope: Surviving gilded seated Great Buddha of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan

sx_zishou.name: Zishou Temple, Lingshi
sx_zishou.sub: Front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings
sx_zishou.yearNote: 1500 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_zishou.lede: Blue-green glazed-tile edging and fine ridge ornaments sit atop gray tiles, and a dark doorway pierces the brick wall. The Hall of Heavenly Kings of Zishou Temple joins Ming hall architecture with the local glazed-tile craft of central Shanxi.
facts: The plate shows the front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings and the central stone steps; the temple's earlier history is not taken as the construction date of the surviving hall.
The blue-green and ocher-yellow glazed tiles on the ridge, the gray brick and the faded red door frame are colored according to their present state in photographs.
The depicted subject belongs to the official fifth-batch national protected site "Zishou Temple"; sources and photo credits are given in the source records.

sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.name: Ruicheng City God Temple
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.sub: Gable side of the main hall
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.era: Original Song structure · Repaired over the centuries
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.yearLabel: Original Song structure · Repaired over the centuries
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted gable side of the main hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.lede: The gable side of the main hall retains broad overhanging eaves and massive bracket sets, and plain red walls support the richly decorated gable pediment of the hip-and-gable roof. Song timberwork remains in view together with later glazed tiles and plastering.
facts: The surviving main hall is an original Song structure; the temple was founded in the Dazhong Xiangfu reign, and its founding, original structure and repairs over the centuries are understood separately.
The plate takes the gable side of the main hall; it does not conjecture the hidden doors and windows behind it, nor does it include the neighboring side halls.
The depicted subject belongs to the official fifth-batch national protected site "Ruicheng City God Temple"; sources and photo credits are given in the source records.

sx_qiao.name: Qiao Family Compound
sx_qiao.sub: Inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard
sx_qiao.yearNote: 1800 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_qiao.lede: Side rooms along both flanks of a long, narrow courtyard lead to the tower court at its end, while gray brick, wood carving and painted decoration unfold the details of a Shanxi merchant residence layer by layer. The spaces of Zaizhong Hall in the Qiao Family Compound grew gradually out of daily domestic life.
facts: This plate takes the inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard, keeping the depth of the courtyard; it does not represent a panorama of the "four halls and one garden."
Zaizhong Hall was enlarged in phases; the timeline uses an approximate Qing position, and a single ordering year cannot be taken as the exact construction date of the whole compound.
The depicted subject belongs to the official fifth-batch national protected site "Qiao Family Compound"; sources and photo credits are given in the source records.

sx_wang.name: Wang Family Compound
sx_wang.sub: Courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort (detail)
sx_wang.yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_wang.lede: Roofs, courtyard walls and small gates stack up on the slope, with light-brown brick walls threading between the gray tiles. A stretch of roofscape at Hongmen Fort in the Wang Family Compound shows the compact, winding spaces of central Shanxi residences.
facts: The plate shows part of the courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort; it is not a bird's-eye reconstruction of the entire Wang Family Compound.
The national protected site list records its period as Ming to Qing; the Qing residential section chosen here is ordered by approximate date, and traces of present-day repair are retained.
The depicted subject belongs to the official sixth-batch national protected site "Wang Family Compound"; sources and photo credits are given in the source records.

sx_daixian_wenmiao.sub: Front and platform of the Dacheng Hall
sx_daixian_wenmiao.era: Ming–Qing buildings · Repaired over the centuries
sx_daixian_wenmiao.yearLabel: Ming–Qing buildings · Repaired over the centuries
sx_daixian_wenmiao.yearNote: 1500 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front and platform of the Dacheng Hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_daixian_wenmiao.lede: A blue glazed-tile roof spreads over the seven-bay hall, and red doors and windows above a pale gray stone platform set off its solemn front. The Dacheng Hall of the Dai County Confucian Temple is the center of Daizhou's Confucian school architecture.
facts: The Dacheng Hall is seven bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the plate keeps the terrace and stone balustrade before the hall and removes the steles and trees in the foreground.

The Confucian Temple was rebuilt at the end of the Yuan and beginning of the Ming and enlarged in the Ming and Qing; the Ming–Qing date of the surviving main structure and the legendary founding year are recorded separately.
The depicted subject belongs to the official sixth-batch national protected site "Dai County Confucian Temple"; sources and photo credits are given in the source records.

sx_ciyun.yearNote: 1450 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the Mahavira Hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_ciyun.lede: Dark bracket sets support a broad gray-tiled roof, and latticed wooden doors and windows extend across the five-bay front. With its restrained colors, the Mahavira Hall of Ciyun Temple in Tianzhen preserves the character of a Ming hall in northern Shanxi.
facts: The depicted subject is the front of the Mahavira Hall and its steps, excluding the side halls on either side and the panorama of the temple.

The national protected site list records Ciyun Temple as Ming architecture; the timeline takes an approximate Ming position, and repairs over the centuries are not equated with the original construction date.

sx_wuyue.name: Wuyue Temple, Jiexiu
sx_wuyue.yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the opera stage on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_wuyue.lede: The upper stage opens outward with wooden columns, carved panels and bracket sets, while arched openings in the lower level connect the courtyard. With its blue-green glazed ridge ornaments, the opera stage of the Wuyue Temple in Jiexiu lets worship and performance share one space.
facts: The plate takes the front of the surviving opera stage: a five-bay upper level, a projecting central roof and gables on the two wings, with a central passage and four side arches in the lower level.
The depicted Qing building is kept distinct from the temple's founding date; scaffolding, clutter and text seen in the photographs are not included in the plate.

sx_pingyao_chenghuang.yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the front hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_pingyao_chenghuang.lede: The central roof of the front hall projects forward, and a stone-arched passage leads into the courtyard behind. Gray brick, dark timber and blue-green glazed tiles set side by side present the fine layering of the Qing architecture of the Pingyao City God Temple.
facts: The plate takes the front of the central front hall, keeping the passage, colonnade and geometric balustrades; it excludes the bell and drum towers on either side and the other temple buildings.

The surviving Qing buildings are kept distinct from the temple's earlier history; the approximate timeline value is only for placement and does not represent an exact construction date for the single hall.
The depicted subject belongs to the official sixth-batch national protected site "Pingyao City God Temple"; sources and photo credits are given in the source records.

sx_rishengchang.name: Former Site of Rishengchang
sx_rishengchang.era: Former Qing draft bank · Surviving street frontage
sx_rishengchang.yearLabel: Former Qing draft bank · Surviving street frontage
sx_rishengchang.yearNote: 1823 is the commonly cited year the draft bank opened; the construction year of the surviving frontage itself is undetermined, and the timeline places it approximately by that period.
sx_rishengchang.lede: A low, gently sloping gray-tiled roof shelters the whole row of street frontage, its dark wooden boards meeting small painted windows above. The Former Site of Rishengchang leads from a central Shanxi shop into the financial history of the Qing draft banks.
facts: This plate shows only the street frontage, not the whole three-courtyard compound; plaques, protection signs and street furnishings are omitted.
1823 is the commonly cited year the draft bank opened; the construction year of the surviving frontage itself is undetermined, and the timeline places it approximately by that period.

id_prambanan_shiva.sub: Single main Shiva temple and steps
id_prambanan_shiva.yearNote: On the same UNESCO page, the brief description gives the 10th century and the detailed description the 9th century; 900 is only for approximate ordering. The surviving main temple has undergone modern reconstruction and restoration.
id_prambanan_shiva.lede: The soaring stone structure tapers inward tier by tier, with niches and tower ornaments arranged around the entrance. The main Shiva temple of Prambanan stands on the Javanese plain with a slender, densely articulated outline.
facts: The plate shows only the main Shiva temple, keeping its crown, body, base and entrance stairs; the other main temples and the small shrines are not included.
Heritage sources give both 9th- and 10th-century dates; the surviving building includes modern reconstruction and restoration, and the approximate value is not taken as an exact completion year.

th_sukhothai_mahathat.yearNote: Reliable sources confirm the Sukhothai period and the lotus-bud form of the main chedi, but the precise year of its remodeling is unknown; 1350 is used only for timeline ordering, and the temple's founding year is not substituted for the age of the surviving main chedi.
th_sukhothai_mahathat.lede: A slender spire rises from the lotus-bud crown, above a brick and stone base that spreads out tier by tier. The main chedi of Wat Mahathat preserves the distinctive lotus-bud outline of Sukhothai architecture.
facts: The plate is limited to the central lotus-bud chedi and the base directly supporting it, excluding the freestanding hall columns and neighboring chedis, and does not reconstruct the lost hall roof.
The date of the surviving main chedi is placed approximately in the Sukhothai period; the precise construction year has not been confirmed, and later restoration is recorded separately.

th_chaiwatthanaram.sub: Central prang, four corner prangs and shared base
th_chaiwatthanaram.yearNote: 1630 is the temple's founding year recorded in historical sources; the plate shows the surviving group of the central prang and four corner prangs, and given the discussion of earlier construction and the modern restoration, not all the brickwork is taken as built in the same year.
th_chaiwatthanaram.lede: The tall, rounded central prang rises from a red-brick base, with smaller corner prangs around it. The central group of Wat Chaiwatthanaram preserves the layering of the Ayutthaya-period temple-mountain layout.
facts: The plate takes the central prang, the four small corner prangs beside it and their shared base; the eight outer structures and the ruined walls in the foreground are excluded.
SAC records the founding in 1630 and describes conservation and restoration in 1987–1992; scholarly discussion of an earlier layout is not rewritten as a proven completion date.

mm_ananda.name: Ananda Temple, Bagan
mm_ananda.sub: Whole temple body, central spire and projecting entrances
mm_ananda.yearNote: The Indian government's conservation project description gives the early 12th century; 1110 is only an approximate placement within that period, and none of the unverified exact years 1090, 1091 or 1105 is chosen. The surviving form includes later restoration.
mm_ananda.lede: Tiers of terraces stack up on the broad temple body, the golden central spire points to the sky, and the entrances project beyond the square main mass. The Ananda Temple shows the outline of a large Bagan Buddhist temple with interior chambers.
facts: The plate includes the whole temple body, the central spire and the projecting entrances, and does not substitute a detail of the central spire for the whole temple; the outer enclosure wall and freestanding gateways are excluded.

The Indian government's description records construction in the early 12th century and notes that after the 2016 earthquake the Archaeological Survey of India took part in its conservation and restoration.

la_xieng_thong_sim.name: Sim of Wat Xieng Thong
la_xieng_thong_sim.sub: The sim (main hall) and its supporting platform
la_xieng_thong_sim.yearNote: Official sources record its founding in about 1560; the main hall was repaired in 1928, in 1952–1960 and at other times, so not all the surviving decoration can be regarded as original 16th-century work.
la_xieng_thong_sim.lede: Low-sweeping roofs spread to either side, and the layered gables and fine gold ornament reflect the lightness of the timber structure. The sim of Wat Xieng Thong rests quietly on its platform beneath the traditional roof curves of Luang Prabang.
facts: The depicted subject is the sim and its supporting platform, excluding the later Royal Funerary Carriage House; the tiles, timberwork and gold ornament are colored from photographs of their present state.
Official tourism sources record the founding of the temple in about 1560 and repeated repairs to the main hall; the founding phase and later decoration are described separately.

vn_po_klong_garai.name: Main Tower of Po Klong Garai
vn_po_klong_garai.sub: Surviving main shrine tower with entrance and base
vn_po_klong_garai.yearNote: Official Khánh Hòa Province sources give the late 13th–early 14th century; 1300 is only for approximate ordering, and the construction date of the tower is not inferred from the life dates of the king worshipped there.
vn_po_klong_garai.place: Khánh Hòa Province · Phan Rang–Tháp Chàm
vn_po_klong_garai.lede: The red-brick tower body is divided by pilasters and false doors, and the layered brick ornament of the upper tiers tapers steadily. The main tower of Po Klong Garai preserves the outline of a Cham temple tower and also carries on local ritual traditions.
facts: The plate shows only the main shrine tower of the three towers, excluding the gate tower and the long-ridged fire tower; the main tower's entrance has an inset stone door frame and a relief of the dancing Shiva.

Official Khánh Hòa Province sources record that the tower group was built in the late 13th–early 14th century. The location is registered under the current Khánh Hòa Province, and the former name, Ninh Thuận Province, is kept for search.

vn_hue_ngo_mon.name: Meridian Gate (Ngọ Môn) of the Huế Imperial City
vn_hue_ngo_mon.sub: Complete gate platform and Five Phoenix Pavilion
vn_hue_ngo_mon.yearNote: 1833 is the construction date of the Meridian Gate; the surviving timber pavilion, roofs and platform have undergone later repairs, and there are also records of modern repairs.
vn_hue_ngo_mon.lede: The broad gate platform folds forward into wings at both sides, and above it the Five Phoenix Pavilion spreads out under roofs of differing heights. The Meridian Gate combines a masonry palace gate with a timber pavilion to form the front outline of the Huế Imperial City.
facts: The platform is U-shaped, with five passages in all: three on the front and two in the side wings; the five passages must not be drawn as five openings on the front.

Official tourism sources record its construction in 1833, with yellow tiles on the central roof and blue-green tiles on either side; the plate includes the complete platform and the Five Phoenix Pavilion.

ph_manila_san_agustin.name: San Agustin Church, Manila
ph_manila_san_agustin.sub: Surviving church facade and bell tower
ph_manila_san_agustin.yearNote: 1607 is the completion date of the surviving stone church, as distinct from the earlier wooden churches. The bell tower and later repairs have their own histories, and the present building as a whole is not dated as original fabric of a single year.
ph_manila_san_agustin.lede: Tiered orders of columns divide the doors and windows of the stone facade, a round window and a cross mark the triangular pediment, and the surviving bell tower adjoins it on the right. San Agustin Church preserves another architectural tradition of old Manila.
facts: The plate shows the surviving main facade and the single bell tower on the right; the low remnant of the lost left tower is kept and not reconstructed as symmetrical twin towers.

The National Museum of the Philippines records that the surviving stone church was completed in 1607; the original wooden church and later repairs are described separately, and the monastery as a whole is not drawn.

kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.name: Sudeoksa Daeungjeon
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.sub: Single Daeungjeon hall and stone platform
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.era: Hall built 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.yearNote: Hall built in 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.lede: A gently sloping overhanging gable roof of tiles rests on the three-bay timber hall, with beam ends projecting tier by tier from the gable side. With its gray-brown timber and simple lattice doors, Sudeoksa Daeungjeon preserves the airy form of a Buddhist hall of the late Goryeo.
facts: The surviving Daeungjeon was built in 1308; the temple's founding and the hall's construction date are recorded separately.
Three bays wide and four bays deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; the columns carry the eaves, and the beam frame on the gable side is an important part of identifying the structure.
The plate shows only the Daeungjeon and its stone platform, excluding the stone lantern in front and the temple's other buildings.

kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.name: Buseoksa Muryangsujeon
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.era: Surviving Muryangsujeon rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.yearNote: The surviving Muryangsujeon was rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.lede: Long eaves extend along the five-bay hall, its timber columns slightly curved, and pale lattice doors line up beneath the deep eaves. Set high within Buseoksa, the Muryangsujeon is an important surviving timber Buddhist hall of the Goryeo period.
facts: The temple was founded in 676, and the surviving Muryangsujeon shown here is assigned to the Goryeo by its 1376 rebuilding date.
Five bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the columns swell at mid-height, and the lattice doors and stone platform are preserved in their present state.
The hall enshrines Amitabha Buddha; the plate takes the exterior of the hall, and the stone lantern in front is not included in this subject.

kr_bulguksa_dabotap.name: Dabotap of Bulguksa
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.sub: Complete Dabotap stone pagoda with stairways on four sides
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.era: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.yearNote: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.lede: Square stone pillars support a pagoda body whose tiers keep changing form, while balustrades and an octagonal canopy shift its scale in the upper part. Carved from granite into a complex outline close to timber construction, Dabotap is entirely different from the common multi-roofed stone pagodas.
facts: Korean authorities officially date Dabotap to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, the ordering uses an approximate value, and no precise completion year is claimed for the pagoda.

Square stone pillars and stairways on four sides below combine with octagonal elements above, and official sources explain that its number of stories is hard to count in the way used for an ordinary pavilion-style pagoda.
Following its present state, the single surviving stone lion is kept, the lost lions are not added back, and the neighboring Seokgatap is not drawn.

kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.name: Changdeokgung Injeongjeon
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.era: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.yearNote: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.lede: Double flying eaves support a broad gray-tiled roof, and red columns and blue-green dancheong painting surround the five-bay hall. With its terrace, central stairway and tall, open interior, Injeongjeon forms the main hall of Changdeokgung where state ceremonies were held.
facts: The National Heritage Portal gives the date of the surviving building as the 4th year of King Sunjo of Joseon (1804), and the palace's founding year is not substituted for it.
Five bays wide and four bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the double eaves outside do not mean there are two separate floors inside.
The plate shows only Injeongjeon and its terrace; the side corridors, the rank stones in the courtyard and other palace buildings are not included.

kp_kaesong_namdaemun.name: Namdaemun of Kaesong
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.sub: Stone gate platform and postwar rebuilt gate tower
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.era: Inner-city gate first built 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.yearNote: The inner-city gate was first built in 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.lede: A single stone arch pierces the gate platform, and the open three-bay gate tower is covered by a broad tiled roof. Namdaemun of Kaesong layers the gate site of the Goryeo capital, the old stone platform and the timber gate tower restored after the war in a single place.
facts: The gate was built together with the inner city wall in 1391–1393; the surviving gate tower is a postwar reconstruction, and the timeline uses 1955.

The ICOMOS evaluation records that the gate tower was destroyed in 1950 and restored from 1954; the caption in the nomination file and the repair notes give 1955, and the dating note keeps both records.
The gate platform has a single arch, and the gate tower is three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a great bell hanging inside; this entry does not include the small shrine nearby.

kp_pothong_gate.name: Pyongyang Pothong Gate
kp_pothong_gate.sub: Gate platform and double-eaved gate tower of Pothong Gate
kp_pothong_gate.era: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
kp_pothong_gate.yearNote: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
kp_pothong_gate.lede: A massive stone platform is pierced by a single arched gateway, and the double-eaved gate tower rises from its top. Pothong Gate preserves the form of the western city gate of old Pyongyang, its masonry platform and painted timber tower forming two clearly distinct upper and lower parts.
facts: Kim Il Sung University sources record that the surviving gate underwent major repairs in 1473, followed by further extensions; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not the exact date of the surviving timberwork.
The gate tower is three bays wide and three bays deep, with two tiers of eaves; the platform is built of granite, with a single semicircular arched gateway at the center.
The depicted subject is the surviving platform and gate tower; the extending city walls are not reconstructed, and the modern streetscape is not included.

kp_sungyang_hall.name: Lecture Hall of Sungyang Academy
kp_sungyang_hall.sub: Five-bay lecture hall of the academy
kp_sungyang_hall.era: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
kp_sungyang_hall.yearNote: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
kp_sungyang_hall.lede: The five-bay lecture hall stands across the academy terrace, its open central wooden floor and end rooms forming a simple hall. Sungyang Academy places teaching and rites at the front and back, and the lecture hall is its space for study.
facts: The academy was established in 1573 and received a royal name in 1575, and the surviving lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the specific construction year of the timberwork is unclear, and about 1600 serves only for timeline placement.

The World Heritage nomination file records the lecture hall as five bays wide and three bays deep; the plan has an open three-bay central hall with rooms on either side, under a single-eaved overhanging gable roof.
The plate shows only the lecture hall, referring to nomination photographs, old photographs and plans; neither the three-door gate in front nor the shrine above is mistaken for the lecture hall.

kp_sonjuk_bridge.name: Sonjuk Bridge, Kaesong
kp_sonjuk_bridge.sub: Old stone beam bridge and 1780 stone balustrades
kp_sonjuk_bridge.era: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
kp_sonjuk_bridge.yearNote: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
kp_sonjuk_bridge.lede: A short granite beam bridge spans a shallow stream, its deck enclosed by round-topped stone posts and rails. Sonjuk Bridge became a memorial site because Jeong Mong-ju was killed there, and the later balustrades also record its withdrawal from everyday traffic.
facts: The nomination file says the stone bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, and its exact construction year has not been confirmed; about 1100 is an ordering position, and 1392 is the year of the killing.
The bridge is 8.35 m long and 3.36 m wide, with stone piers carrying stone beams topped by stone slabs; it is not an arch bridge. The surviving stone balustrades on both sides were added in 1780.
Only the old Sonjuk Bridge and its later balustrades are drawn; the separate bridge built alongside for traffic, the stele pavilion and the inscribed steles are not part of the subject.

jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.name: Karamon of Ueno Tōshō-gū
jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1651 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.lede: An undulating karahafu gable spreads above the doors, and gilded carving is concentrated on the small, intricate entrance. The plate takes the Karamon of Ueno Tōshō-gū, built in 1651.
facts: Cultural Heritage Online dates the Karamon to 1651 and records it as a mukaikaramon gate one bay wide and one bay deep, with copper-tile roofing.
The plate shows only the Karamon; the shrine buildings behind it, the openwork fences on either side and the lanterns along the approach are outside its scope.
The gold leaf and painted color are taken from photographs of the present state, and the surface colors after restoration cannot be directly equated with the original state of 1651.

jp_nezu_romon.name: Rōmon of Nezu Shrine
jp_nezu_romon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1706 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_nezu_romon.lede: Vermilion columns support the upper story and a broad tiled roof, and the central passage is flanked by two niches for guardian figures. The Rōmon of Nezu Shrine covers its two-story gate with a single large roof, in compact proportions.
facts: The Rōmon belongs to the building of Nezu Shrine completed in 1706; Cultural Heritage Online records it as a three-bay, single-passage two-story gate with an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof and pantile roofing.
The lower story has only a single central passage, with niches for zuishin guardian figures on either side; a balustrade runs around the outer edge of the upper story.
The plate takes the front of the Rōmon and does not merge in the shrine's Karamon, main sanctuary or Senbon Torii.

jp_asakusa_jinja.name: Asakusa Shrine
jp_asakusa_jinja.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1649 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_asakusa_jinja.lede: On the east side of Sensō-ji, this shrine preserves early Edo shrine buildings. The low, broad worship hall spreads out in vermilion columns and gold ornament, on a scale quite different from the nearby main hall of Sensō-ji.
facts: The surviving shrine buildings were built and donated by Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1649 and have come through disasters and war.

The main sanctuary (honden), offering hall (heiden) and worship hall (haiden) form the core of the shrine, with the main sanctuary linked to the offering hall and worship hall by a connecting passage.
This plate shows only the front of the worship hall. Asakusa Shrine and Sensō-ji are separate entries, and their dates and personal records are kept separately.

jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.name: Sangedatsumon of Zōjō-ji
jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1622 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.lede: Two tiers of deep eaves and a horizontal balustrade weigh down on the broad gate front, and three passages run through the lower story. The Sangedatsumon of Zōjō-ji preserves the grand scale of an early Edo temple entrance.
facts: The temple officially records the construction date of the surviving Sangedatsumon as 1622.
The gate is a five-bay, three-passage nijūmon (two-story gate); the plate keeps the upper and lower roofs and the three central passages.

The plate is drawn from photographs taken before the conservation repairs and omits the temporary curtains; the temple has announced conservation repairs from 2025, and the illustration does not represent what is currently visible on site.

jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.name: Kiyomizu Kannon-dō of Kan'ei-ji
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.sub: Kannon Hall and the stage in front
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1631 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding. It was moved to its present site in 1694, and conservation repairs were completed in 1996.
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.lede: The vermilion Kannon Hall overlooks the slopes of Ueno, its wooden stage projecting toward Shinobazu Pond. It borrows the concept of Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto, yet has survived through Tokyo's own history of construction and relocation.
facts: The Kannon Hall was built by Tenkai in 1631 and moved to its present site in 1694 for the construction of Kan'ei-ji's Konponchūdō.
The temple officially records conservation repairs to the cultural property from 1990 to 1996, restoring its appearance at the time of the Genroku-era relocation.
The plate shows the Kannon Hall and the stage in front, omitting the Moon Pine (Tsuki no Matsu) and the hillside scenery; the raised stage of Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto is not applied to this hall.

jp_gokokuji_hondo.name: Main Hall of Gokoku-ji
jp_gokokuji_hondo.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1697 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_gokokuji_hondo.lede: The copper-plate roof has oxidized to blue-green, and the broad curved roof covers a solid timber structure. The main hall of Gokoku-ji carries on the scale and craftsmanship of an Edo prayer temple of the Genroku period.
facts: Gokoku-ji was founded in 1681; the surviving Kannon Hall shown was completed in 1697, and the founding year of the temple cannot be substituted for the building's date.
Cultural Heritage Online records the main hall as seven bays wide and seven bays deep, with an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof, a three-bay kōhai (front canopy) and batten-seam copper-plate roofing.
The plate includes only the main hall, its veranda and steps, and does not merge in the later tahōtō pagoda or the relocated Gekkō-den.

jp_ikegami_pagoda.name: Five-Story Pagoda of Ikegami Honmon-ji
jp_ikegami_pagoda.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1608 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_ikegami_pagoda.lede: The five-story wooden pagoda rises from the Ikegami cemetery grounds, its dark tiled eaves tapering tier by tier. The old vermilion of the body and the bronze sōrin finial give its early Edo outline a clear, quiet presence.
facts: The official cultural property list of Ikegami Honmon-ji records the five-story pagoda as dating to the 13th year of Keichō, that is, 1608.
The pagoda has five tiers of eaves topped by a sōrin finial; the plate keeps the complete body, finial and base.
This plate does not include gravestones, the surrounding temple buildings or modern facilities; the present colors of the materials are rendered from daytime photographs.
captions: Five-Story Pagoda of Ikegami Honmon-ji · Surviving five-story wooden pagoda

jp_shofukuji_jizodo.name: Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.sub: Single-story Zen Buddhist hall with mokoshi
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1407 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.lede: The great eaves of the main roof are raised high, with a low mokoshi skirt roof encircling the building below. With its compact square mass, the Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji preserves the form of a Muromachi-period Zen Buddhist hall in the Kantō region.
facts: Based on an ink inscription dated the 14th year of Ōei found during repairs, Cultural Heritage Online records the Jizō Hall's construction date as 1407.

The building is a Buddhist hall three bays square, single-story with a mokoshi, under an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof; the upper roof is covered with wood shingles and the mokoshi with copper plate. The two tiers of eaves do not mean two stories.
It stands in Higashimurayama, Tokyo; the plate shows only the Jizō Hall, not the other buildings of Shōfuku-ji.
